title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
### Check yourself
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. Total momentum before is 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s, so the joint speed is 6 / 3 = 2 m/s. Show the momentum equation even when the speed looks obvious.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Integration reverses differentiation. Questions want a general antiderivative, a specific curve through a point, a definite integral, or an area. Most lost marks come from the constant of integration, the limits, and the sign of a region below the axis.

Start from a question

A curve passes through (1, 1) and has dy/dx = 3√x − 2/x² for x > 0.

  1. Find y in terms of x.
  2. Evaluate the integral of (3√x − 2/x²) from x = 1 to x = 4.
  3. Find the area between the curve y = x² − 4 and the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3.

Part 1. Integrate term by term: 3x^(1/2) gives 2x^(3/2), and −2x⁻² gives 2x⁻¹. So y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x + c. Substituting (1, 1) gives 2 + 2 + c = 1, so c = −3 and y = 2x^(3/2) + 2/x − 3.

Part 2. The antiderivative at 4 is 16 + ½ = 33/2. At 1 it is 4 = 8/2. The definite integral is 33/2 − 8/2 = 25/2. No +c is needed.

Part 3. The curve y = x² − 4 crosses the x-axis at x = 2. Between 0 and 2 it lies below the axis, so that part of the integral is negative. The area is |∫ from 0 to 2| + ∫ from 2 to 3. The first integral is [x³/3 − 4x] from 0 to 2 = −16/3, so its area is 16/3. The second is [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = −3 − (−16/3) = 7/3. The total is 23/3. Taking the integral from 0 to 3 directly gives −3, which is the wrong answer for an area.

Indefinite integrals

∫axⁿ dx = a xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c, for n ≠ −1. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and write +c. Multiply out brackets and rewrite roots as powers first. Example: ∫(x − 2)(x + 4) dx = ∫(x² + 2x − 8) dx = x³/3 + x² − 8x + c.

Area between two curves

Find where the curves meet, then integrate the upper curve minus the lower curve between those x-values. Example: y = 2x and y = x² meet at x = 0 and x = 2. Between them 2x ≥ x², so the area is ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x − x²) dx = [x² − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 4/3.

Trapezium rule

With strips of width h and ordinates y₀, y₁, …, yₙ, the estimate is (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ]. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x² + 1) dx with h = 1. The ordinates are 1, 2 and 5, so the estimate is ½(1 + 4 + 5) = 5. The exact value is 14/3. The curve bends upwards, so the estimate is too large.

Traps that cost marks

  • Integrating a product term by term without expanding the brackets first.
  • Writing +c in a definite integral, or forgetting it in an indefinite one.
  • Subtracting the limits in the wrong order.
  • Quoting a negative answer for an area that lies below the x-axis.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks
For combined events, each branch probability with the changed denominator earns a mark: write 3/5 then 2/4 for no-replacement draws. For expectation, probability times trials stated earns the mark even with arithmetic slips. For conditional probability, restricting the denominator to the given condition earns the method mark: write 12/20 before simplifying. For P(A or B), the overlap subtracted earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: unchanged denominator after a no-replacement draw. Correction: both numerator and denominator drop. Error: dividing by 50 for a given-glasses probability. Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.
### Worked example
In a group of 30 students, 18 play football, 12 play hockey and 5 play both. The number who play at least one sport is n(F ∪ H) = 18 + 12 − 5 = 25. The number who play neither is 30 − 25 = 5. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting those 5 students twice.
### Check yourself
Given n(A) = 14, n(B) = 9 and n(A ∩ B) = 4, find n(A ∪ B). It is 14 + 9 − 4 = 19. Then find how many elements are outside both sets if the universal set has 25 elements.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Circular Motion Recap

Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Simple Harmonic Motion

Acceleration is proportional to displacement and opposite: a = −ω²x.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt (start at centre) or x = x₀ cos ωt (start at extreme), with ω = 2πf.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m, f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

E = ½mω²x₀² total (constant), exchanged between KE (max at centre) and PE (max at extremes).

Damping and Resonance

Damping removes energy: light damping → slow decay; critical → fastest return without oscillation. Resonance: driving at the natural frequency gives maximum amplitude (microwave ovens, swing pushing, bridge disasters).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition; time period questions often need only T = 2π/ω.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.

title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that connect the way organisms coordinate and respond to stimuli with the ways we now use gene technology. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples, drawings and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. The point of the topic: coordination, response, homeostasis and gene technology together

This topic is really about how living systems detect change and deal with it. Nervous and hormonal coordination are the two main ways animals coordinate a response, and they have different speeds, ranges and durations, which is why both exist. Sensory reception is the entry point for information from the environment. Muscle and gland effectors are where the response happens. The endocrine system adds a hormonal layer that can act on a longer timescale. Homeostatic control systems keep the internal environment within limits. Gene technology is the modern set of tools that lets us read, copy and manipulate DNA and that has reshaped medicine, agriculture and research. The parts are connected because the same logic of detection, processing and response applies whether the signal is electrical, chemical or genetic.

A good answer sees the topic as one system of control at several levels: from receptor to coordinator to effector, and from the molecular handling of DNA to the applications that result from it. If you can see those links, you can answer the questions that cross the parts, which are often where the higher marks are. If you treat the parts as unrelated lists, you lose the reasoning that the specification is after.

2. Nervous coordination as detection, transmission and response

Nervous coordination begins with a receptor detecting a stimulus and ending with an effector producing a response, and the signal is usually an electrical impulse carried by neurones. The system is fast, short-range in duration and usually localised in its effect, which is why it suits rapid responses to specific stimuli. The key point is that the nervous system transmits information as action potentials along neurones, and that the response is often fast and specific, such as a reflex or a voluntary movement.

A good answer says that nervous coordination involves a receptor, a coordinator such as the central nervous system, and an effector such as a muscle or gland, and that the signal is an electrical impulse along neurones. It also says that the nervous system is fast and usually produces a specific response. It does not say that the nervous system is slow or diffuse, because that is the opposite of its main feature for many responses. The contrast with hormonal coordination is useful because it explains why we have both systems. If you can say that, you have the coordination idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Hormonal coordination as a slower, often longer-lasting chemical signal

Hormonal coordination uses chemical signals, hormones, carried in the blood to target organs. Hormones are produced by endocrine glands and act on target cells that have the right receptors. Hormonal responses are often slower to start than nervous responses and can be longer-lasting and more widespread, which is why hormones suit processes such as growth, development, metabolism and reproduction. The key point is that hormones are chemical messengers in the bloodstream and that they act only on cells with the right receptors.

A good answer says that hormones are chemical messengers released by endocrine glands into the blood, that they act on target organs with the right receptors, and that hormonal responses are often slower and longer-lasting than nervous ones. It does not say that hormones act on every cell, because they do not; they act only on cells with the right receptors. It also does not say that hormonal responses are always slow in every sense, because some are fast enough to matter physiologically, but the general contrast with nervous coordination is the important exam point. If you can say that, you have the hormonal idea in a form that scores marks.

4. Sensory reception and the structure behind the senses: rods, cones and Pacinian corpuscles

Sensory reception happens in receptors that detect specific stimuli and convert them into nerve signals. In the eye, rods and cones are the photoreceptors on the retina. Rods are sensitive to light intensity and work well in dim light; cones detect colour and work best in brighter light. In the skin and other tissues, receptors such as Pacinian corpuscles detect pressure and vibration. The important point is that receptors are specialised to detect particular stimuli and to transduce them into action potentials.

The Pacinian corpuscle is a good example because it illustrates how a receptor works structurally. It has a connective tissue capsule around a nerve ending, so that pressure deforms the capsule and stimulates the nerve ending. The receptor is not the nerve ending alone; the capsule shapes the response so that the receptor detects vibration and pressure rather than constant touch. A good answer describes the Pacinian corpuscle as a pressure receptor with a connective tissue capsule and a nerve ending, and says that pressure deforms the capsule and stimulates the ending. It does not say that the corpuscle detects all touch equally, because it is tuned to vibration and deep pressure. If you can say that, you have the receptor idea in a form that scores marks.

In the eye, rods and cones contain the visual pigments that respond to light. In rods, the pigment is rhodopsin; light bleaches rhodopsin and triggers a generator potential. Cones have pigments sensitive to different wavelengths. A good answer says that rods are more sensitive and work in dim light, that cones detect colour and work best in brighter light, and that the pigments respond to light by bleaching. It does not say that rods detect colour or that cones work well in dim light. Those are the opposite of the real properties. If you can keep them straight, you can avoid the most common mistake.

5. The organisation of the retina and the pathway from light to signal

The retina is built so that light reaches the photoreceptors and the signals are processed before they leave the eye. The photoreceptors are at the back of the retina, and the signals pass through other retinal cells before reaching the neurones that leave the eye as the optic nerve. The fovea is the region of highest cone density and sharpest vision, and it is adapted for detailed daylight vision. A good answer says that the retina contains rods and cones, that the fovea is the area of sharpest vision with many cones, and that the signals from the photoreceptors are processed within the retina before being carried to the brain by the optic nerve.

The structure of the rod cell is also worth knowing because it shows how a receptor works. A rod cell has an outer segment packed with discs containing rhodopsin, a cell body, and a synapse that connects to the neurone. Light causes rhodopsin to change and hyperpolarise the cell, which reduces neurotransmitter release and so signals the change. The point is that the receptor does not work like a simple wire; it transduces the light signal into a change in the cell. If you can say that, you have the transduction idea rather than just a list of parts.

6. Reflexes, the reflex arc and why they are useful

A reflex is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not need conscious thought. A simple reflex arc includes a receptor, a sensory neurone, an interneurone in the spinal cord or brain, a motor neurone and an effector. Reflexes protect the body from harm and help with rapid adjustments, and their value is partly that they are fast and do not need conscious processing. A good answer describes a reflex arc, names the parts, and says that a reflex is fast and automatic and useful for protection and rapid adjustment. It does not say that a reflex involves conscious decision, because it does not; the arc bypasses conscious processing. If you can say that, you have the reflex idea in a form that scores marks.

An example such as the withdrawal reflex, moving a hand away from a painful stimulus, shows the point. The sensory neurone brings the information to the spinal cord, the interneurone connects to the motor neurone, and the muscle contracts to withdraw the limb, often before the brain is even fully aware of the stimulus. A good answer can use a concrete example and still explain the general principle. That is the kind of answer the examiners like, because it shows understanding rather than just recall.

7. The synapse and the neuromuscular junction, and why the presynaptic Ca2+ entry matters

A synapse is the junction between a neurone and another cell, and the neuromuscular junction is the special case where a motor neurone synapses with a muscle fibre. At a chemical synapse, an action potential arrives at the presynaptic membrane, calcium ions enter the presynaptic neurone, vesicles fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, the neurotransmitter binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, and an action potential or other response is generated in the postsynaptic cell. The calcium entry is what triggers neurotransmitter release, so it is the key step that links the electrical signal to the chemical signal.

The neuromuscular junction is essentially a chemical synapse between a motor neurone and a muscle, and it works on the same principle: the motor neurone releases a neurotransmitter that binds to the muscle fibre, and this starts contraction. The basic idea is the same as at a neurone-to-neurone synapse, but the postsynaptic cell is a muscle fibre rather than another neurone. A good answer says that an action potential arriving at the presynaptic membrane causes calcium ions to enter, that the calcium triggers neurotransmitter release, that the neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds to receptors, and that the calcium entry is essential for release. It also says that the neuromuscular junction is a synapse between a motor neurone and a muscle. If you can say that, you have the synapse and neuromuscular junction idea in a form that scores marks.

A common mistake is to say that the neurotransmitter is released simply because the action potential arrives, without mentioning calcium. It is not; the action potential opens calcium channels and the calcium triggers the vesicle fusion. If you remember the calcium step, you avoid one of the most common mark-losers on synapses. It is also a useful example of how the system can be controlled pharmacologically and physiologically, because anything that affects calcium entry or receptor binding can change synaptic transmission.

8. Muscle contraction at the molecular level: filaments, cross-bridges and ATP

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament mechanism, in which actin and myosin filaments slide past one another so the sarcomere shortens. The myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and release in a cycle that pulls the thin filament past the thick one. The cycle needs ATP and calcium. ATP is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the head, and to provide the energy for the next stroke after the head resets. Calcium exposes the binding sites on actin so the myosin heads can bind in the first place. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

The filament arrangement matters. The sarcomere has a defined banding pattern, with the A band, I band and H zone, and these change during contraction because of the sliding. A good answer describes the sliding filament model, says that the filaments do not shorten but slide, and uses the banding pattern to show what happens. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it explains that the overlap increases and the zones change because of the sliding. That is the difference between a correct answer and a common mistake that loses marks.

The energy story is ATP for the cycle and calcium for the trigger. ATP is used both for the power stroke and for detachment and resetting, and calcium is needed for the binding. A good answer says that ATP and calcium are both required, and that relaxation depends on calcium removal and the covering of the binding sites. It does not say that ATP alone drives contraction without calcium, because it does not. That distinction is one of the things the examiners check, because it shows that the student understands the control of the cycle, not just the energy.

9. The endocrine system, the pancreas and the insulin-glucagon system

The endocrine system uses hormones to regulate many processes, and the insulin-glucagon system is one of the clearest examples of homeostatic hormonal control. The pancreas has endocrine tissue that secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood. Insulin lowers blood glucose by increasing the uptake of glucose by cells, by promoting glycogenesis and by other effects that remove glucose from the blood. Glucagon raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and by other effects that add glucose to the blood. The two hormones work in opposite directions to keep blood glucose within limits.

A good answer says that insulin and glucagon are secreted by the pancreas, that insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it, and that they work in opposition to maintain homeostasis. It does not say that insulin and glucagon both raise glucose, or that either alone can manage the system, because the system depends on the balance between the two. It also does not say that insulin and glucagon are produced by the same cells; they come from different cells of the islets. If you can keep the direction and the source correct, you have the endocrine control idea in a form that scores marks.

The hormone action is also worth understanding. Insulin binds to receptors and changes the activity of cells so that glucose is taken up and stored. Glucagon acts mainly on the liver and promotes the release of glucose. A good answer says that the hormones act on target cells in different ways to move glucose in opposite directions. It does not just say “insulin lowers glucose” without saying how; a specification answer usually benefits from a little mechanism, not just a label. If you can give the direction and a little of the mechanism, you have a better answer than a one-line label.

10. Homeostasis and negative feedback, and why the blood glucose system matters as an example

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the main control principle: a change from the set point is detected and effectors act to reduce the change and return the variable toward the set point. The insulin-glucagon system is a good example of negative feedback in a hormone system, because a rise in blood glucose stimulates insulin release, which lowers glucose back toward normal, and a fall in blood glucose stimulates glucagon release, which raises glucose back toward normal. A good answer describes homeostasis as maintenance of stability within limits, explains negative feedback as a response that opposes the change, and uses the insulin-glucagon system as an example. It does not say that the system produces constancy all the time; it says that the variable is kept within limits by opposing the deviation. That is the right way to describe negative feedback.

The point of using insulin and glucagon as an example is that the two hormones oppose each other and the set point is kept by their balance. If the question asks for a hormonal example of homeostasis, insulin and glucagon are the right example. If the question asks for the general principle, say that negative feedback reduces the deviation from the set point. If the question asks how insulin works, say that it promotes glucose uptake and storage. If you can do those, you can answer the question at the right level and avoid the trap of treating homeostasis as no change at all.

11. The basics of the endocrine control of reproduction and the hormones involved

Hormonal control of reproduction involves several hormones, including FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in females and testosterone in males, and also pituitary hormones such as ADH for water balance. The key idea is that reproduction is coordinated by hormones that act on the reproductive system and on the secondary sexual characteristics, and that the pattern of hormone levels changes across the cycle. A good answer says that reproductive hormones coordinate the development and function of the reproductive system and the secondary sexual characteristics, that FSH and LH are pituitary hormones involved in gamete production and hormone release, that oestrogen and progesterone are involved in the female cycle and in maintaining pregnancy, and that testosterone is involved in male development and spermatogenesis.

A good answer also says that ADH, anti-diuretic hormone, regulates water balance by controlling water reabsorption in the kidney, and that this is a homeostatic function. It does not confuse ADH with the reproductive hormones, because they are different systems. The reproductive hormones are about gametes and secondary characteristics; ADH is about water balance. If you can keep the systems separate, you can answer the questions without mixing them up.

The pattern of hormone levels across the female cycle is an exam point in some specifications, but the core idea is that the hormones are coordinated and that the balance changes with the cycle. If the question asks for the hormones, name them and say what they do at the level of the system, and do not over-specify without a clear reason. If you can keep the system-level idea clear, you can answer the reproductive hormone questions correctly.

12. Plant coordination: hormones and tropic responses

Plants also coordinate responses, but they do it with hormones and growth rather than with nerves. Plant hormones such as auxins coordinate growth responses, and tropic responses such as phototropism and gravitropism are classic examples. Phototropism is growth toward light; gravitropism is growth in relation to gravity. Auxins are involved in these responses by redistributing in the plant and causing differential growth. A good answer says that plants coordinate responses with hormones, gives auxins as an example, and explains that tropic responses are growth responses to a directional stimulus, with auxins involved in the redistribution that causes the differential growth. It does not say that plants have nerves, or that tropic responses are movement of whole organs in the animal sense, because they are growth responses. If you can say that, you have the plant coordination idea in a form that scores marks.

The difference between animal and plant coordination is worth knowing because it is a common comparison. Animals use nerves and hormones; plants use hormones and growth, and their responses are slower and often involve bending rather than rapid movement. A good answer says that plant coordination is chemical and growth-based, while animal coordination includes electrical signalling and muscle effectors. It does not say that plants have no coordination, because they do; it says that the mechanisms are different. If you can make that distinction, you can answer the comparison questions.

13. Gene technology: what it is and why it is part of a biology topic

Gene technology is the set of techniques that let us study and manipulate DNA, and it is now part of biology because it is a practical tool for medicine, agriculture and research. The core ideas are that DNA can be cut, copied, separated and inserted, and that these operations let us identify genes, make copies of them, and put them into other organisms for study or use. A good answer says that gene technology includes techniques such as cutting DNA with restriction enzymes, copying DNA by the polymerase chain reaction, separating DNA fragments by gel electrophoresis, and inserting DNA into other organisms, and that the techniques are used in medicine, agriculture and research. It does not just say that gene technology is “genetic engineering” as a label; it says what we do with DNA and why.

The point of the topic is not only that DNA can be manipulated, but that the manipulation has consequences we can reason about. If you understand what PCR does, what a vector does, what transformation does and what gel electrophoresis shows, you can answer the questions that ask for the principles rather than just the names of techniques. The applications come after the principles, because you cannot judge the applications without the principles. If you can keep that order clear, you can answer the gene technology questions well.

14. Restriction enzymes, DNA cutting and sticky ends

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, and the cuts can produce sticky ends, short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with complementary sticky ends from another piece of DNA cut with the same enzyme. The useful point is that the specificity of a restriction enzyme lets us cut DNA predictably, and that sticky ends make it easier to join a piece of DNA into another DNA molecule, because the complementary overhangs can base-pair and then be sealed with DNA ligase. A good answer says that restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, that some cuts produce sticky ends, and that sticky ends allow two pieces of DNA cut with the same enzyme to be joined by base-pairing and ligated by DNA ligase. It does not say that restriction enzymes cut at random sites, or that any two pieces of DNA will join regardless of the enzyme used, because that is not how specificity works. If you can say that, you have the restriction enzyme idea in a form that scores marks.

The sticky end idea is important because it is one of the ways gene technology is made practical. If you want to insert a gene into a plasmid, you cut both with the same restriction enzyme so the ends match, then you ligate them. A good answer describes that process without pretending that the joining is automatic; it needs the matching ends and the ligase. If you can describe the cut, the matching ends and the ligation, you have the cloning step in a form that scores marks.

15. Polymerase chain reaction and the logic of copying DNA in vitro

The polymerase chain reaction, PCR, is a way to copy and amplify a specific DNA sequence in vitro, using repeated cycles of heating, cooling and polymerisation. The basic idea is that a DNA sample is denatured by heat, primers anneal to the target sequences, and a heat-stable polymerase extends the primers to make new copies, so that the target sequence doubles each cycle. A good answer says that PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence through repeated cycles, that the cycles involve heating to separate the strands, cooling to let primers anneal, and warming for the polymerase to synthesise new DNA, and that the amount of target DNA increases exponentially. It does not say that PCR copies the entire genome randomly, because it amplifies a target sequence by using primers that define the region. If you can say that, you have the PCR idea in a form that scores marks.

The practical importance of PCR is that it lets you get enough DNA from a small sample to study or use. A good answer says that PCR is used to amplify small samples of DNA, and gives examples such as forensic or diagnostic use, without pretending that PCR by itself identifies the source. The amplification is one step; identification depends on what you do with the product. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the questions without overclaiming. The heat-stable polymerase is another key idea, because it lets the enzyme survive the repeated heating. If you can say that, you have the right level of detail.

16. Gel electrophoresis, separation by size, and the blotting ideas behind gene probes

Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments, or RNA or protein, by movement through a gel in an electric field, so that fragments of different sizes travel different distances. DNA fragments are negatively charged and move toward the positive electrode, with smaller fragments moving faster through the gel matrix. The result is a pattern of bands that can be compared with a standard or used to detect a specific fragment when combined with a probe. A good answer says that electrophoresis separates fragments by size, that DNA moves toward the positive electrode, that smaller fragments move faster, and that the result is a banding pattern. If a probe is used, it hybridises to a complementary sequence and reveals a specific band. It does not say that electrophoresis identifies a sequence by itself; it separates by size, and identification needs a probe or a comparison with a known standard. If you can say that, you have the electrophoresis idea in a form that scores marks.

The combining of electrophoresis with a gene probe is the basis of techniques such as Southern blotting, in which DNA fragments are separated, transferred to a membrane and probed with a labelled complementary DNA or RNA sequence to detect a specific fragment. A good answer says that gene probes are used to detect specific sequences by hybridisation, and that the probe is complementary to the target. It does not say that a probe works by size alone; it works by base-pairing with the target sequence. If you can say that, you have the probing idea, which is the link between the separation and the identification.

17. Vectors and transformation, and the role of a selectable marker

When DNA is inserted into another organism, a vector is used to carry the DNA. A plasmid is a common vector; it is cut with a restriction enzyme, the wanted DNA is inserted, and the plasmid is put back into a host cell, where it can be replicated and expressed. Transformation is the process of getting the DNA into the host cell. A selectable marker such as an antibiotic resistance gene lets you identify the cells that took up the vector or the recombinant DNA, because only those cells will survive the selection. A good answer says that a vector carries foreign DNA into a host cell, that transformation is the uptake of the DNA, and that a selectable marker lets you identify the transformed cells. It does not say that transformation happens to all cells or that every cell takes up the vector; only some do, and the marker is what lets you find them. If you can say that, you have the vector and transformation idea in a form that scores marks.

The insertional inactivation idea is often tested alongside the marker idea. If a gene is inserted into a marker gene, the marker may be disrupted, so that the recombinant cells have a different phenotype from the non-recombinant ones. A good answer says that inserting DNA into a marker gene can inactivate it, giving a way to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant cells. It does not say that the insertion has no effect on the marker; it says that it can inactivate it and that this is useful for selection. If you can say that, you have the selection logic as well as the terminology.

18. Genetic screening, gene probes and the ethics of knowing

Genetic screening uses techniques such as probes and PCR to detect alleles or mutations associated with a condition, and it can be applied to individuals and populations. The practical point is that screening can identify people at risk of a genetic condition, which can affect medical decisions, family planning and the psychological experience of the person tested. A good answer says that genetic screening uses gene probes or PCR to detect disease-related alleles, that it can identify people at risk, and that this has medical and ethical implications. It does not say that screening is always beneficial without qualification, because screening raises issues about privacy, anxiety, discrimination and the meaning of a result, as well as the medical benefit. If you can keep the benefits and the issues both in view, you can answer the screening questions well.

The ethics are part of the topic, because gene technology is not only a technical subject. A good answer can mention that knowing a genetic risk can be useful and burdensome at the same time, and that the meaning of a result depends on the condition, the test and the person. If the question asks for issues, list a few that are real: privacy, the effect on family members, the possibility of discrimination, and the psychological effect. If the question asks for benefits, list a few that are real: early detection, informed choices, and targeted management. If you can do both, you have the balanced answer that the specification wants.

19. Gene therapy, germ-line and somatic treatment, and the limits of the idea

Gene therapy is the use of gene technology to treat a condition by introducing, removing or altering genetic material in cells. In somatic gene therapy, the change affects the treated individual’s body cells and not the germ cells, so it does not pass to offspring. In germ-line gene therapy, the change would be heritable, which raises different and greater ethical issues. A good answer says that gene therapy aims to correct or compensate for a faulty gene, that somatic treatment affects only the individual and is not inherited, that germ-line treatment would be inherited and raises ethical concerns, and that gene therapy is still limited in what it can achieve for many conditions. It does not say that gene therapy is a cure-all, or that somatic and germ-line therapy are the same ethically, because they are not. If you can say that, you have the gene therapy idea in a form that scores marks.

The detail of delivery matters too: the therapeutic DNA has to get into the right cells, which is not trivial in many cases, and that is one reason gene therapy is challenging. A good answer can say that delivery is a problem and that the immune system, targeting and expression all matter. It does not need to describe every method in detail to answer at the right level, but it should recognise that delivery is part of the difficulty. If you can say that, you have a realistic view of gene therapy, which is better than a hopeful or dismissive one.

20. Genetically modified organisms and the main applications

Genetically modified organisms are organisms whose DNA has been altered by gene technology. Common applications include producing human proteins in microorganisms, improving crops for yield, pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and producing animals or cell lines for research or medicine. A good answer says that GM organisms are made by inserting or altering genes, and that applications include therapeutic protein production, crop improvement and research. It does not say that every GM organism is identical in purpose, because the applications differ. It also does not say that all genetic modification is the same as selective breeding, because selective breeding works within existing variation over generations, while gene technology can move genes across species and is much faster and more direct. If you can make that distinction, you can answer the GMO questions well.

The plant applications are a common exam area. A good answer can mention insect resistance, herbicide tolerance, and improved nutritional content as separate aims, and can say that the same general approach, transfer of a useful gene, can serve different purposes. It does not say that all GM crops are the same, because the trait matters. If you can name a couple of concrete aims and say how gene technology enables them, you have a stronger answer than a vague label. The value of the answer is in the reasoning, not in the buzzword.

21. The ethics and practical concerns of GM organisms

GM organisms raise practical and ethical issues. Among the practical issues are gene flow to wild relatives, effects on non-target organisms, resistance development, and control of the product. Among the ethical issues are concerns about altering organisms, ownership and control of genes, food labelling and consumer choice, and the distribution of benefits and risks. A good answer says that GM organisms raise both practical and ethical concerns, gives examples from both categories, and does not present the same answer for every situation, because different GM uses raise different issues. If the question asks for concerns about a specific use, answer for that use rather than giving a generic list. If you can do that, you have the evaluation in the right form.

A common mistake is to treat every GM issue as equally important in every case, or to treat the issues as obviously one-sided. The better answer distinguishes the technical, the environmental and the ethical, and says that the importance depends on the case. A good answer also says that some concerns are shared with conventional breeding and agriculture, such as unintended effects or resistance, while some are more specific to gene technology, such as the transfer of genes across wide species boundaries. If you can separate those, you can answer more accurately.

22. Gene technology as a tool for answering biological questions and for medicine

Gene technology is not only about applications; it is also a way of doing biology. By making copies of genes, probing genomes, sequencing DNA, and knocking out or modifying genes, we can ask and answer questions that were hard or impossible before. The same tools are used to understand disease, to develop diagnostics, and to produce therapies. A good answer says that gene technology is a research tool as well as a practical technology, and that it lets us study gene function, identify disease-related genes, and develop medical and agricultural uses. It does not say that gene technology and genetics are the same thing; genetics is the study of heredity and gene function, and gene technology is the set of manipulation tools. If you can say that, you have the relationship between the science and the tools clear.

The important reasoning skill is to link a technique to its purpose. PCR amplifies a target for analysis; restriction enzymes cut at specific sites so pieces can be joined; vectors carry DNA; electrophoresis separates; probes detect. If you can match technique to purpose, you can answer the “explain how” questions, which are where the marks often sit. The topic rewards that linkage, not just the vocabulary. If you can do the linkage, you are doing the topic at the right level.

23. How the parts fit together: detection, coordination, control and manipulation of information

The topic is unified by the idea of information and its control. Sensory receptors detect information; nervous and hormonal systems transmit and coordinate that information; effectors carry out the response; homeostatic systems regulate the internal environment by comparing the current state with a set point and responding to deviations; and gene technology manipulates the DNA that encodes the instructions for all of this. If you see the topic as a set of control systems at different levels, the parts fit together, and the exam questions that ask for connections become easier to answer.

A good answer can trace the chain for a concrete case: a stimulus is detected by a receptor, the signal is processed, a response is made by a muscle or gland, and where hormones are involved the response is slower and more widespread, and where homeostasis is involved the response opposes the change. It can separate nervous and hormonal coordination by speed, range and duration. It can describe the synapse and the neuromuscular junction as chemical junctions that translate electrical signals into other signals. It can describe gene technology as the manipulation of the DNA that underlies all of it. If you can do that, you have the topic as a connected system, which is what the examiners are looking for when they ask for an explanation rather than a list.

24. How to answer the coordination and gene technology questions

For nervous and hormonal coordination, say what each is, where the signal goes, and why the two systems are both needed. For receptors, give a concrete example with the right structural detail, such as rods, cones or a Pacinian corpuscle, and say what the receptor detects and how the signal starts. For synapses and the neuromuscular junction, include the calcium step and the neurotransmitter release. For muscle contraction, include sliding filaments, ATP and calcium, and the fact that the filaments do not shorten. For homeostasis, define it as stability within limits and say that negative feedback opposes the change, and use insulin and glucagon as the example if the question allows it. For gene technology, match each technique to its purpose and distinguish principle from application, and where the question asks for ethics, give a balanced set of issues rather than a single slogan. If you can do that, you can handle most of the question types in this topic.

25. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe nervous and hormonal coordination and contrast them; describe sensory reception with rods, cones or a Pacinian corpuscle; describe the retina, the fovea and the photoreceptor structure; describe the reflex arc and why reflexes are useful; describe the synapse and the neuromuscular junction including calcium entry and neurotransmitter release; describe muscle contraction by sliding filaments with the roles of ATP and calcium; describe the insulin-glucagon system and homeostasis with negative feedback; describe the endocrine control of reproduction at the level of the hormones and their functions; describe plant coordination with hormones and tropic responses; describe gene technology techniques including restriction enzymes, PCR, gel electrophoresis, vectors, transformation, probes and screening; describe gene therapy and GM organisms with their applications and the issues they raise. After this topic, revise the related systems, because the associations matter and the best questions ask for the links.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology behind coordination and response and the molecular biology and applications of gene technology. A revision note has to cover both the organism-level coordination and the molecular techniques in enough detail to be useful, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the nervous system is slow and diffuse, when its main feature for many responses is that it is fast and specific.
  • Saying hormones act on every cell, when they act only on cells with the right receptors.
  • Saying rods detect colour or that cones work best in dim light, when the opposite is true.
  • Saying the Pacinian corpuscle detects all touch equally, when it is tuned to vibration and deep pressure.
  • Saying a reflex involves conscious thought, when it is automatic and bypasses conscious processing.
  • Saying neurotransmitter is released just because the action potential arrives, without mentioning calcium entry at the presynaptic membrane.
  • Saying the muscle filaments shorten during contraction, when they slide past each other.
  • Saying ATP alone drives contraction without calcium, when calcium exposes the binding sites first.
  • Saying insulin and glucagon have the same effect, or that either alone controls blood glucose, when they oppose each other.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, rather than being kept within limits by negative feedback.
  • Confusing ADH’s role in water balance with the reproductive hormones.
  • Saying plants have nerves, or that tropic responses are rapid muscle-like movements rather than growth responses.
  • Saying restriction enzymes cut at random sites, when they cut at specific recognition sequences.
  • Saying PCR copies the whole genome randomly, when it amplifies a target sequence defined by primers.
  • Saying electrophoresis identifies a sequence by itself, without a probe or standard, when it separates by size.
  • Saying transformation happens to every cell, when only some take up the vector and a marker is used to find them.
  • Saying gene therapy is a cure-all, or treating somatic and germ-line therapy as ethically identical.
  • Saying all genetic modification is the same as selective breeding, when gene technology can move genes across species and is much faster and more direct.
  • Giving a single-sided ethical answer for every GM use, instead of matching the issues to the specific case.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe nervous and hormonal coordination and give one way in which they differ. Answer: Nervous coordination uses electrical impulses along neurones from receptor to coordinator to effector, and produces fast, specific responses, such as a reflex or voluntary movement. Hormonal coordination uses hormones released by endocrine glands into the blood, acting on target cells with the right receptors, and produces responses that are often slower, longer-lasting and more widespread, such as growth or metabolic control. Difference: nervous responses are fast and local, hormonal responses are often slower and more widespread. (5 marks)
  2. Describe the structure of a rod cell and explain how it responds to light. Answer: A rod cell has an outer segment packed with discs containing the pigment rhodopsin, a cell body and a synapse. Light bleaches rhodopsin, which changes the membrane potential of the rod cell and reduces neurotransmitter release at the synapse, so the change is signalled to the rest of the visual system. Rods are more sensitive to light and work well in dim light, but do not detect colour. (5 marks)
  3. Describe the structure of the Pacinian corpuscle and explain how it detects pressure or vibration. Answer: The Pacinian corpuscle is a pressure receptor with a connective tissue capsule around a nerve ending. Pressure deforms the capsule, which stimulates the nerve ending and generates a nerve signal. The capsule means the receptor responds to changes in pressure and vibration rather than constant touch. (4 marks)
  4. Describe a simple reflex arc and explain why reflexes are useful. Answer: A reflex arc includes a receptor, a sensory neurone, an interneurone, a motor neurone and an effector. The sensory neurone brings information from the receptor to the central nervous system, the interneurone connects to the motor neurone, and the effector responds. Reflexes are fast and automatic, so they protect the body and make rapid adjustments without waiting for conscious thought. (5 marks)
  5. Describe how an action potential at a synapse leads to neurotransmitter release, and state the role of calcium ions. Answer: An action potential arriving at the presynaptic membrane opens calcium ion channels, calcium ions enter the presynaptic neurone, and the calcium causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, triggering an action potential or other response. Calcium entry is essential to trigger release. (5 marks)
  6. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the roles of ATP and calcium. Answer: Muscle contraction uses the sliding filament model: actin and myosin filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, while the filaments themselves do not shorten. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and release, pulling the thin filament. Calcium exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin can bind; ATP is used to break the cross-bridge, re-cock the myosin head and provide energy for the cycle. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and binding sites are covered again. (5 marks)
  7. Describe the roles of insulin and glucagon in the control of blood glucose concentration, and explain how they illustrate homeostasis. Answer: Insulin is secreted when blood glucose rises and lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake by cells and glycogenesis and by other effects; glucagon is secreted when blood glucose falls and raises blood glucose by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. They work in opposition to keep blood glucose within limits. This illustrates homeostasis and negative feedback because each hormone opposes the deviation of blood glucose from the set point. (5 marks)
  8. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback, using one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward normal. Example: in temperature control, if body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point; if it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)
  9. Describe the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the human female, and the role of testosterone in the male. Answer: FSH and LH are pituitary hormones involved in controlling the reproductive system and sex hormone release; in females, oestrogen and progesterone are involved in the female reproductive cycle, including control of the cycle and maintenance of pregnancy; in males, FSH and LH are involved in spermatogenesis and testosterone is involved in male development and spermatogenesis. (5 marks)
  10. Describe ADH and explain its role in homeostasis. Answer: ADH, anti-diuretic hormone, is released when the body needs to conserve water; it acts on the kidneys to increase water reabsorption, reducing water loss in urine and helping maintain water balance. This is a homeostatic function because it keeps the internal water balance within limits. (4 marks)
  11. Describe plant coordination with hormones and explain what is meant by a tropic response. Answer: Plants coordinate responses with hormones such as auxins, which control growth. A tropic response is a directional growth response to a stimulus; phototropism is growth toward light, and gravitropism is growth in relation to gravity. Auxins redistribute in the plant and cause differential growth, so the organ bends. (5 marks)
  12. Explain the role of restriction enzymes and sticky ends in gene technology. Answer: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. Some cuts produce sticky ends, short single-stranded overhangs. If two pieces of DNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, their sticky ends are complementary and can base-pair, allowing them to be joined by DNA ligase and made into a recombinant molecule. (4 marks)
  13. Describe the polymerase chain reaction and explain why it is useful. Answer: PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles in which the DNA is heated to separate the strands, primers anneal at cooler temperatures, and a heat-stable polymerase extends the primers to make new copies, so the target sequence doubles each cycle. It is useful because it allows a small DNA sample to be amplified enough to study or use in diagnosis or forensics. (5 marks)
  14. Describe gel electrophoresis and explain how a gene probe can be used with it. Answer: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field; DNA moves toward the positive electrode, and smaller fragments move faster, giving a banding pattern. A gene probe is a labelled single-stranded DNA or RNA sequence complementary to a target sequence; it hybridises to the target fragment so the specific band can be detected. Electrophoresis separates by size; the probe identifies a specific sequence by base-pairing. (5 marks)
  15. Describe the use of a vector and a selectable marker in genetic modification, and explain insertional inactivation. Answer: A vector such as a plasmid carries foreign DNA into a host cell; the DNA is inserted into the vector, the vector is introduced into the host by transformation, and a selectable marker such as an antibiotic resistance gene lets only transformed cells survive. If the foreign DNA is inserted into the marker gene, the marker may be inactivated, so recombinant cells can be distinguished from non-recombinant ones by their phenotype. (5 marks)
  16. Give the main applications of genetically modified organisms and one concern about them. Answer: Applications include producing human proteins in microorganisms, improving crops for pest resistance, herbicide tolerance or nutrition, and producing organisms for research or medicine. A concern could be gene flow to wild relatives, effects on non-target organisms, development of resistance, or ethical issues such as ownership of genes, labelling and consumer choice, and the distribution of benefits and risks. The concern depends on the specific use. (5 marks)
  17. Describe gene therapy and distinguish somatic from germ-line gene therapy, including one ethical issue with germ-line therapy. Answer: Gene therapy uses gene technology to treat a condition by introducing, removing or altering genetic material in cells. Somatic gene therapy affects body cells and is not inherited; germ-line gene therapy would alter heritable DNA and would be passed to offspring. A germ-line ethical issue is that changes to the germ line are heritable, so they affect future generations, raising questions about consent, unforeseen consequences and how far it is right to alter the inheritable genome. (5 marks)
  18. Explain how gene technology is useful both as a research tool and as a practical technology. Answer: As a research tool, gene technology lets us copy genes, probe genomes, sequence DNA, and modify genes to study gene function and disease. As a practical technology, it lets us produce therapeutic proteins, improve crops, and develop diagnostics and therapies. The same techniques are used for both understanding biology and for applications. (5 marks)
  19. Describe the main stages in producing a genetically modified bacterium that makes a human protein. Answer: The human gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme, or otherwise obtained; a plasmid vector is cut with the same enzyme so the ends match; the gene is inserted into the plasmid and the recombinant plasmid is sealed with DNA ligase; the plasmid is introduced into bacterial cells by transformation; transformed cells are selected using a marker; and the bacteria are grown to produce the human protein, which is then harvested. (5 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one example and one reason. Practise the receptor examples, the synapse and neuromuscular junction with the calcium step, the sliding filament contraction with ATP and calcium, the insulin-glucagon system with homeostasis, and the gene technology techniques matched to their purposes. Check that you can say where each thing happens and why, not just what it is. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.
content:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that connect the way organisms coordinate and respond to stimuli with the ways we now use gene technology. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples, drawings and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. The point of the topic: coordination, response, homeostasis and gene technology together

This topic is really about how living systems detect change and deal with it. Nervous and hormonal coordination are the two main ways animals coordinate a response, and they have different speeds, ranges and durations, which is why both exist. Sensory reception is the entry point for information from the environment. Muscle and gland effectors are where the response happens. The endocrine system adds a hormonal layer that can act on a longer timescale. Homeostatic control systems keep the internal environment within limits. Gene technology is the modern set of tools that lets us read, copy and manipulate DNA and that has reshaped medicine, agriculture and research. The parts are connected because the same logic of detection, processing and response applies whether the signal is electrical, chemical or genetic.

A good answer sees the topic as one system of control at several levels: from receptor to coordinator to effector, and from the molecular handling of DNA to the applications that result from it. If you can see those links, you can answer the questions that cross the parts, which are often where the higher marks are. If you treat the parts as unrelated lists, you lose the reasoning that the specification is after.

2. Nervous coordination as detection, transmission and response
