title:
Appendix U — Cross-strand reasoning in one long integrated answer

A question that crosses the strands is the one that tests whether the topic is a connected whole or three separate lists. The best way to answer such a question is to write one integrated answer that moves between the strands without losing the thread, and the best way to practise that is to take a cross-strand question and write the integrated answer from the durable ideas and the cross-strand appendix. Suppose the question asks you to relate the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, and to say what the two kinds of recognition have in common and what they do not. A good integrated answer says that both are about telling things apart by recognising specific features, and that the immune system recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies and memory cells, while DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA and uses the differences between individuals to identify or exclude. A good answer then says that the common point is recognition and comparison, while the differences are that one is a biological response inside the body and the other is a technical comparison of extracted DNA, and that one is about defence and the other is about identification. If you can write that, you have the cross-strand answer, and you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you only write two separate descriptions, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

If you write that integrated answer with the common point and the differences in the right places, you hit the marks that the cross-strand question is after. You hit the recognition-and-comparison idea, which is the common point. You hit the biological-response-versus-technical-comparison idea, which is one of the differences. You hit the defence-versus-identification idea, which is the other of the differences. You hit the connection, because you have said both the common point and the differences without treating them as unrelated. If you can write that under time pressure, you are ready for the cross-strand question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write only a description of immunity and a description of DNA profiling without the connection, you have the labels but not the connection, and the mark is in the connection. The cross-strand appendix and the durable ideas are there to help you write that answer, and the practice is to write it from them under time pressure until it comes out integrated rather than separate.

The practice for the cross-strand answer is also good practice for the single-strand questions, because it forces you to say the distinctions clearly, and the distinctions are what the single-strand questions are often after as well. If you can say what immunity and DNA profiling have in common without blurring the differences, you can usually say what antibodies and antigens are without blurring the distinction between recognition and killing, and what B cells and T cells are without blurring the difference between the humoral and the cell-mediated arm. The cross-strand practice is therefore good practice for the whole topic, not just for the cross-strand questions, because it builds the precision that all the questions want. If you do the cross-strand practice once or twice under time pressure, you are practising the precision that the whole topic rewards, and that is the use of the cross-strand practice: to build the precision for everything, not just for the cross-strand questions.

Appendix V — The last long answers to practise before the exam and why these are the ones

The last long answers to practise before the exam are the ones that test the most integrated understanding, because if you can answer those under time pressure, the less integrated ones are usually easier. The first is the immune-response long answer with the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order. The second is the gene technology long answer with the principle and the purpose for each technique and the application and the limit if the question asks for it. The third is the coordination long answer with a receptor, a synapse or neuromuscular junction, and a muscle contraction, depending on what the question gives. The fourth is the cross-strand answer that relates, for example, immunity and DNA profiling, or microbiology culturing and forensic evidence. If you can write those four under time pressure, you can answer most of the long questions the topic is likely to set, because those four are the shapes the long questions most often take. If you can only write some of them, the others are the ones to practise before the exam, and the note is there to practise them from.

The reason these are the last long answers to practise is that they are the ones that require the most integration, and integration is the skill that the higher marks are after. The immune-response long answer requires integration of the non-specific and specific arms, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link. The gene technology long answer requires integration of the technique, the purpose, the application and the limit. The coordination long answer requires integration of the receptor, the synapse or neuromuscular junction, and the muscle contraction, depending on the question. The cross-strand answer requires integration of two or more strands. If you can integrate across each of those, you have the skill the higher marks are after, and the skill is the thing that is hardest to recover on the day without practice. The note is long enough to give you the integrated answers to practise, and the practice is to write them from the durable ideas and the appendices under time pressure until they come out integrated rather than separate.

The last long-answer practice is also the last chance to check the distinctions that matter most, because those are the ones that are most often lost when writing fast. For the immune-response long answer, the distinctions are non-specific versus specific, B versus T, primary versus secondary, memory cells, and the vaccination link. For the gene technology long answer, the distinctions are the principle and the purpose for each technique, and the application versus the limit. For the coordination long answer, the distinctions are the receptor structure, stimulus and transduction, the calcium step at the synapse, and the sliding-filament idea with ATP and calcium. For the cross-strand answer, the distinctions are the common point and the differences. If you can write the long answers with those distinctions in the right places under time pressure, you are ready for the long questions, because you have the distinctions the marks are after. If you can only write them with some of the distinctions missing, the missing ones are the ones to practise before the exam, and the note is there to practise them from.

Appendix W — What to leave out on the day and why that is a skill

On the day, one of the skills is knowing what to leave out, because the exam rewards a precise answer of the right length more than a long imprecise one, and the long imprecise answer is the one that most often loses marks by running out of time or losing focus. The first thing to leave out is padding that does not add a distinction, because padding of that kind is what turns a precise answer into a vague one without adding marks. If the question is about the non-specific first line, do not spend the answer on the specific response unless the question asks for both, because the marks are in the non-specific first line and the padding will only eat the time. If the question is about a receptor, do not spend the answer on the whole nervous system unless the question asks for the whole system, because the marks are in the receptor and the padding will only eat the time. If the question is about one gene technology technique, do not spend the answer on all of them unless the question asks for all of them, because the marks are in the one technique and the padding will only eat the time. If you can leave out the padding, you save the time and the focus for the marks that are actually there, and that is the skill the exam rewards.

The second thing to leave out is the temptation to over-explain a correct point until it becomes wrong, because over-explanation is one of the most common ways to lose a mark on a correct answer. If you have said that the filaments slide and do not shorten, do not keep going until you say something like “the filaments shorten a little” or “the filaments really do get shorter in a way,” because that is exactly the kind of over-explanation that turns a correct point into a wrong one. If you have said that the secondary response is faster and stronger because of memory, do not keep going until you say something that implies the memory is a vague feeling rather than cells, because that is the kind of over-explanation that loses the mark. If you have said that the restriction enzyme cuts at a specific sequence, do not keep going until you say something that implies it cuts at any sequence, because that is the kind of over-explanation that loses the mark. If you can stop at the correct point, you keep the mark, and that is the skill the exam rewards. The note is written to give you the correct points to stop at, and the practice is to stop at them rather than to keep going until you lose them.

The third thing to leave out is the urge to answer a question from memory of the note rather than from the question in front of you, because the exam is not a test of whether you remember the note but of whether you can answer the question that is actually there. If the question asks about the neuromuscular junction, do not answer about the synapse in general unless the question asks for the general synapse, because the marks are in the neuromuscular junction. If the question asks about herd immunity, do not answer about vaccination in general unless the question asks for vaccination, because the marks are in the herd immunity. If the question asks about the secondary response, do not answer about the primary response unless the question asks for both, because the marks are in the secondary response. If you can answer the question that is actually there, you are answering for the marks, and that is the skill the exam rewards. The note is there to give you the material to answer the question that is actually there, not to be recited regardless of the question. The skill is to use the note as a source, not as a script.

The final thing to leave out is the urge to check every answer against the note at the last minute, because the last minute is too late to change much and too easy to panic. If you have written the answer and checked the distinctions during the exam, that is the time to trust it and move on, rather than to go back and second-guess every word. If you have written the answer and you know the distinctions are there, that is the time to move on, because the marks are in the distinctions and the distinctions are there. The last-minute check is the one that most often leads to crossing out a correct point or adding a wrong one, and that is the kind of last-minute check that loses marks rather than gaining them. If you can leave out the last-minute rewriting, you save the marks you already have, and that is the skill the exam rewards. The note is for the revision and the practice, not for the last-minute rewriting, and the practice is to leave the note behind on the day and write the answer from the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions you have practised.

Appendix X — The four-hour review structure that makes the note usable in one sitting

If you have four hours for the topic, the structure that makes the note usable in one sitting is to spend the first hour on the durable ideas and the anchors, the second hour on the description and comparison questions, the third hour on the evaluation questions, and the fourth hour on one timed integrated answer of each of the four shapes. The first hour is the framework hour, because you want the framework in place before you go into the detail. Say the four durable ideas with their anchors and their distinctions, and check that you can say them under time pressure. If one is weak, spend the rest of the hour on that one, because a weak framework will cost you across the topic, not just on one question. If all four are sound, move on, because the rest of the sitting is then filling in the detail under the framework, and the framework is the thing that lets you find the detail under time pressure. Appendix U — Cross-strand reasoning in one long integrated answer

A question that crosses the strands is the one that tests whether the topic is a connected whole or three separate lists. The best way to answer such a question is to write one integrated answer that moves between the strands without losing the thread, and the best way to practise that is to take a cross-strand question and write the integrated answer from the durable ideas and the cross-strand appendix. Suppose the question asks you to relate the immune recognition of antigens to the forensic comparison of DNA patterns, and to say what the two kinds of recognition have in common and what they do not. A good integrated answer says that both are about telling things apart by recognising specific features, and that the immune system recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies and memory cells, while DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA and uses the differences between individuals to identify or exclude. A good answer then says that the common point is recognition and comparison, while the differences are that one is a biological response inside the body and the other is a technical comparison of extracted DNA, and that one is about defence and the other is about identification. If you can write that, you have the cross-strand answer, and you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you only write two separate descriptions, you have lost the connection, and the connection is what the question is after.

If you write that integrated answer with the common point and the differences in the right places, you hit the marks that the cross-strand question is after. You hit the recognition-and-comparison idea, which is the common point. You hit the biological-response-versus-technical-comparison idea, which is one of the differences. You hit the defence-versus-identification idea, which is the other of the differences. You hit the connection, because you have said both the common point and the differences without treating them as unrelated. If you can write that under time pressure, you are ready for the cross-strand question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write only a description of immunity and a description of DNA profiling without the connection, you have the labels but not the connection, and the mark is in the connection. The cross-strand appendix and the durable ideas are there to help you write that answer, and the practice is to write it from them under time pressure until it comes out integrated rather than separate.

The practice for the cross-strand answer is also good practice for the single-strand questions, because it forces you to say the distinctions clearly, and the distinctions are what the single-strand questions are often after as well. If you can say what immunity and DNA profiling have in common without blurring the differences, you can usually say what antibodies and antigens are without blurring the distinction between recognition and killing, and what B cells and T cells are without blurring the difference between the humoral and the cell-mediated arm. The cross-strand practice is therefore good practice for the whole topic, not just for the cross-strand questions, because it builds the precision that all the questions want. If you do the cross-strand practice once or twice under time pressure, you are practising the precision that the whole topic rewards, and that is the use of the cross-strand practice: to build the precision for everything, not just for the cross-strand questions.

On the day, one of the skills is knowing what to leave out, because the exam rewards a precise answer of the right length more than a long imprecise one, and the long imprecise answer is the one that most often loses marks by running out of time or losing focus. The first thing to leave out is padding that does not add a distinction, because padding of that kind is what turns a precise answer into a vague one without adding marks. If the question is about the non-specific first line, do not spend the answer on the specific response unless the question asks for both, because the marks are in the non-specific first line and the padding will only eat the time. If the question is about a receptor, do not spend the answer on the whole nervous system unless the question asks for the whole system, because the marks are in the receptor and the padding will only eat the time. If you can leave out the padding, you save the time and the focus for the marks that are actually there, and that is the skill the exam rewards.

The second thing to leave out is the temptation to over-explain a correct point until it becomes wrong, because over-explanation is one of the most common ways to lose a mark on a correct answer. If you have said that the filaments slide and do not shorten, do not keep going until you say something like “the filaments shorten a little” or “the filaments really do get shorter in a way,” because that is exactly the kind of over-explanation that turns a correct point into a wrong one. title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.

Worked example: midpoint, distance and the perpendicular bisector

Let A = (2, 5) and B = (8, −1). The midpoint is ((2 + 8)/2, (5 − 1)/2) = (5, 2). The length AB is √((8 − 2)² + (−1 − 5)²) = √(36 + 36) = 6√2.

The gradient of AB is (−1 − 5)/(8 − 2) = −1. The perpendicular bisector has gradient 1 and passes through (5, 2), so its equation is y − 2 = x − 5, which gives y = x − 3. Check that C = (0, −3) lies on it: 0 − 3 = −3, so it does.

Intersection of two lines

To find where y = 2x + 1 meets y = −x + 7, set the two right-hand sides equal: 2x + 1 = −x + 7, so 3x = 6 and x = 2. Substitute back: y = 2(2) + 1 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5). Always substitute back into the second equation as a check.

Area of a triangle from coordinates

For the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 4), the base from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4 and the height is the vertical distance from (3, 4) to that base, which is 3. The area is ½ × 4 × 3 = 6 square units.

When the base is not horizontal, use the shoelace method: list the coordinates in order, multiply diagonally, subtract, and halve the absolute value. It works for any triangle, so it is safer than estimating the height.

Parallel and perpendicular lines in exam questions

  • Parallel lines have equal gradients, so 2y = 4x + 1 and y = 2x − 7 are parallel.
  • Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3.
  • If a question asks for a line through a given point perpendicular to a line, find the gradient first, then substitute the point into y = mx + c or y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Common errors that lose marks

  • Subtracting the coordinates in different orders for the gradient, for example using (−1 − 5)/(2 − 8), which gives the wrong sign.
  • Stating the distance as the difference of the x-coordinates only, rather than using Pythagoras on both differences.
  • Leaving a midpoint as a fraction when it is a whole number, or giving a line equation in a form that is not what the question asks for.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

Ohm's law and resistors

For a conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR. In a series circuit, the current is the same at every point and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same and the current divides between the branches.

For two equal resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is half the value of one resistor. A fuse or circuit breaker protects the wiring by breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.

Exam tip: state whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying a resistance rule.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as light, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. An actuator does the opposite: it converts an electrical signal into physical movement, for example by turning a motor. A robot or automated system uses sensors to read its environment, a processor to decide what to do, and actuators to act.

A feedback loop compares the measured value with the required value and adjusts the output to close the gap. A thermostat is a simple example: it switches the heater off when the room reaches the set temperature. Feedback allows a system to correct itself, but a poorly set loop can overshoot or oscillate.

Exam tip: name a sensor and an actuator in any automated system you describe, and explain what the feedback corrects.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A hash function maps each key to a storage address. If the file has 100 slots and the key is an integer n, the address could be n mod 100. Two keys that give the same address are a collision, and the file must provide a method such as an overflow area to store the second record. ### Check yourself Compare serial and random file organisation. Serial files store records in the order they were added, so searching is slow. Random files use a hash or index to reach a record directly, so retrieval is fast but collisions must be handled.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

This A2 Level Biology revision note covers Edexcel IAL Topic 6, focusing on culturing microorganisms, immunity, antibiotics, decomposition, forensic DNA profiling, and determining the time of death.

  • 6.1 Culturing microbes requires strict aseptic technique using autoclaved equipment and nutrient agar to prevent contamination.
  • 6.2 Microbial growth is measured via cell counts, dilution plating, mass, and optical turbidity methods.
  • 6.3 Bacterial growth curves consist of lag, exponential, stationary, and death phases; exponential growth rate constants are calculated using (ln(N_t) − ln(N_0)) / t.
  • 6.4 Core Practical 13 investigates the growth rate of liquid cultures safely and ethically.
  • 6.5 Pathogens include bacteria and viruses (Ebola, TMV, HIV, lambda phage), exhibiting lytic cycles or latency.
  • 6.6 M. tuberculosis and HIV infect host cells, destroying immune cells and causing fatal systemic symptoms.
  • 6.7 Pathogen entry routes are protected by physical and chemical barriers including skin, stomach acid, and flora.
  • 6.8 Non-specific responses feature inflammation, lysozyme action, interferon release, and phagocytosis.
  • 6.9 Antigens provoke immune responses involving macrophages, antigen-presenting cells, plasma cells, and specific antibodies.
  • 6.10 B cells and T cells (helper, killer, memory) coordinate humoral and cell-mediated immune responses.
  • 6.11 Immunity is acquired naturally or artificially, through active or passive mechanisms.
  • 6.12 Pathogen evasion mechanisms drive an evolutionary race between hosts and pathogens.
  • 6.13 Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacterial reproduction while bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria outright.
  • 6.14 Core Practical 14 investigates the inhibition zones of different antibiotics on bacteria.
  • 6.15 Hospital-acquired infection prevention requires strict hygiene codes and controlled antibiotic prescription.
  • 6.16 Microorganisms decompose organic matter, recycling carbon within ecosystems.
  • 6.17 Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifies DNA fragments exponentially using thermal cycling.
  • 6.18 Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by length through an agarose gel using an electric current.
  • 6.19 DNA profiling uses short tandem repeats to identify individuals and establish genetic relationships.
  • 6.20 Time of death is estimated using decomposition stages, succession, forensic entomology, body temperature, and rigor mortis.

Worked example

Calculate the exponential growth rate constant for a bacterial culture where the initial cell number N_0 is 1000 cells, rising to 50000 cells after 4 hours. Using the formula k = (ln(N_t) − ln(N_0)) / t, we get k = (ln(50000) − ln(1000)) / 4 = (10.82 − 6.91) / 4 = 3.91 / 4 = 0.978 per hour.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics; remember bacteriostatic prevents division whereas bactericidal causes cell lysis. When calculating exponential growth, ensure you use natural logarithms (ln) rather than base-10 logs unless converting appropriately. In PCR, remember the steps of denaturation at 95 °C, annealing at 55 °C, and extension at 72 °C using Taq polymerase. For forensics, remember that rigor mortis is temporary muscle contraction caused by ATP depletion, which peaks and then reverses as decomposition begins.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

title:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI15. Use it to organise the detail in the full notes, not to replace them. The summary repeats the specification points by number so you can see at a glance what each paragraph is there for, and it keeps the same three-part split the full notes use: the laboratory methods for growing and measuring microbes, the host-pathogen-immune story, and the DNA and forensic methods.

Growing and measuring microorganisms

The first idea is that microbes are handled with aseptic technique so the culture stays pure and stays contained. The technique is not a checklist you tick; it is a set of linked practices — working near a flame, sterilising the loop until it glows, cooling it before it touches the culture, flaming the necks of containers, and taping plates without sealing them completely. Sterility of the medium matters too, because an inoculated medium should bring only one organism into growth.

  • 6.1 The point of aseptic technique is purity and safety at the same time. Work near a flame so airflow carries unwanted microbes away; sterilise loops in a flame; let them cool before use; flame the necks of bottles and plates before opening; tape plates down but do not seal them.
  • 6.2 Microbial growth can be measured four ways. Direct cell counts use a counting chamber of known volume; dilution plating estimates viable count as colony-forming units per cm3 and is the standard for living cells; mass and turbidity give proxies; dry mass is used when cells are small, numerous or clumped. Choose the method by what you actually want to know.
  • 6.3 The bacterial growth curve has lag, exponential, stationary and death phases. In the exponential phase the population doubles in a fixed time, and the exponential formula N = N0 e^(kt) applies, with doubling time t_d = ln 2 / k. The calculation only works if both counts belong to the exponential phase.
  • 6.4 Core Practical 13 follows growth in liquid culture using turbidity or viable counts, with safe and ethical use of a non-pathogenic species, sealed plates and sterilisation before disposal.

Bacteria, viruses and the cycles of infection

Bacteria are prokaryotic cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a circular chromosome and often plasmids. Viruses are not cells; they have a nucleic acid core and a protein capsid, sometimes with an envelope. The named examples matter because they illustrate different architectures: Ebola is an enveloped RNA virus; tobacco mosaic virus is a rod-shaped plant virus; HIV is a retrovirus that reverse-transcribes and integrates; lambda phage is a bacterial virus with a head and tail.

  • 6.5 (i) Compare bacteria and viruses by structure and by independence: bacteria are cells that can metabolise and reproduce in suitable conditions; viruses are not cells and can only reproduce inside a host.
  • 6.5 (ii) The lytic cycle replicates and lyses the host; latency, or lysogeny in phages, lets the viral genome persist without producing particles for a time. Latency matters because it hides the infection and complicates clearance and diagnosis.

How pathogens enter and how the body resists at first

Pathogens enter through defined routes — respiratory, digestive, skin, sexual, parenteral — and the body defends at those entry points. Skin is the main physical barrier; mucous and cilia clear the respiratory tract; stomach acid and lysozyme in secretions are chemical defences; and the normal flora competes with pathogens, so disrupting it can itself cause problems.

  • 6.7 (i) Routes of entry include inhaled droplets, ingested material, breaches of skin, the sexual route and direct inoculation into blood or tissues.
  • 6.7 (ii) Barriers include skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme, and the competitive effect of normal flora on skin and gut.

Non-specific and specific defence

The non-specific response is fast, local and not specific: inflammation brings blood and defences to the site; lysozyme breaks down bacterial cell walls in secretions; interferon warns neighbouring cells to resist virus replication; and phagocytes engulf and digest microbes, also linking to the specific response by presenting antigen. The specific response is slower but targeted and produces memory, using B cells against extracellular threats and T cells against cells presenting antigen.

  • 6.8 (i) Inflammation is the local response with vasodilation and increased permeability, bringing defences to the site.
  • 6.8 (ii) Lysozyme is in tears and secretions and attacks peptidoglycan.
  • 6.8 (iii) Interferons are released by virus-infected cells and make nearby cells more resistant to viral replication.
  • 6.8 (iv) Phagocytosis is carried out by macrophages and neutrophils: recognition, engulfment into a phagosome, fusion with lysosomes, and destruction, with antigen presentation linking to the adaptive system.
  • 6.9 (i) Antigen is a molecule recognised by the immune system; antibody is a Y-shaped protein that binds a specific antigen; plasma cells secrete antibody; macrophages also act as antigen-presenting cells.
  • 6.9 (ii) Specific binding means B and T cells respond to a particular antigen, and antibodies can neutralise, block entry, opsonise and activate complement.
  • 6.10 (i) B cells act against extracellular threats, differentiating into plasma cells and memory B cells.
  • 6.10 (ii) T helper cells coordinate by recognising antigen on class II; T killer cells kill infected cells presenting antigen on class I; T memory cells give faster re-exposure responses.

Types of immunity

Immunity can be natural or artificial and active or passive. Active means the body makes its own response and memory; passive means antibodies are supplied and the protection is temporary. Active gives long-term protection; passive gives fast but short-lived protection.

  • 6.11 (i) Natural active: from infection, memory formed, often long-lasting.
  • 6.11 (ii) Artificial active: from vaccination, memory formed without disease.
  • 6.11 (iii) Natural passive: antibodies from mother to infant, temporary, no memory.
  • 6.11 (iv) Artificial passive: injected antibodies such as antivenom, temporary, no memory.

The evolutionary race and antibiotics

Pathogens evade defences by mutation, latency, intracellular hiding and immune suppression. The host and pathogen are in a continuing race, and the same logic applies to antibiotic resistance: use of a drug is selection pressure, and resistant variants are favoured. Antibiotics themselves come in two functional kinds: bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and rely on the host, while bactericidal drugs kill. That distinction matters when the host's defences are weak.

  • 6.12 (i) The evolutionary race is supported by evasion mechanisms such as rapid antigenic change, latency, intracellular life and interference with host signalling.
  • 6.12 (ii) Antigenic variation is a powerful evasion because changed antigens escape existing memory; HIV mutation is a classic case.
  • 6.13 (i) Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop growth and division without necessarily killing.
  • 6.13 (ii) Bactericidal antibiotics kill, often by damaging cell wall or membrane.
  • 6.14 Core Practical 14 tests antibiotic effects with disc diffusion on agar, measuring zones of inhibition, controlling the conditions so comparisons are valid, and using safe organisms and aseptic technique.
  • 6.15 Hospital-acquired infections arise from vulnerable patients, breached barriers, antibiotic use and cross-infection; the codes of practice — careful prescribing, hand hygiene, asepsis, sterilisation and isolation — follow directly from those causes.

Decomposition, PCR, gels, profiling and time of death

Microorganisms are also the agents of decomposition and carbon recycling; they break down dead organic matter, respire, and return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, completing the carbon cycle. PCR amplifies a chosen DNA region through repeated denaturation, annealing and extension cycles using a thermostable polymerase; gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size toward the positive electrode because DNA is negatively charged; DNA profiling compares variable regions for identification and relatedness; and time of death is estimated from several indicators — decomposition stage, insect succession, body temperature and rigor mortis — because no single one is precise enough and each is affected by conditions such as temperature.

  • 6.16 (i) Microorganisms decompose organic matter; (ii) decomposition returns carbon to the atmosphere through microbial respiration and closes the carbon cycle.
  • 6.17 (i) PCR amplifies a specific DNA region from a tiny sample through repeated cycles; (ii) the cycle is denaturation, primer annealing, and extension by a thermostable polymerase.
  • 6.18 (i) Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by length; (ii) fragments move toward the positive electrode, smaller ones faster, and are visualised by staining.
  • 6.19 (i) DNA profiling is used for identification in forensics; (ii) it is used to assess genetic relationships in plants and animals.
  • 6.20 (i) Decomposition extent, (ii) insect succession, (iii) body temperature, and (iv) rigor mortis are combined indicators; time of death is an estimate from several changing features, not a single test.

Rapid checkpoints

Before an exam, check these quick contrasts. Direct count versus viable count: total versus living. Active versus passive immunity: memory versus no memory, long versus short, self-made versus supplied. B cells versus T cells: extracellular versus cell-presenting, antibody secretion versus killing or coordinating. Lytic versus latent: immediate kill of host versus quiet persistence. Static versus cidal: stop growth versus kill. PCR versus gel: amplification versus separation; one makes copies, the other sorts them. Time of death: use more than one indicator because each is condition-dependent.

  • 6.5: bacteria are cells, viruses are not; named viruses show different architectures and lifestyles.
  • 6.8: non-specific is fast and local, specific is targeted and gives memory.
  • 6.11: active gives memory, passive does not.
  • 6.17: PCR needs a thermostable polymerase so the enzyme survives the denaturation step.
  • 6.18: DNA moves to the positive electrode; smaller fragments move faster.
  • 6.20: time of death uses several indicators, not one.

Typical mistakes in a hurry

  • Counting all cells and calling it viable: haemocytometer counts total cells unless a viability stain is used.
  • Applying N = N0 e^(kt) outside the exponential phase: the formula assumes constant doubling.
  • Calling a virus a cell or saying it metabolises: viruses are not cells and have no independent metabolism.
  • Mixing help and kill: T helper cells coordinate; T killer cells destroy infected cells.
  • Expecting passive immunity to last: it does not, because no memory is formed.
  • Saying DNA runs to the negative electrode: it runs to the positive one.
  • Using a single forensic indicator as if it were exact: time of death is a combined estimate with uncertainty.
  • Blurring static and cidal: static holds growth, cidal kills, and the choice depends on the host.

The fast version of this topic is: culture and measure microbes with the right method, remember that bacteria are cells and viruses are not, track the race between pathogen evasion and host defence, know the four kinds of immunity and the static-versus-cidal split, and be clear on what PCR, gels and profiling actually do. Use this summary alongside the full notes and the Core Practicals, and practise the calculations and the B-versus-T and active-versus-passive distinctions until they are automatic.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Mathematics — OL. area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

  • 1. Area of a triangle
  • 2. Sine rule
  • 3. Cosine rule
  • 4. Bearing problems
  • 5. 3-D trigonometry

Formulas to learn

  • Area of a triangle: one half of a b sin C.
  • Sine rule: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.
  • Cosine rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc).

Worked example

In a triangle with sides 7 and 9 and included angle 40 degrees, the area is one half of 7 x 9 x sin 40, about 20.2. The angle opposite the side 9 is then found by the sine rule, so check the answer against the cosine rule before you finish.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Radians

One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.

Common angles: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 2π.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²

Exam tips: never mix degrees into s = rθ; convert first. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing, and check whether a question asks for the major or minor sector.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

Worked method for pressure questions

Step 1: write down the force in newtons and the area in m². Step 2: divide, p = F/A. Step 3: if the question is about a liquid, use p = hρg with h in metres, ρ in kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, and remember that the pressure is the same at equal depths in the same liquid. Atmospheric pressure is added to the liquid pressure when a question asks for total pressure at depth.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 2.1, explain why serial transmission is reliable over distance and describe the benefits of packet switching, including robustness and shared lines. For 2.2, state the purpose of checksums and explain how they detect errors. For 2.3, describe the process of encryption and justify its importance in secure data transmission. For 3.4, describe the functions of network hardware components, including routers, switches, and gateways.
### Traps
Error: confusing MAC and IP addresses. Correction: MAC addresses are burned-in and used for layer 2 communication, while IP addresses are assigned and used for layer 3 communication. Error: assuming parallel transmission is always faster. Correction: parallel transmission is faster over short distances, but serial transmission is more reliable over long distances. Error: thinking that HTTPS is a protocol. Correction: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, a secure protocol for data transmission.
### Memory hooks
Use the mnemonic 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' to remember the layers of the TCP/IP stack: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application. To compare MAC and IP addresses, use a table to highlight their differences. To remember the functions of network hardware components, associate each component with its function, such as routers 'routing' traffic between networks.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on networking and communication. Make sure to allocate time to read the questions carefully and plan your answers before starting to write.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons

E = hf = hc/λ, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

Example: green light 550 nm: E ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 2.3 eV.

The Photoelectric Effect

Light above a threshold frequency ejects electrons instantly; intensity alone does nothing below f₀.

  • Einstein: hf = φ + KE_max (φ = work function)
  • KE_max = eV_s (stopping potential)

Example: sodium φ = 2.3 eV needs λ < 540 nm; 400 nm light gives KE_max = 3.1 − 2.3 = 0.8 eV.

Wave–Particle Duality

de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Electrons diffract like waves — electron microscopes exploit short electron wavelengths.

Example: an electron at 10⁶ m s⁻¹: λ ≈ 0.7 nm.

Energy Levels and Line Spectra

Atoms absorb/emit photons matching level gaps: hf = E₁ − E₂. Emission lines are bright; absorption dark.

Example: the Hα line: 3 → 2 transition, 656 nm.

Exam tips: one photon interacts with one electron — that is why intensity cannot release electrons below threshold; convert eV ↔ J with 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.

Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan

45°√2/2√2/21

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title: Probability and Statistics I
content:
Probability and Statistics I

Permutations and Combinations

  • Permutations (order matters): ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!
  • Combinations (order irrelevant): ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Example: choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: C(8,3) = 56. Arranging 3 of 8 books on a shelf: P(8,3) = 336.

Probability Rules

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
  • Independent events: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
  • Complement: P(A′) = 1 − P(A)

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Tree diagrams multiply along branches and add across outcomes.

Example: P(two reds without replacement from 5 red + 3 blue) = (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14.

Discrete Random Variables

E(X) = Σ x P(X = x); Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

Example: die: E(X) = 3.5; E(X²) = 91/6, so Var(X) ≈ 2.92.

Exam tips: decide permutation vs combination by testing whether swapping two items changes the outcome; always verify tree-branch probabilities sum to 1.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.
