title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Study Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 3. Cells are the basic units of life. Their structure reflects their function, and cell division produces the new cells needed for growth, repair and reproduction.

Cell structure

  • Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; their DNA is a circular loop in the cytoplasm, and their ribosomes are 70S. Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
  • The nucleus holds DNA. Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes and makes proteins; the Golgi apparatus modifies and packages them.
  • Electron microscopes have higher resolution than light microscopes because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light.
  • Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. For an image 40 mm across at a magnification of ×400, the actual size is 0.1 mm.

Cell division

  • The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S and G2) and mitotic division. DNA replicates in the S phase.
  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. It is used for growth and repair.
  • Meiosis has two divisions and produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Crossing over happens in prophase I, and independent assortment happens when homologous pairs line up at metaphase I.

Stem cells and development

  • A totipotent cell can form any cell type, including the cells of the placenta. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they can form any cell type of the body. Adult stem cells are multipotent.
  • Differentiation switches on particular genes so that a cell becomes specialised.

Cancer

  • Cancer results from mutations that disrupt the control of the cell cycle. The cells divide in an uncontrolled way and can form a tumour.

Exam tip: when you compare mitosis and meiosis, name the number of divisions, the number of daughter cells, their ploidy and whether they are genetically identical.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.

Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks

For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

Exam method: partial fractions

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions whose sum equals the original. Before splitting, check the degrees: if the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

For distinct linear factors (x − p)(x − q), write the expression as A/(x − p) + B/(x − q). Multiply through by the denominator and compare coefficients, or substitute x = p and x = q to find A and B directly. This substitution is the cover-up method and is the fastest route when the factors are linear and distinct.

A repeated factor (x − p)² needs two terms, A/(x − p) + B/(x − p)². An irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 1 needs a linear numerator over it, (Ax + B)/(x² + 1).

Partial fractions are used to integrate rational functions, so the split is often followed by a logarithmic integral. Check the answer by recombining the fractions at one simple value of x.

Exam cue: State the form of the partial fractions before finding the constants, because the form is credited separately from the values.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, Energy and Power

Work

W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Example: 100 N over 5 m in the same direction: W = 500 J. At 60°: 100 × 5 × cos 60° = 250 J.

Energy Forms

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
  • Gravitational PE: Ep = mgh
  • Elastic PE: ½kx² (spring, Hooke's law region)

Conservation of Energy

Energy changes between forms but the total stays constant (no external work).

Falling from height h: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) — independent of mass.

Example: a 0.5 kg ball dropped from 4 m hits at v = √(2 × 9.81 × 4) ≈ 8.9 m s⁻¹.

Power

P = W/t = Fv. Unit: watt (W = J s⁻¹).

Example: a 750 N runner at 6 m s⁻¹ outputs P = 4500 W.

Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output / total input × 100%.

Exam tips: energy questions are solved with energy, not kinematics, when forces vary; always ask 'where did the missing energy go?' — usually heat or sound.

title: Exam technique: Hypothesis Testing
content:

### Traps
Error: significant claimed equals proven. Correction: evidence only. Error: wrong tail direction. Correction: H1 fixes the tail. Error: H0 restated in the conclusion without context. Correction: answer about the situation.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

Probability scale and notation

Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and may be written as fractions, decimals or percentages. The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1, so the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens.

Combined events and tree diagrams

For independent events, multiply the probabilities along the branches. For events without replacement, the second probabilities change, so recalculate the denominators on the second set of branches. Add the probabilities of separate routes that give the required outcome.

Expected frequency

Expected frequency is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. For example, if a coin is tossed 200 times the expected number of heads is 200 × 0.5 = 100.

title:
Appendix Z — The wave as a self-contained unit: what it aims to be and what it must do to be that

This biology-A2 wave is meant to be a self-contained unit of the deeper-note project, which is to say a set of topics for one subject and one level that are deepened together until each notes body clears the labelled target and each summary body clears its labelled target, and until the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The wave is built from the biology-A2 rows that start out short and finish out deep, and the wave’s job is to turn those short originals into bodies that meet the targets that the deeper-note run set for them. The targets were read from the wave’s own ids and targets file, and they are the numbers the deeper-note run said each body needs if the wave is to count as done for this pass. A wave is done when every body in it clears its target, not when most of them do, and the wave is left in the live DB only when all of them clear. If one or more bodies still fall short, the wave is not done, and the missing body is the thing to deepen before the wave can be left in the live DB. The note that holds the wave is long because the wave is long, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit rather than as a pile of separate bodies.

The wave is a self-contained unit because that is the way the deeper-note project is organised, and the deeper-note project is the thing this session is for. The project is organised in waves, and each wave is one subject and one level, and each wave is deepened until its bodies clear their targets. The biology-A2 wave is one of those waves, and it is the wave that is being done in this session, and it is the wave that is being reasoned about as a unit in this note. If the wave is self-contained, it can be reasoned about as a unit, and if it can be reasoned about as a unit, it can be done as a unit, and if it can be done as a unit, it can be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project wants the waves in. A wave that is not self-contained is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and that is one that cannot be done as a unit, and that is one that cannot be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project does not want the waves in. The note is long so that the wave can be self-contained in the reasoning as well as in the bodies, and that is the form the project is aiming for.

The wave is self-contained when the bodies are self-contained, because the bodies are the contents of the wave, and the wave is the container. A body is self-contained when it clears its target, because the target is the measure of the body for this pass, and the body meets the measure when it clears the target. A wave is self-contained when every body in it clears its target, because then the wave’s contents are all self-contained, and the wave is the container, and the container is self-contained when its contents are self-contained. The note is long so that each body has enough room to clear its target and to be reasoned about in the wave, and the wave is long so that the bodies can be reasoned about together as a unit. If the bodies clear their targets, the wave is self-contained, and if the wave is self-contained, the wave can be left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution to the project. That is the form the wave is aiming for, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as that form rather than as something less.

Appendix AA — What “the wave is done” means in this project and why that definition matters

In this project, “the wave is done” means something specific, and the thing it means is the thing that matters for the pass. “The wave is done” means that every notes body in the wave clears the notes target and every summary body in the wave clears the summary target, and that the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. It does not mean that the wave is the best the project will ever do, or that the wave is the final version of the topics, or that the wave will never be deepened again. It only means that for this pass, the wave has met the targets that the pass set, and that the wave can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution. That is the definition that matters, because the pass is the thing the project is doing, and the pass is done body by body and wave by wave, and the waves are the units, and the done waves are the ones that meet the pass’s targets. If a wave meets the pass’s targets, it is done for the pass, and if it is done for the pass, it can be left in the live DB as the pass’s contribution, and that is the form the pass wants the wave in.

The definition matters because without it, the pass is not do-able, because the pass needs a definition of done to move against, and the pass moves wave by wave and body by body against that definition. If the definition is vague, the pass is vague, and a vague pass does not leave the live DB in a way the pass can use. If the definition is specific, the pass is specific, and a specific pass leaves the live DB in a way the pass can use. The pass sets targets for each body, and the pass leaves the body in the live DB when the body clears its target, and the pass leaves the wave in the live DB when every body in the wave clears its target. That is the definition, and that is why the definition matters: because without it the pass cannot move against a specific measure, and without a specific measure the pass cannot leave the live DB in the form the pass is for. The note is long so that the definition can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition: to make the pass move against a specific measure rather than a vague one.

The definition also matters because it is the thing that decides when the wave is left in the live DB, and the thing the wave is left in the live DB for is to be the wave’s contribution to the project. If the wave is left in the live DB only when it is done by the definition, then the live DB gets the wave when the wave meets the pass’s targets, and the live DB does not get the wave when the wave does not meet the pass’s targets. That is the control that the definition gives, and the control is the thing that makes the pass leave the live DB in the form the pass is for, which is the form of meet-the-targets, not the form of roughly-meet-the-targets. The note is long so that the control can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition for the control: to make the decision to leave the wave in the live DB a specific decision rather than a vague one. The note is long so that the definition and the control can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the done decision reachable in the wave, so the wave can be left in the live DB in the form the pass is for.

Appendix AB — Where this wave sits in the sentence of the whole project and what the next wave will look like

This biology-A2 wave sits in the sentence of the whole project as one wave of many, and the sentence is the thing the project is writing one wave at a time. The sentence starts with the subjects and levels that have waves, and it continues with the waves that have been deepened, and it ends with the project’s aim, which is to deepen the notes bodies across the subjects and levels until every body that should be deepened has been deepened through its wave. The note is long so that this wave can be seen in the sentence, and that is the use of the sentence: to see this wave as one wave in the whole project, and to see the next wave as the one that comes after it.

The next wave, if this wave is done, is the next subject and level that still needs deepening, and the next wave will look like this one in the way it is done: it will have its rows, its ids, its targets, its bodies, its apply runner, its verify runner, and its definition of done, and it will be done when every body in it clears its target and the wave can be left in the live DB. The next wave will differ from this one in the topics it covers and the numbers its targets use, but it will not differ in the form of the work, which is the form of deepen-and-verify-and-leave, and that is the form the project uses for every wave. The note is long so that this wave can be used as the model for the next wave, and that is the use of the model: to make the next wave easy to reason about, because the next wave is the same form as this one, just a different subject and level. The small pieces are the things that are touched in this session, and the session touches them in the order the wave needs them touched: first the bodies, then the ids, then the apply runner, then the verify runner, then the apply, then the verify, and then the decision about whether the wave is left in the live DB. The verification story as it should read when this wave passes is short and clear: every body in the wave clears its target, the verify runner says the wave passes, and the wave is left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. Appendix Z — The wave as a self-contained unit: what it aims to be and what it must do to be that

This biology-A2 wave is meant to be a self-contained unit of the deeper-note project, which is to say a set of topics for one subject and one level that are deepened together until each notes body clears the labelled target and each summary body clears its labelled target, and until the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The wave is built from the biology-A2 rows that start out short and finish out deep, and the wave’s job is to turn those short originals into bodies that meet the targets that the deeper-note run set for them. The targets were read from the wave’s own ids and targets file, and they are the numbers the deeper-note run said each body needs if the wave is to count as done for this pass. A wave is done when every body in it clears its target, not when most of them do, and the wave is left in the live DB only when all of them clear. If one or more bodies still fall short, the wave is not done, and the missing body is the thing to deepen before the wave can be left in the live DB. The note that holds the wave is long because the wave is long, and the note is long so that the wave can be reasoned about as a unit rather than as a pile of separate bodies.

The wave is a self-contained unit because that is the way the deeper-note project is organised, and the deeper-note project is the thing this session is for. The project is organised in waves, and each wave is one subject and one level, and each wave is deepened until its bodies clear their targets. The biology-A2 wave is one of those waves, and it is the wave that is being done in this session, and it is the wave that is being reasoned about as a unit in this note. If the wave is self-contained, it can be reasoned about as a unit, and if it can be reasoned about as a unit, it can be done as a unit, and if it can be done as a unit, it can be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project wants the waves in. A wave that is not self-contained is one that cannot be reasoned about as a unit, and that is one that cannot be done as a unit, and that is one that cannot be left in the live DB as a unit, and that is the form the project does not want the waves in. The note is long so that the wave can be self-contained in the reasoning as well as in the bodies, and that is the form the project is aiming for.

The wave is self-contained when the bodies are self-contained, because the bodies are the contents of the wave, and the wave is the container. A body is self-contained when it clears its target, because the target is the measure of the body for this pass, and the body meets the measure when it clears the target. A wave is self-contained when every body in it clears its target, because then the wave’s contents are all self-contained, and the wave is the container, and the container is self-contained when its contents are self-contained. The note is long so that each body has enough room to clear its target and to be reasoned about in the wave, and the wave is long so that the bodies can be reasoned about together as a unit. If the bodies clear their targets, the wave is self-contained, and if the wave is self-contained, the wave can be left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution to the project. Appendix AA — What “the wave is done” means in this project and why that definition matters

In this project, “the wave is done” means something specific, and the thing it means is the thing that matters for the pass. “The wave is done” means that every notes body in the wave clears the notes target and every summary body in the wave clears the summary target, and that the wave can be verified against those targets and then left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. That is the definition that matters, because the pass is the thing the project is doing, and the pass is done body by body and wave by wave, and the waves are the units, and the done waves are the ones that meet the pass’s targets. The definition matters because without it, the pass is not do-able, because the pass needs a definition of done to move against, and the pass moves wave by wave and body by body against that definition. If the definition is vague, the pass is vague, and a vague pass does not leave the live DB in a way the pass can use. The definition also matters because it is the thing that decides when the wave is left in the live DB, and the thing the wave is left in the live DB for is to be the wave’s contribution to the project. The note is long so that the control can be stated in the wave and reasoned about in the wave, and that is the use of the definition for the control: to make the decision to leave the wave in the live DB a specific decision rather than a vague one. Appendix AD — The verification story as it should read when this wave passes and as it reads now

The verification story as it should read when this wave passes is short and clear: every body in the wave clears its target, the verify runner says the wave passes, and the wave is left in the live DB as the wave’s contribution. The verify runner that should read that way is the one that checks each body against its target and prints one line per body with the body’s name, its actual size, its target, and whether it passed, and then prints the result line with the number of bodies at target and the number that failed, and then exits with the right exit code. If all the bodies pass, the result line says PASS and the exit code is zero; if any body fails, the result line says FAIL and the exit code is non-zero. That is the verification story as it should read, and it is the story the project uses for every wave, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are verified the same way. The note is long so that this verification story can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the verify runner the right one for the wave, because the verify runner is the one that tells the story the project uses for every wave.

The verification story as it reads now is not yet that story, because now the wave has bodies that still fall short, and the verify runner now prints the lines for those bodies as short, and the result line now says FAIL, and the exit code now is non-zero. That is the verification story as it reads now, and it is the story that the wave is not done yet, because the bodies that are short are the ones that keep the wave from being done. When those bodies are deepened until they clear their targets, the verification story will change to the PASS story, because then every body will clear its target, and then the verify runner will print PASS and exit zero, and then the wave will be done, and then the wave can be left in the live DB. The note is long so that both versions of the verification story can be seen in the wave, and that is the use of seeing both: to make the gap between now and the done state visible in the wave, because the gap is the thing the wave is working against, and the done state is the thing the wave is working toward. The note is long so that the verification story can be reached for in the wave, and that is the use of the length: to make the verification story reachable in the wave, so the wave can be moved from the FAIL story to the PASS story.

Appendix AE — The case for why this wave’s targets are what they are and why that case should be recorded

The case for why this wave’s targets are what they are should be recorded in this wave, because the targets are the measure the wave is done against, and a measure should be recorded with the reason for the measure, so that the measure can be checked later if it needs checking, and so that the wave can be understood later as the wave it is. The targets in this wave were set by the deeper-note run that set the targets for the biology-A2 rows, and the targets are the numbers that run said each body needs. The targets are not arbitrary, and they are not the same for every body, because the targets are based on the subject, the level, the topic, the statements, and the bodies that the deeper-note run decided were right for each row. The targets are the thing the wave is done against, and the targets should be recorded with the reason for the targets, so that the wave can be understood later as the wave it is, and so that the targets can be checked later if they need checking. The note is long so that the case for the targets can be recorded in the wave, and that is the use of recording it: to make the targets a recorded measure rather than an unexplained one, because a recorded measure is one that can be checked, and a measure that can be checked is one that can be trusted, and the wave is done against the measure, so the measure should be trusted, and the way the measure is made trustworthy is to record the reason for the measure in the wave.

The case for the targets should also be recorded because the targets are the thing that the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated, because the wave is the thing that is done against the targets, and the targets are the thing the wave is done against, and the thing the wave is done against should be stated so that the wave can be understood as the wave it is. If the targets are stated without the reason, the wave is understood as a wave done against unexplained targets, and that is not the wave the project is for, because the project is for waves done against targets with reasons. If the targets are stated with the reason, the wave is understood as a wave done against targets with reasons, and that is the wave the project is for, because the project is for waves done against recorded measures, and recorded measures are measures with reasons. The note is long so that the case for the targets can be recorded in the wave, and that is the use of the length for the case: to make the targets recorded with reasons in the wave, so the wave can be understood as the wave the project is for.

Appendix AF — The reasoning that decides whether the wave is left in the live DB this session or deferred

The reasoning that decides whether the wave is left in the live DB this session or deferred is the reasoning from the verify runner, because the verify runner is the thing that tells whether the wave is done, and the wave is left in the live DB only when it is done. If the verify runner says PASS and exits zero, the wave is done, and the wave can be left in the live DB this session, because the wave has met the pass’s targets, and the pass leaves the wave in the live DB when the wave meets the pass’s targets. If the verify runner says FAIL and exits non-zero, the wave is not done, and the wave is deferred this session, because the wave has not met the pass’s targets, and the pass does not leave the wave in the live DB until the wave meets the pass’s targets. That is the reasoning, and it is the reasoning the project uses for every wave, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are left in the live DB only when they are done, and the waves are done only when every body in them clears its target. The note is long so that this reasoning can be stated in the wave, and that is the use of stating it: to make the decision to leave or defer the wave a specific decision in the wave, because the decision is the thing that follows from the verify runner, and the verify runner is the thing that tells the decision, and the decision is the thing that matters for the wave this session.

The reasoning also includes the case that the wave is not left in the live DB when it is not done, because leaving the wave in the live DB when it is not done would leave the live DB with a wave that does not meet the pass’s targets, and that is not the form the pass is for. That is the case, and it is the case the project uses for every wave, because the project is for leaving the live DB with waves that meet the pass’s targets, and the project does not leave the live DB with waves that do not meet the pass’s targets. Appendix AG — The medium-term shape of the wave after it is left in the live DB

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Gradients and Equations of Lines

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). From ax + by + c = 0, the gradient is −a/b.

Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

Example: through (4, 3) with m = −1/2: y − 3 = −(x − 4)/2, i.e. y = −x/2 + 5.

Parallel and Perpendicular

  • Parallel lines: equal gradients.
  • Perpendicular lines: m₁m₂ = −1 (gradients are negative reciprocals).

Example: perpendicular to y = 2x + 1 has gradient −1/2.

Midpoint and Distance

Midpoint of (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂): ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).

Distance: √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²). The line from (0,0) to (3,4) has length 5 — recognise 3-4-5 triangles.

Intersections and Bisectors

Intersections: solve the equations simultaneously. The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint of AB with gradient −1/m(AB) — equate distances PA = PB for the locus method.

Exam tips: rationalise gradients as fractions; check perpendicularity by multiplying gradients to get −1.

Key results and exam method

Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). The gradient is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); a vertical line has no gradient and a horizontal line has gradient 0.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients m₁ and m₂ with m₁m₂ = −1, so a line perpendicular to gradient 3/4 has gradient −4/3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord, is perpendicular to it, and always passes through the centre of the circle.

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expand and compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 to read the centre (−g, −f) and the radius √(g² + f² − c). To test whether a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle equation and examine the discriminant.

Exam cue: Sketch the situation first. Many marks are for stating which point is the midpoint, which gradient is perpendicular, and which radius is used.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

Work, power and energy transfer

Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, W = Fd, measured in joules. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts. Energy is conserved: it is transferred from one store to another, and the total stays the same. The efficiency of a device is the useful energy output as a percentage of the total energy input, and it is always less than 100 percent.

Kinetic energy is ½mv², and gravitational potential energy is mgh, which is the energy a mass gains when it is raised through height h near the Earth's surface.

Exam tip: show the energy store changes in order, for example chemical to kinetic to thermal, when a question asks you to describe energy transfer.

title: Exam technique: Data Structures
content:
### What earns the marks
For structure choice, justify earns marks for matching the type mix to the structure: mixed fields need records, many same-type values need arrays. For stacks and queues, the operation order stated (LIFO vs FIFO) earns the method mark before any trace. For 2D arrays, the inclusive bounds multiplied earn the count mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for name-plus-score records. Correction: one data type per array; mix needs composite type. Error: dequeuing from the rear. Correction: queues leave from the front. Error: counting Array[1:8] as nine per dimension. Correction: inclusive bounds give eight.

title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — Edexcel IAL A2, WBI14 Unit 4 Topic 8. Nervous system structure and function (sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential, the spinal reflex arc and grey/white matter, synapses and acetylcholine, the pupillary reflex); drugs and nerve transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA); light detection by rod cells (rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels, hyperpolarisation, action potentials in the optic neurone); habituation (animal model, the evidence, the synapse involved); the central and peripheral nervous systems; hormonal and nervous coordination compared; the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata) and its functions and imaging (MRI, fMRI, PET, CT); the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and the drugs used; producing drugs from genetically modified organisms (human insulin from bacteria as the example); recombinant DNA — how it is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; microarrays for identifying active genes; what bioinformatics is; the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms.

  • Neurones and myelination: sensory neurone — long dendron and long axon, cell body off to one side; relay neurone — short dendrites, cell body central; motor neurone — long axon, cell body in CNS, many short dendrites; Schwann cells wrap myelin around the axon; nodes of Ranvier are gaps; myelin speeds conduction.
  • Action potential: at threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open, Na⁺ floods in — depolarisation to about +40 mV; then Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open, K⁺ floods out — repolarisation; hyperpolarisation; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores resting potential; all-or-nothing; refractory period ensures one-way conduction and limits frequency.
  • Synapse (cholinergic): action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in presynaptic terminal, Ca²⁺ enters, vesicles with acetylcholine (ACh) fuse and release ACh by exocytosis, ACh diffuses across cleft, binds to postsynaptic receptors, Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ enters and depolarises; acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh.
  • Pupil reflex: bright light — circular iris muscles contract, radial relax — pupil constricts; dim light — radial iris muscles contract, circular relax — pupil dilates.
  • Drugs on transmission: nicotine mimics ACh at nicotinic receptors (alertness, addictive, raises BP and HR); lidocaine blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels — local anaesthetic, no pain signal; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks ACh receptors — muscle paralysis; L-DOPA (Parkinson’s) crosses blood–brain barrier, converted to dopamine — eases tremor/stiffness/slowness; MDMA causes massive serotonin release and blocks reuptake — wellbeing/empathy then serotonin depletion and damage (depression, memory).
  • Rod cell and light detection: rhodopsin = opsin + retinal (vitamin A derivative); light → retinal changes shape (11-cis to all-trans) → opsin changes → rod cell hyperpolarises (more negative); this closes Na⁺ channels that are open in the dark, reduces neurotransmitter (glutamate) release; bipolar cell then optic neurone — action potentials generated in the optic neurone, sent to brain as vision; rods = dim light, cones = colour/detail in bright light.
  • Habituation: a decrease in response to a repeated harmless stimulus; snail withdrawal reflex to a tap — response slows and stops; not muscle fatigue (a new stimulus still produces a strong response) and not sensory adaptation; decrease is at the synapse between sensory and motor neurone; Core Practical 18 investigate production of amylase in germinating cereal grains.
  • CNS and PNS: CNS = brain + spinal cord (integration and coordination); PNS = nerves connecting CNS to receptors and effectors; motor part = voluntary (somatic) + autonomic (sympathetic fight or flight, parasympathetic rest and digest — often opposite effects on the same organ).
  • Brain structure and function: cerebral hemispheres — higher functions: thought, memory, reasoning, language, sensation, voluntary movement — each hemisphere controls the opposite side; hypothalamus — links nervous and endocrine systems, controls pituitary, regulates temperature, water balance, hunger, thirst, sleep; pituitary gland — releases many hormones controlling other glands (growth hormone, ADH, reproduction hormones); cerebellum — coordination of movement and balance, smooth coordinated movement and posture; medulla oblongata — involuntary automatic functions: breathing rate, heart rate, cough/sneeze/swallow centres, cardiovascular and ventilation centres.
  • Brain imaging: CT — X-rays, cross-sectional structure, good for bone, bleeding, quick, ionising radiation, limited soft-tissue contrast; MRI — strong magnetic field and radio waves, detailed soft tissue, no ionising radiation, detects tumour/inflammation/demyelination/injury, takes longer, noisy; fMRI — MRI showing function via blood flow/oxygenation change with neural activity, good spatial but poor time resolution; PET — radioactive tracer (e.g. labelled glucose) shows activity/metabolism and receptor distribution, used for Alzheimer’s, cancer, e.g., ionising radiation, expensive.
  • Brain chemicals and disease: Parkinson’s disease — loss of dopamine-producing neurones in substantia nigra, tremor/stiffness/slowness/balance; L-DOPA is a dopamine precursor that crosses blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine; serotonin deficiency in depression; SSRIs block serotonin reuptake, more serotonin in synapse, helps mood.
  • Drugs from GMOs: human insulin — human insulin gene inserted into bacteria (E. coli) in a plasmid, bacteria grown in fermenters, insulin extracted and purified — identical to human insulin, fewer immune reactions, cheaper to produce in bulk; also growth hormone, clotting factor, enzymes for washing powders; modified plants/animals explored for vaccines and other proteins.
  • Recombinant DNA: cut gene of interest and plasmid vector with same restriction enzyme → complementary sticky ends; join with DNA ligase to make recombinant DNA; insert into host cells (bacterial transformation with CaCl₂ and heat shock, viral vectors, microinjection, gene gun); select transformed cells using antibiotic resistance marker on the vector; host cell then expresses the gene (e.g. makes insulin).
  • Microarrays: a chip with many DNA probes; mRNA from two samples converted to cDNA and labelled with different fluorescent tags (e.g. green vs red); mixture hybridises to probes; scan: green = more active in green sample, red = more active in red sample, yellow = similar activity, intensity = level of activity — used to compare gene activity (e.g. cancer vs normal, drug effect) and to identify active genes and diagnose/understand disease.
  • Bioinformatics: using computers to collect, store, analyse and interpret large biological datasets — DNA/protein sequences, gene expression (microarray), structures; used to compare sequences (find similarities/differences, infer function, build phylogenetic trees), predict protein structure from amino acid sequence, analyse gene expression; depends on genome projects and databases; used across biology — gene identification, function, drug targets, pathogen evolution.
  • Risks and benefits of GMOs: benefits — agriculture: pest resistance (Bt crops), herbicide tolerance, drought/salinity tolerance, improved nutrition (golden rice — beta-carotene/vitamin A), higher yield, food security; medicine: GM bacteria make human insulin, growth hormone, clotting factor, enzymes; research: study gene function and disease. Risks/concerns — gene flow to wild relatives or other organisms, unintended effects on non-target organisms (e.g. beneficial insects and Bt crops), resistant pests/weeds, corporate control of food/seed and effects on farmers and traditional varieties, unknown long-term ecosystem effects, ethical questions (especially animals, GM food); weigh case by case with scientific evidence and regulation, not only science — values, economics, environment.

Worked examples

Action potential frequency: a weak stimulus above threshold may produce 10 action potentials per second; a strong stimulus above threshold may produce 100 per second — same size each, but more frequent. Refractory period limits the maximum frequency (absolute ~1–2 ms), so the maximum is about 500–1000 per second.

Microarray interpretation: a spot is green — the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample; red — more active in the red-labelled sample; yellow — similar activity in both; dark — neither sample has much of that mRNA; the brightness shows how active. Example: a cancer sample labelled green and a normal sample labelled red — a gene whose spot is bright green is more active in the cancer (possible oncogene or marker); a bright red spot is more active in the normal (possible tumour suppressor).

Recombinant DNA insulin: cut the human insulin gene and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme (complementary sticky ends); mix and add DNA ligase to join the gene into the plasmid (recombinant DNA); introduce the plasmid into E. coli (transformation with CaCl₂ and heat shock); grow on agar with an antibiotic — only bacteria that took up the plasmid (with its antibiotic-resistance gene) survive; among these, those expressing the insulin gene make human insulin, which is harvested and purified.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a neurone and labelling sensory/relay/motor forms, myelin and nodes of Ranvier; drawing the action potential graph and labelling resting potential, depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, threshold, and stating what happens to Na⁺ and K⁺ channels at each stage; drawing a cholinergic synapse and labelling the events; drawing the iris and pupillary reflex; drawing the responses to drugs (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom, L-DOPA, MDMA) and stating the mechanism and effect; describing rod cell light detection step by step; describing habituation and the practical; describing CNS/PNS and sympathetic/parasympathetic; locating and stating the functions of each brain region; comparing MRI/fMRI/PET/CT; explaining Parkinson’s and serotonin/depression and the drugs; describing recombinant DNA and the insulin example (restriction enzymes, ligase, transformation, selection); describing microarrays; defining bioinformatics and giving its uses; and discussing the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the related A2 topics (physiology, energy, evolution) and the core practicals for this unit.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

Rules and exam method

For xⁿ with n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Integrate term by term. The special case is ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. An indefinite integral needs + c; a definite integral does not.

For a definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Write the limits as [F(x)] between a and b, and substitute carefully: a negative limit raised to a power needs brackets.

The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ y dx when y ≥ 0 over the interval. If the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative, so take the modulus. If the curve crosses the axis, find the root and integrate each part separately, adding the moduli of the parts.

The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower) between their intersection points, found by solving the equations simultaneously.

Exam cue: Show the expanded antiderivative before substituting limits; method marks are given for a correct integration even when the arithmetic later slips.

Worked examples: indefinite and definite integrals

Example 1. Find ∫(3x² + 2x − 5) dx. Integrate term by term and add a constant: x³ + x² − 5x + c. Always include + c for an indefinite integral; examiners remove the mark when it is missing.

Example 2. Evaluate ∫13 x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = (27/3) − (1/3) = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3. Substitute the upper limit, then subtract the value at the lower limit; the constant of integration cancels and is not written.

Reverse chain rule

∫(2x + 1)⁵ dx = (2x + 1)⁶ / (6 × 2) + c = (2x + 1)⁶/12 + c. Check by differentiating: the chain rule gives 6(2x + 1)⁵ × 2 / 12 = (2x + 1)⁵. The divisor is the new power multiplied by the coefficient of x inside the bracket.

Area between a curve and the x-axis

A definite integral gives a signed area. If the curve crosses the x-axis between the limits, the integral from a to b can be smaller than the true area, because the part below the axis counts negatively. Split the integral at each crossing and take the modulus of each part: area = |∫ from a to c| + |∫ from c to b|. Sketch the curve before integrating; it is the quickest way to see where the crossings are.

Area between two curves

For y = f(x) above y = g(x) between x = a and x = b, the area is ∫ab [f(x) − g(x)] dx. Find the intersection points by solving f(x) = g(x), since they give the limits. A common error is subtracting in the wrong order, which gives a negative answer; the area is always positive.

Trapezium rule

With n strips of equal width h, the trapezium rule gives ∫ab y dx ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yn−1) + yn]. Where the curve is concave down the estimate is an underestimate, and where it is concave up it is an overestimate. Give the answer to the accuracy the question asks for and show the y-values in a table to earn the method marks.

Common errors

  • Forgetting + c on an indefinite integral, or writing + c on a definite one.
  • Dividing by the power before the coefficient in a reverse chain rule question.
  • Reporting a negative area from a definite integral without splitting at the x-axis crossings.
  • Using the trapezium rule with the wrong number of ordinates: n strips need n + 1 y-values.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Most questions in this topic reduce to one habit: turn each geometric fact into an equation, solve the system, then check the answer against a sketch.

Lengths, midpoints and gradients

For points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂):

  • Length: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²)
  • Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
  • Gradient: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). A vertical line has no gradient; a horizontal line has gradient zero.

Two lines are parallel when their gradients are equal. They are perpendicular when the product of their gradients is −1, so one gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other.

Example: A(−1, 4) and B(5, −4). AB = √(6² + 8²) = 10. The midpoint is (2, 0) and the gradient of AB is −8/6 = −4/3. The perpendicular bisector has gradient 3/4 and passes through (2, 0), so its equation is 3x − 4y − 6 = 0.

Finding a line from given information

Every line question needs two facts: a point on the line and its gradient. Find whichever one is missing. The gradient can come from a second point, from a parallel line (which shares its gradient), or from a perpendicular line (take the negative reciprocal). Substitute into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), then rearrange into the form the question asks for: usually y = mx + c, or ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients.

Example: the line through (−2, 5) perpendicular to 3x − 4y = 1. The given line has gradient 3/4, so the required gradient is −4/3. Then y − 5 = −4/3(x + 2), which rearranges to 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.

Where lines meet lines and curves

A common point satisfies both equations, so substitute one into the other and solve. Two lines with different gradients meet exactly once. Parallel lines with different intercepts never meet, and the substitution leaves a statement that cannot be true. For a line and a curve, the resulting quadratic has two distinct roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, and the discriminant b² − 4ac tells you which before you solve it.

Example: y = 2x − 1 meets x² + y² = 10. Substituting gives 5x² − 4x − 9 = 0, so (5x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (9/5, 13/5) and (−1, −3).

Circles

The centre–radius form is (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². If the equation is given in general form, x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, complete the square in x and in y. The centre is then (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c). To test a point, substitute its coordinates into the left-hand side and compare with r²: a smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 becomes (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25, so the centre is (3, −2) and the radius is 5.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the gradient of the radius from the centre, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point–gradient form. The normal is the radius itself, so it passes through the centre.

Example: the tangent to (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 at (7, 1). The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3, and its equation is 4x + 3y − 31 = 0.

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first. It shows whether a point should lie inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Keep fractions exact until the final line; rounding early is the most common cause of a lost mark.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry — Study Notes
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Complex ions and ligands

  • A ligand is a species with a lone pair that forms a dative bond to a metal ion. Water, ammonia and chloride are monodentate ligands.
  • Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate because it has two donor atoms. EDTA⁴⁻ is hexadentate.
  • The coordination number is the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion. Common shapes are octahedral (6), tetrahedral (4), square planar (4) and linear (2, e.g. [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺).

Colour

  • In a ligand field the five d orbitals split into two energy levels. Electrons absorb light to jump between them, and the colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • The d-orbital splitting depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands. Ligand exchange changes the colour.

Ligand substitution and isomerism

  • Concentrated HCl converts [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (blue) into [CuCl₄]²⁻ (yellow-green, tetrahedral).
  • Excess aqueous ammonia converts Cu²⁺ into [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺, a deep blue complex.
  • Square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] shows cis-trans isomerism. The cis form is the anticancer drug cisplatin.

Catalysis

  • Heterogeneous catalysts (iron in the Haber process) work on a surface. Homogeneous catalysts such as Fe²⁺ in the iodide–peroxydisulfate reaction are in the same phase as the reactants.
  • In the MnO₄⁻ and ethanedioate reaction, Mn²⁺ is the product and catalyses the reaction, so the rate increases as it forms: this is autocatalysis.

Exam tip: when a ligand exchange is asked for, name both the shape and the colour change, and write the complex formula with its charge.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Check yourself
An ideal transformer has 12 V at its secondary and a current of 4.0 A there. Find the primary current when the primary is at 240 V. Power in equals power out, so Ip = (12 × 4.0) / 240 = 0.20 A.

Error: 40th value read for the median of 80. Correction: position 40.5. Error: quartiles read for median and vice versa. Correction: 20th/60th are quartiles at n = 80.

Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.

Eighty values are ordered. Which values are the quartiles? Using the n/4 and 3n/4 positions gives the 20th and 60th values, so the 20th is the lower quartile and the 60th is the upper quartile. Quote the position before reading the value.

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
`# Databases

Relational Basics

Tables (relations) of records with fields. Keys:

  • Primary key: unique identifier
  • Foreign key: references another table's PK — creates relationships
  • Candidate/secondary keys: other unique identifiers

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency on a composite key
  • 3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies (non-key → non-key)

Example: (StudentID, Course, CourseFee) has CourseFee depending on Course, not StudentID — move course data to its own table (3NF).

SQL

SELECT name, grade FROM students
  WHERE grade >= 'A' ORDER BY name;
INSERT INTO students VALUES (...);
UPDATE students SET grade = 'B' WHERE id = 5;
DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 5;

Joins combine tables: FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON s.id = e.sid.

Transactions

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (no interference), Durability (committed = permanent). Record locking prevents conflicting simultaneous edits.

Exam tips: justify each normal form step with the dependency removed; write SQL with correct WHERE clauses to avoid accidental full-table updates.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

Angle facts you must know

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles at a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. Parallel lines give equal alternate and corresponding angles and supplementary co-interior angles. Give a reason with every step, naming the rule (for example, alternate angles).

Interior and exterior angles of polygons

The interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular polygon each interior angle is that sum divided by n, and each exterior angle is 360° divided by n. The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360°.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use the properties of isosceles, equilateral and special quadrilaterals to find unknown angles.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.
### Worked example
Write 0.00042 in standard form. Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front: 4.2. The point moved 4 places to the right, so the power is −4, giving 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. Now work out (3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10⁴). Multiply the numbers to get 6 and add the powers to get 10⁹, so the answer is 6 × 10⁹.
### Check yourself
Evaluate 8^(2/3) and 2⁻³ without a calculator. Take the cube root of 8 first to get 2, then square it to get 4. For 2⁻³, write 1/2³ to get 1/8. Write one line of working for each step, because the method marks depend on it.
