title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Inequalities
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, calculate earns marks for each correct rearrangement step with the inequality sign carried through, and the final solution as an inequality or integer list as demanded. For integer-solution questions, list earns marks only for the complete correct set: show the solved inequality first, then enumerate. For combined inequalities, handle each side separately and intersect at the end.
### Traps
Error: forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. Correction: circle every division by a negative and flip immediately. Error: answering x < 9 with 9 for the largest integer. Correction: step down one for strict inequalities. Error: including -1 in -1 < n <= 3. Correction: strict ends exclude, slack ends include.
### Worked example
Solve −2x > 6. Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the sign, giving x < −3. For a quadratic x² − 4 < 0, factorise to (x − 2)(x + 2) < 0. The product is negative between the roots, so −2 < x < 2.
### Check yourself

For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.

In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.

State the value of the digit 6 in 4 706 325, then calculate 20 − 2 × (3 + 4)². The 6 is worth 6000. The second is 20 − 2 × 49 = 20 − 98 = −78, which shows why the brackets must be done first.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

title: Redox Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Redox Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 16. Redox reactions transfer electrons. Standard electrode potentials let you predict whether a reaction is feasible and quantify the reducing and oxidising power of species.

Oxidation and reduction

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised; the oxidising agent is reduced.

Standard electrode potentials

  • Each half-cell has a standard electrode potential, E⁰, measured under standard conditions: 298 K, 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions and 100 kPa for gases.
  • E⁰ is measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, which is defined as 0 V.
  • A more positive E⁰ means a stronger oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation. A more negative E⁰ means a stronger reducing agent.

Predicting feasibility

  • E⁰cell = E⁰(reduction) − E⁰(oxidation). A positive E⁰cell means the reaction is feasible under standard conditions.
  • ΔG = −nFE. A negative ΔG (positive E⁰cell) means the reaction is spontaneous.

Redox titrations

  • Manganate(VII) is its own indicator: it is purple in solution and becomes colourless at the end point when Mn²⁺ forms.
  • Acidified dichromate(VI) turns from orange to green as Cr³⁺ forms. Iodine and thiosulfate use starch, which turns blue-black with iodine and loses that colour at the end point.

Exam tip: write the ion-electron half-equations first, balance the electrons, then combine them. The ratio of electrons sets the mole ratio in titration calculations.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks

For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Study Notes
content:
Sampling and Estimation

Populations, Samples, Statistics

A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Unbiased Variance

The estimator with divisor (n − 1) is the unbiased sample variance:

  • s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1)

Why n − 1: deviations are measured from x̄ rather than μ, slightly underestimating spread; the smaller divisor corrects it. At A2, state which estimator you are using — the unbiased one is the default.

Distribution of the Sample Mean

For a sample of size n from a population with mean μ and variance σ²:

  • E(x̄) = μ and Var(x̄) = σ²/n

Averaging shrinks spread — bigger samples give steadier estimates.

Central Limit Theorem

Whatever the population shape, for large n (rule of thumb n ≥ 30) the sample mean is approximately normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n). This is why the normal appears constantly in inference.

Example: population mean 50, s.d. 12, n = 36. Then x̄ ~ N(50, 4) and P(x̄ > 51) = P(Z > 0.5) = 0.3085.

Using x̄ to Estimate

Given sample data, estimate μ by x̄ and σ² by the unbiased s². When the population is normal, x̄ is exactly normal for any n — the CLT is only needed for non-normal populations.

Exam tips: distinguish σ²/σ (population) from s²/s (sample) in notation. Standard error means √(σ²/n) — smaller with larger n. Quote probabilities for x̄ with the variance divided by n; forgetting that division is the classic error.

Exam method: estimators and sample variance

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean μ. The unbiased estimate of the population variance is s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1), which divides by n − 1 rather than n. Using n gives the population variance of the sample, which tends to underestimate the true value.

When the sum of squared deviations is given, divide it by n − 1 directly. When the raw data are given, it is quicker to compute s² = (Σx² − n x̄²)/(n − 1).

A random sample gives each member of the population an equal chance of selection. Bias means the estimator does not equal the parameter on average, so the sample must be random to make the estimate reliable.

The standard error of the sample mean is σ/√n. It decreases as the sample size grows, so larger samples give more precise estimates.

Exam cue: Name the estimator and state whether it is unbiased, because the question often asks for both the value and the reason.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

title: Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development - Edexcel IAL AS-Level Biology Revision Notes
content:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development - Edexcel IAL AS-Level Biology Revision Notes

This revision note covers Edexcel International AS-Level Biology WBI12 Topic 3, examining the ultrastructure of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, microscopy, the cell cycle, mitosis, meiosis, gamete specialisation, fertilisation, stem cells, gene expression, epigenetics, inheritance, and variation.

Cell Ultrastructure and Organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, sharing common features such as a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and genetic material. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into hierarchical structures: specialised cells work together to form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs coordinate to form organ systems.

  • Eukaryotic cells possess membrane-bound organelles. The nucleus contains chromatin (DNA and histones) and directs cellular activities via transcription; the nucleolus synthesises ribosomal RNA (rRNA). Ribosomes (80S in eukaryotes, 70S in prokaryotes) are the sites of protein synthesis.
  • The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is studded with ribosomes and folds and processes proteins. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) synthesises and processes lipids and carbohydrates.
  • Mitochondria feature a double membrane, folded inner cristae, and a central matrix containing enzymes for aerobic respiration and ATP production.
  • Centrioles are cylindrical bundles of microtubules involved in spindle fibre formation during cell division. Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes to digest worn-out cell components or engulfed pathogens.
  • The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins received from the rER, adding carbohydrate chains to form glycoproteins, and packages them into vesicles for secretion or transport.
  • Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus. They possess a rigid cell wall made of peptidoglycan, an outer protective capsule, small loops of DNA called plasmids, a flagellum for locomotion, pili for adhesion, 70S ribosomes, and a single circular DNA molecule free in the cytoplasm.

Microscopy and Core Practical 5

Microscopy allows the visualisation of cellular ultrastructure. Magnification is how many times larger an image is compared to the actual specimen. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two separate points that are very close together.

  • Light microscopes use visible light and glass lenses, achieving a maximum resolution of about 200 nm and magnification up to x1500. Electron microscopes use a beam of electrons focused by electromagnets, achieving much higher resolution (transmission electron microscopes up to 0.1 nm; scanning electron microscopes up to 0.5 nm) due to the extremely short wavelength of electrons.
  • Staining specimens with coloured dyes (such as methylene blue or acetocarmine) increases contrast, making colourless or transparent structures visible under the light microscope.
  • Magnification formula: Magnification = Image size ÷ Actual size (I = A × M). Ensure units are consistent (convert mm to micrometres by multiplying by 1000).
  • Core Practical 5: Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells (such as squamous epithelial cells from the cheek). Use an eyepiece graticule calibrated with a stage micrometer to measure cell dimensions and understand scale.

Protein Transport and Secretion

Proteins destined for extracellular release or membrane insertion undergo a precise pathway involving transcription and translation at the rER. Ribosomes on the rER synthesise polypeptide chains, which pass into the cisterna of the rER where they are folded into their tertiary structure.

  • Transport vesicles bud off the rER containing the newly folded proteins and travel to the Golgi apparatus.
  • The vesicles fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus. Inside the Golgi, proteins are modified, such as by the addition of carbohydrate groups to form glycoproteins.
  • Modified proteins are packaged into secretory vesicles that bud off the trans face of the Golgi apparatus.
  • These secretory vesicles move towards and fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing their contents (such as extracellular enzymes) outside the cell via exocytosis.

The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, and G2) and mitotic division. Interphase involves cell growth, organelle replication, and DNA replication during the S phase.

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells from one parent cell, ensuring exact genetic replication for growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction.
  • The stages of mitosis are prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes align at the equator, attached to spindle fibres via centromeres), anaphase (sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles as centromeres divide), and telophase (nuclear envelopes reform around the two sets of chromosomes, which uncoil).
  • Core Practical 6: Prepare and stain a root tip squash (using acetic orcein) to observe the stages of mitosis under a light microscope.
  • Mitotic index calculation: Mitotic Index = (Number of cells in mitosis ÷ Total number of cells observed). Multiply by 100 to express as a percentage.

Meiosis and Genetic Variation

Meiosis is a form of nuclear division that halves the chromosome number, producing four genetically non-identical haploid gametes from a diploid parent cell, ensuring genetic stability across generations while introducing variation.

  • Independent assortment of chromosomes occurs during metaphase I, where homologous chromosome pairs line up randomly along the equator, resulting in diverse combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in daughter cells.
  • Crossing over of alleles between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes occurs during prophase I, breaking and rejoining chromatids to exchange genetic material and create new allele combinations.

Mammalian and Plant Gametes and Fertilisation

Gametes are specialised haploid cells adapted for sexual reproduction and successful fertilisation.

  • Sperm cells are specialised with an acrosome containing digestive enzymes to break through the egg layers, a flagellum for swimming powered by numerous mitochondria in the midpiece, and a haploid nucleus.
  • Egg cells (secondary oocytes) are large, non-motile cells containing food reserves, a haploid nucleus, cortical granules, and a protective extracellular glycoprotein coat called the zona pellucida.
  • Mammalian fertilisation involves the acrosome reaction, where enzymes released from the sperm acrosome digest the zona pellucida. This is followed by the fusion of the sperm and egg cell membranes. The cortical reaction then occurs: cortical granules release enzymes that harden the zona pellucida, preventing polyspermy. Finally, the sperm and egg haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote.
  • Flowering plant fertilisation begins with pollination, followed by the growth of a pollen tube down the style driven by a tube nucleus and directed by chemical signals. Upon reaching the micropyle of the ovule, the pollen tube enters the embryo sac. Two male gametes are discharged: one fuses with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote, and the other fuses with two polar nuclei to form a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (double fertilisation).

Stem Cells, Differentiation, and Gene Expression

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can divide by mitosis to produce more stem cells and cells that can differentiate into specialised cell types.

  • Potency definitions: Totipotent stem cells can differentiate into any cell type, including placental cells (e.g., zygote and early embryo cells up to the morula stage). Pluripotent stem cells (found in the blastocyst) can differentiate into almost all cell types of the body, but not placental cells. Multipotent stem cells can differentiate into a limited range of cell types within a specific tissue (e.g., adult bone marrow stem cells). A morula is a solid ball of cells formed by early cleavage divisions; a blastocyst is a hollow ball of cells with an inner cell mass containing pluripotent embryonic stem cells.
  • Society uses scientific knowledge of stem cells to make ethical and medical decisions regarding therapeutic cloning, regenerative medicine, and the moral status of embryos.
  • Cell specialisation occurs through differential gene expression. Although all cells in an organism contain the same genome, different cells transcribe different genes, producing active mRNA. This leads to the synthesis of specific proteins that determine cell structure (e.g., haemoglobin in red blood cells) and control cell processes.
  • Post-transcriptional changes to mRNA allow a single gene to give rise to more than one protein. During splicing, non-coding introns are removed and coding exons are joined in different combinations, producing multiple variant mRNA transcripts from one primary mRNA transcript.

Genetics, Epigenetics, and Variation

Phenotype is the observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from a complex interaction between genotype (genetic makeup) and the environment.

  • A locus is the specific physical location of a gene on a chromosome. Gene linkage refers to genes situated on the same chromosome; linked genes tend to be inherited together during meiosis unless separated by crossing over.
  • Epigenetic modification alters the activation of genes without changing the underlying DNA nucleotide sequence. DNA methylation (addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases) typically represses gene transcription by preventing transcription factor binding. Histone modification (such as acetylation or methylation of histone tails) alters chromatin packing, making DNA more or less accessible to RNA polymerase. Epigenetic modifications can be passed on following cell division, affecting daughter cells.
  • Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene (e.g., human ABO blood groups) or by polygenic inheritance, where multiple genes interact to determine a single characteristic. Polygenic inheritance combined with environmental influence gives rise to phenotypes that show continuous variation (e.g., human height or skin colour), forming a normal distribution curve.

Worked Examples

Calculate the actual size of a mitochondrion measuring 15 mm in an electron micrograph with a magnification of x30,000.

  • State the formula: Actual size = Image size ÷ Magnification.
  • Substitute values: Actual size = 15 mm ÷ 30,000.
  • Convert to micrometres: 15 mm = 15,000 micrometres.
  • Calculate actual size: 15,000 ÷ 30,000 = 0.5 micrometres.

Calculate the mitotic index of an onion root tip where 45 cells out of a total of 250 counted are undergoing mitosis.

  • State the formula: Mitotic Index = (Number of cells in mitosis ÷ Total number of cells) × 100.
  • Substitute values: (45 ÷ 250) × 100.
  • Calculate value: 0.18 × 100 = 18.0 percent.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing magnification and resolution: Students often state that electron microscopes magnify more when the key advantage is their superior resolving power due to electron wavelength.
  • Mixing up embryonic and adult stem cell potency: Remember that embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, whereas adult stem cells are multipotent.
  • Forgetting the cortical reaction: Students often omit the role of cortical granules in hardening the zona pellucida to prevent polyspermy during mammalian fertilisation.
  • Assuming phenotype is purely genetic: Always state that phenotype is the interaction between genotype and environmental factors.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain how the rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus work together to produce and secrete an extracellular enzyme. Answer: Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum translate mRNA to synthesise the polypeptide chain. The protein is folded inside the rER lumen and transported in vesicles to the cis face of the Golgi apparatus, where it is modified (e.g., carbohydrate added) and packaged into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane for exocytosis.
  2. Describe how meiosis contributes to genetic variation in gametes. Answer: Independent assortment of homologous chromosome pairs occurs during metaphase I, creating random combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Crossing over between non-sister chromatids occurs in prophase I, exchanging alleles and producing novel recombinant chromatids.
  3. Compare the potency of totipotent, pluripotent, and multipotent stem cells. Answer: Totipotent cells can differentiate into any cell type including placental cells. Pluripotent cells can differentiate into almost all body cell types except placenta. Multipotent cells can differentiate into a limited range of specialised cells within a specific tissue type.
  4. Explain how post-transcriptional changes allow one gene to code for multiple proteins. Answer: During mRNA processing, pre-mRNA undergoes splicing where non-coding introns are removed and exons are re-joined in different combinations, producing diverse mature mRNA transcripts and hence different protein isoforms.
  5. Distinguish between continuous and discontinuous variation with respect to genetic control. Answer: Discontinuous variation is controlled by a single gene or a few genes with little environmental influence, producing distinct categories. Continuous variation is controlled by polygenic inheritance (many genes) interacting with the environment, producing a continuous range of phenotypes.

Use these revision notes alongside past paper practice questions and core practical write-ups. Ensure you can recognise all listed eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell structures from electron micrographs before moving on to Topic 4 (Biodiversity and Conservation).

title: Information Representation — Study Notes
content:
`# Information Representation

Number Systems and Ranges

Unsigned binary with n bits stores 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. Two's complement represents negatives: the MSB has value −2ⁿ⁻¹.

Example: 8-bit two's complement of −5: 11111011 (−128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1).

SystemBaseDigits
Binary20–1
Hexadecimal160–9, A–F
BCD—4 bits per decimal digit

Binary Arithmetic

Add: 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1, 1+1+1=1 carry 1. Overflow happens when a result exceeds the word size.

Subtraction uses two's complement addition (A − B = A + (−B)).

Text

  • ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters, English only
  • Unicode: universal scripts; UTF-8 is variable-width (1–4 bytes)

Images and Sound

  • Bitmap: pixels with colour depth (bits per pixel). File size = width × height × depth.
  • Sound: sampling rate (Hz) × bit depth × duration × channels.
  • Resolution trade-off: fidelity vs size.

Compression

  • Lossless (ZIP, run-length encoding): exact reconstruction — required for text/code
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — smaller files

Example: RLE of AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C.

Exam tips: show working for two's complement conversions; state why compression type suits the data (text must be lossless).

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes — Study Notes
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18. Benzene is an arene. Its delocalised ring of six pi electrons makes it stable, so it reacts by electrophilic substitution rather than addition.

Structure and stability

  • Benzene is C₆H₆ with a planar ring. All six C–C bonds are the same length (0.139 nm), intermediate between single and double bonds.
  • The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with −360 kJ mol⁻¹ for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. The difference, about 150 kJ mol⁻¹, is the delocalisation energy.

Electrophilic substitution

  • The pi electron cloud is electron-rich, so the ring is a nucleophile and attacks electrophiles.
  • Nitration: concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 50 °C. The electrophile is NO₂⁺, and nitrobenzene forms.
  • Halogenation: Br₂ with an AlBr₃ or FeBr₃ halogen carrier. The carrier polarises Br₂ to give Br⁺.
  • Friedel–Crafts alkylation uses a haloalkane and AlCl₃ to add an alkyl group. Friedel–Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride and AlCl₃ to form a phenyl ketone.

Directing effects

  • Alkyl groups, including –CH₃, direct a second substituent to the 2- and 4- (ortho and para) positions.
  • A –NO₂ group directs to the 3- (meta) position.
  • –OH and –NH₂ are strongly activating: phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Side-chain oxidation

  • Hot, acidified KMnO₄ oxidises an alkyl side chain on the ring to a carboxylic acid group. Methylbenzene forms benzoic acid.

Exam tip: when describing a mechanism, show the electrophile, the arenium intermediate with its positive charge spread over the ring, and the loss of H⁺ to restore the delocalised ring.

title: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Study Notes
content:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 7. Respiration releases energy as ATP for muscle contraction. Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable, and the kidney is central to this. The topic links biochemistry to physiology.

Aerobic respiration

  • Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm. Glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules, with a small net gain of ATP and reduced NAD.
  • The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO₂.
  • The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix. It releases CO₂ and produces reduced NAD and FAD, and a little ATP.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation takes place on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons pass along the electron transport chain, a proton gradient forms, and ATP synthase makes ATP. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor.

Anaerobic respiration in mammals

  • Without oxygen, pyruvate is reduced to lactate. This regenerates NAD so that glycolysis can continue, but it gives far less ATP.
  • The oxygen debt is the extra oxygen needed after exercise to oxidise the lactate.

Respiratory quotient

  • RQ = volume of CO₂ produced ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. Carbohydrate gives an RQ of about 1.0 and fat gives about 0.7.

Muscle contraction

  • A sarcomere is the unit between two Z lines. Thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin slide past each other; the sarcomere shortens but the filaments do not change length.
  • Myosin heads bind to actin, and the power stroke pulls the actin along. ATP binds to myosin to break the link, and hydrolysis of ATP resets the head.
  • Calcium ions bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the binding sites on actin.

Homeostasis and the kidney

  • Negative feedback corrects a change from the set point. Receptors detect the change, and effectors bring the level back.
  • In the nephron, ultrafiltration occurs at the Bowman's capsule under high hydrostatic pressure. Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed by active transport in the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • The loop of Henle creates a salt gradient in the medulla. ADH increases the permeability of the collecting duct, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

Exam tip: when you describe the link between ADH and water reabsorption, follow the steps in order: osmoreceptors, ADH release, collecting duct permeability, water reabsorption.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: Deformation

Hooke's Law

Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Springs in series share the load (k_total < each); in parallel, k_total adds.

Stress, Strain, Young Modulus

  • Stress σ = F/A (Pa)
  • Strain ε = x/L (no unit)
  • Young modulus E = σ/ε (Pa) — a material property, independent of shape

Example: a wire of length 2 m, cross-section 1 × 10⁻⁶ m², extends 1 mm under 100 N: E = (F/A)/(x/L) = (10⁸)/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa — steel-like.

Force–Extension Graphs

  • Gradient of the linear region = k
  • Area under graph = elastic PE stored = ½Fx (for linear) = ½kx²
  • Beyond the yield point the wire deforms plastically and will not return

Breaking Stress

The maximum stress a material withstands — strong materials have high breaking stress, stiff materials have high E.

Exam tips: convert mm to m and mm² to m² before substituting; the area under a stress–strain graph gives energy per unit volume.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

Area formulae

Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Trapezium: ½(a + b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides. Circle: πr², and circumference 2πr. Leave answers in terms of π when asked, or round to the accuracy stated.

Volume and surface area

Prism volume is cross-sectional area × length. Cylinder volume is πr²h. Cone volume is ⅓πr²h and sphere volume is ⁴⁄₃πr³. Surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh. Sketch the solid and label radii and heights before you substitute.

Units and compound measures

Convert units before calculating: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Density is mass ÷ volume, and speed is distance ÷ time. Keep the units with the answer.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.
### Check yourself
Share £45 in the ratio 1 : 4. Find each share and check that they add up to £45. The shares are £9 and £36, because there are 5 parts and each is £9.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

title: Exam technique: Binomial Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For probabilities, the term C(n,k) p^k q^(n-k) written with values earns the method mark before evaluation. For mean and variance, np and npq quoted earn a mark each. For tail probabilities, the complement route stated earns the method mark over direct summation.
### Traps
Error: p and q swapped. Correction: track which outcome counts as success. Error: variance quoted as np. Correction: multiply by q as well. Error: continuity correction applied to exact binomial work. Correction: corrections belong to approximations only.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

Making accurate measurements

The SI base unit of length is the metre (m), and common multiples and submultiples are given in kilometres, centimetres and millimetres. A micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths to about 0.01 mm. A zero error is a reading that is not zero when it should be, and every reading must be corrected by it. Parallax error occurs when the eye is not directly in line with the scale, and it is avoided by reading the scale straight on.

Repeating a measurement and calculating the mean reduces random error. Time many oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number, to reduce the effect of reaction time on a stopwatch.

Exam tip: give a reading to the same precision as the instrument, and state the unit.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and Equilibrium

Free-Body Diagrams

Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Resolving Forces

Any force F at angle θ splits into F cos θ (along) and F sin θ (perpendicular).

Example: a 50 N pull at 30° above horizontal drags with 50 cos 30° ≈ 43.3 N horizontally.

An object on a slope of angle θ has components mg sin θ down the slope and mg cos θ into it.

Equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force is zero in every direction and the resultant moment is zero.

Moments and the Principle of Moments

Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.

For equilibrium: Σ clockwise moments = Σ anticlockwise moments.

Example: a 600 N child 2 m from a pivot balances an adult 1.2 m away: 600 × 2 = W × 1.2, so W = 1000 N.

Centre of Gravity

The point where the weight appears to act. For stable equilibrium the line of action must pass through the base.

Exam tips: take moments about the point with the most unknown forces; include the normal reaction and friction of any support, and check units of perpendicular distance.

title: Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics — Study Notes
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 6. Pathogens cause disease, and the immune system defends the body against them. Knowledge of microbes also allows antibiotics, vaccines and forensic DNA analysis.

Pathogens and antibiotics

  • Bacteria have 70S ribosomes, a cell wall made of peptidoglycan and circular DNA. Antibiotics such as penicillin block cell wall synthesis; others block 70S ribosomes.
  • Viruses have no cell structure of their own. They are obligate parasites that use the host cell machinery to replicate, so antibiotics do not act on them.
  • Antibiotic resistance spreads by natural selection. Bacteria with resistance alleles survive and reproduce, and the resistant population grows when antibiotics are overused.

Immune response

  • Phagocytes engulf pathogens by phagocytosis. Antigens on the pathogen surface are recognised as foreign.
  • B lymphocytes with complementary receptors undergo clonal selection and clonal expansion. Plasma cells produce antibodies, which bind to specific antigens.
  • T helper cells release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
  • Memory cells persist after an infection, so the secondary response is faster and larger.

Vaccination

  • A vaccine contains an antigen, often as a weakened or inactivated pathogen, or a harmless fragment. It stimulates a primary response without causing the disease.
  • Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated when a high proportion of the population is immune.

HIV

  • HIV attacks and destroys helper T cells. Over time the immune system fails, and the person develops AIDS.
  • The virus carries RNA and uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA copies inside the host cell.

Forensic DNA profiling

  • Short tandem repeats (STRs) are short sequences that repeat a variable number of times at specific loci. The number of repeats differs between people.
  • PCR amplifies the STR regions from a small sample. The products are separated by gel electrophoresis, where DNA moves towards the positive electrode according to size.

Exam tip: when you explain antibiotic resistance, describe the variation, the selection pressure and the change in the population over generations.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For conduction, free electrons named earn the explanation mark. For convection, rise of hot less-dense fluid earns the mark. For radiation, matt black as best emitter and absorber earns the mark; Q = mcT quoted earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: convection claimed in solids. Correction: conduction only in solids. Error: shiny surfaces called best emitters. Correction: matt black emits and absorbs best. Error: evaporation cooling unexplained. Correction: fastest molecules escape.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation Revision Notes
content:
Quick revision: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

Biology — AS. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 4. Plant tissues are arranged to transport water, move sugars and carry out photosynthesis. Biodiversity measures and conservation methods show how ecosystems are monitored and protected.

Key areas to revise

  • Plant tissues
  • Stomata and transpiration
  • Measuring biodiversity
  • Sampling
  • Conservation

Worked example

Calculate the index of diversity (D) for a habitat containing 5 species with individual counts of 10, 25, 5, 40 and 20. First find N, the total number of organisms: 10 + 25 + 5 + 40 + 20 = 100. Next, calculate n(n − 1) for each species: 10(9) = 90, 25(24) = 600, 5(4) = 20, 40(39) = 1560, 20(19) = 380. Sum these values to get the denominator: 90 + 600 + 20 + 1560 + 380 = 2650. Now calculate N(N − 1): 100 × 99 = 9900. Divide 9900 by 2650 to get D = 3.74.

Key points to remember

Plant cells possess a rigid cell wall made of cellulose microfibrils, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, amyloplasts for starch storage, a large permanent vacuole bounded by a tonoplast, plasmodesmata for cytoplasmic connection, pits, and a middle lamella acting as an adhesive layer. Animal cells lack cell walls, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, large vacuoles, tonoplasts, plasmodesmata, pits and middle lamellae.

Cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose molecules joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, where alternate glucose monomers are inverted by 180 degrees. Hydrogen bonds form between adjacent chains, grouping together to form microfibrils, which bundle into macrofibrils with secondary thickening to give high tensile strength to xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres.

Xylem vessels provide structural support and transport water and mineral ions upwards. Sclerenchyma fibres provide mechanical support with thick lignified walls. Phloem sieve tubes transport organic solutes by translocation. Roots, stems and leaves show distinct tissue arrangements visible under light microscopes using stained transverse section sections.

Sustainable use of plant materials involves replacing oil-based plastics with plant-based starches and fibres. Plants require inorganic ions: nitrates for amino acids and proteins, calcium ions for calcium pectate in the middle lamella, and magnesium ions to form chlorophyll. Deficiencies in these ions cause characteristic symptoms in plant growth.

Bacterial growth requires an appropriate temperature, moisture, pH, oxygen availability, and nutrient supply. Plants produce antimicrobial substances tested using aseptic techniques. Drug testing protocols have evolved from William Withering's digitalis soup to modern clinical trials involving double-blind trials, placebos, and three distinct phases.

Biodiversity includes species richness and genetic diversity measured via the heterozygosity index (number of heterozygotes divided by total individuals). The index of diversity formula is D = N(N − 1) / sum of n(n − 1). The Hardy-Weinberg equation (p squared + 2pq + q squared = 1 and p + q = 1) tracks allele frequency changes driven by mutation, natural selection, and reproductive isolation leading to speciation. Conservation employs zoos and seed banks via scientific research, captive breeding, reintroduction, and education.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

title: Exam technique: Astronomy and Cosmology
content:
### What earns the marks
For parallax, 1 over p in arcseconds earns the method mark with parsecs stated. For Hubble, v = H0 d quoted earns both marks. For evidence, CMB and redshift each linked to the model earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallax inverted. Correction: distance is 1 over angle. Error: standard candle reasoning skipped. Correction: period gives luminosity, brightness gives distance. Error: fusion claimed for white dwarfs. Correction: degeneracy pressure supports them.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For keys, primary identified as unique plus foreign as the link earns one mark each. For SQL, SELECT plus FROM plus WHERE in order earns each mark. For flat versus relational, one concrete drawback of duplication earns the discussion mark.
### Traps
Error: SELECT * claimed as precise. Correction: name the fields asked for. Error: primary key assigned to a non-unique field. Correction: keys must be unique. Error: flat file praised for large data. Correction: duplication corrupts it.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

title: Abstract Data Types — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Abstract Data Types

Computer Science — A2. An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Key areas to revise

  • What is an ADT?
  • Linked Lists
  • Stacks and Queues
  • Binary Search Trees
  • Hash Tables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). State which item is returned and what remains. The result is A, and the queue now holds B.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.
### Method marks
Pressure = force ÷ area, and the area must be in m² for the answer in pascals. Density = mass ÷ volume. For an irregular solid, find the volume from the displacement of water.
### Explain, do not just name
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because the weight of the column above increases. Write p = hρg and name each symbol in the explanation.
### Traps
Using cm² without converting: 1 cm² = 10^-4 m². Forgetting that the pressure in a fluid at a given depth acts equally in all directions.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.
### Worked example
Two triangles have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and a second triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The second triangle is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Each length is multiplied by 2, so each area is multiplied by 2² = 4. If the lengths are scaled by 2.5, the areas are scaled by 6.25.
### Check yourself
Two triangles have all three angles equal. Are they similar, congruent, or neither? They are similar, because equal angles give equal shape but not necessarily equal size. They are congruent only if the side lengths also match, which you check using SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sampling and Estimation

Mathematics — A2. A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Key areas to revise

  • Populations, Samples, Statistics
  • Unbiased Variance
  • Distribution of the Sample Mean
  • Central Limit Theorem
  • Using x̄ to Estimate

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. Circuits

Current and Charge

I = Q/t — charge per second, in amperes. Conventional current flows + to − (electrons drift the other way).

I = nAvq links microscopic drift to macroscopic current (n = carrier density).

Voltage and Power

  • V = W/Q (joules per coulomb)
  • P = VI = I²R = V²/R

Resistance and Resistivity

R = V/I; R = ρL/A. Resistivity ρ is a material property (Ω m). Metals' resistance rises with temperature; thermistors' falls (NTC).

Example: a wire 2 m long, 0.5 mm² cross-section, ρ = 5 × 10⁻⁷: R = 2 Ω.

Series and Parallel

  • Series: same current, R_total = R₁ + R₂ + …
  • Parallel: same voltage, 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …

EMF and Internal Resistance

ε = I(R + r) — some voltage is 'lost' inside the battery. Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as load current rises.

Potential Dividers

V_out = V_in × R₂/(R₁ + R₂). Used with LDRs/thermistors to make sensor circuits.

Exam tips: redraw messy networks with clean junctions; always account for internal resistance in 'maximum power' questions.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch-execute cycle, each stage in order earns stepwise credit. For CPU parts, control unit versus ALU roles stated earn one mark each. For sensors, the named sensor matched to its use earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: RAM and ROM roles swapped. Correction: RAM is working memory, ROM holds boot code. Error: control unit claimed to compute. Correction: the ALU computes, the CU coordinates. Error: stages given out of order. Correction: fetch, decode, execute, store.

title: Exam technique: Databases and Data Definition
content:
### What earns the marks
For DDL vs DML, purpose decides: structure changes are DDL, row changes are DML. For transactions, atomicity (all-or-nothing rollback) and durability (surviving crashes) each earn a mark when tied to the failure. For concurrency, the lost-update mechanism described earns the mark before locking is prescribed.
### Traps
Error: SELECT classed as DDL. Correction: queries read rows, so DML. Error: half-applied transfers accepted. Correction: atomicity rolls them back. Error: views claimed as backups. Correction: views are access windows, not copies.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.

title: Exam technique: Bearings and Loci
content:
### What earns the marks
For bearings, measure earns marks for the angle taken clockwise from north with three figures in the final answer: add leading zeros (075, 008). For back bearings, the 180-degree adjustment stated earns the method mark. For scale drawings, the scale multiplication shown earns a mark independent of arithmetic. For loci, construct earns marks for the correct locus type (circle, bisector, parallel pair) drawn and labelled.
### Traps
Error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong datum. Correction: north line up, clockwise. Error: dropping leading zeros. Correction: three figures always. Error: one angle bisector instead of the pair for intersecting lines. Correction: two lines cross, so two bisectors. Error: dividing by the scale instead of multiplying. Correction: real distances exceed map distances.
### Worked example
A boat sails from A on a bearing of 065° and reaches B. Its back bearing from B to A is 065 + 180 = 245°. Draw the north line at both points, because the angles at the two north lines are alternate and the back bearing follows from that.
### Check yourself
Describe the locus of points exactly 3 cm from a fixed point P, and the locus of points equidistant from two points A and B. The first is a circle of radius 3 cm centred on P. The second is the perpendicular bisector of the line AB. State both in words and draw them with compasses and a ruler.
