title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a. ### Check yourself Solve 5(y + 1) = 2y + 13 and verify your answer. Expand to 5y + 5 = 2y + 13, so 3y = 8 and y = 8/3. Check: 5(8/3 + 1) = 5 × 11/3 = 55/3, and 2 × 8/3 + 13 = 16/3 + 39/3 = 55/3.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

title: Molecules, Transport and Health Revision Notes
content:
Molecules, Transport and Health AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International AS Level Biology specification, covering biological molecules, transport mechanisms, gas exchange, and cardiovascular health.

Water and Its Biological Importance

Water is essential for life due to its chemical properties. It acts as an important solvent in transport because of its dipole nature, where the oxygen atom has a partial negative charge and hydrogen atoms have partial positive charges. This allows polar molecules and ionic substances to dissolve and be transported easily in blood and plant sap.

  • Dipole nature: polar molecule with uneven charge distribution.
  • Solvent properties: allows chemical reactions and transport of dissolved ions and molecules.

Carbohydrates and Sugars

Carbohydrates exist as monosaccharides, disaccharides, and polysaccharides. Monosaccharides include glucose, fructose, and galactose. They join via condensation reactions, forming glycosidic bonds and releasing water molecules, creating disaccharides such as maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose), and lactose (glucose + galactose), and polysaccharides such as glycogen, amylose, and amylopectin. Glycosidic bonds can be split through hydrolysis reactions using water molecules. Amylose has a helical structure formed by 1,4-glycosidic bonds, while amylopectin is branched with 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds, making both suited for energy storage in plants. Glycogen is highly branched with many 1,4 and 1,6-glycosidic bonds for rapid hydrolysis to release glucose in animals.

  • Monosaccharides: single sugar units like glucose, fructose, galactose.
  • Disaccharides: two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond via condensation.
  • Polysaccharides: long chains of monosaccharides acting as energy stores (starch, glycogen).
  • Hydrolysis: breaks glycosidic bonds using water.

Core Practical 1: Estimating Sugar and Starch Concentrations

Semi-quantitative methods use colour standards to estimate concentrations. For reducing sugars, add Benedict's reagent to the sample, heat in a water bath, and observe the colour change from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red. Compare against standard known concentrations. For starch, add iodine dissolved in potassium iodide solution and observe the colour change from browny-orange to blue-black, comparing with standard concentrations.

  • Reducing sugars test: Benedict's reagent, heat, observe colour change from blue to brick-red.
  • Starch test: iodine solution, observe colour change from orange-brown to blue-black.
  • Colour standards: compare unknowns against solutions of known concentrations.

Lipids and Triglyceride Synthesis

Triglycerides are synthesised by condensation reactions between one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, forming ester bonds. Saturated lipids contain only single carbon-carbon bonds in their hydrocarbon chains, whereas unsaturated lipids contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds, causing kinks that prevent tight packing.

  • Triglyceride: 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids linked by 3 ester bonds.
  • Saturated fatty acids: no carbon-carbon double bonds, solid at room temperature.
  • Unsaturated fatty acids: contain carbon-carbon double bonds, liquid at room temperature.

Proteins and Amino Acids

Proteins are polymers made of amino acid monomers. An amino acid consists of a central carbon atom bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a variable R group. Amino acids join by peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions to create polypeptides. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. This determines the secondary structure (alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets held by hydrogen bonds), which further folds into the three-dimensional tertiary structure held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, and hydrophobic interactions. Globular proteins, such as haemoglobin, are folded into spherical, soluble shapes with hydrophilic groups on the outside, and function in metabolic roles. Fibrous proteins, such as collagen, form long, strong, insoluble fibres made of triple helices with cross-linking, providing structural strength.

  • Amino acid structure: central carbon, amine group, carboxyl group, hydrogen, R group.
  • Peptide bond: formed between amine and carboxyl groups via condensation.
  • Primary structure: amino acid sequence.
  • Secondary structure: alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet formed by hydrogen bonding.
  • Tertiary structure: 3D folding stabilised by hydrogen, ionic, disulfide, and hydrophobic interactions.
  • Globular vs Fibrous: globular is soluble and spherical (haemoglobin); fibrous is structural and insoluble (collagen).

Enzymes and Biological Catalysts

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up metabolic reactions by lowering the activation energy without being used up. They are globular proteins with a specific active site whose three-dimensional shape is complementary to a specific substrate. Intracellular enzymes catalyse reactions inside cells, while extracellular enzymes are secreted to catalyse reactions outside cells. Enzyme action depends on temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, and substrate concentration.

  • Mechanism: substrate binds to active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
  • Activation energy: lowered by enzymes, increasing the rate of reaction.
  • Specificity: determined by the precise 3D shape of the active site.

Core Practical 4: Investigating Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

To investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, or substrate concentration on the initial rate of reaction, measure the formation of products or disappearance of substrate over time using continuous or initial rate sampling.

  • Independent variables: temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration.
  • Dependent variable: initial rate of reaction, calculated from the linear steepest part of a product against time graph.
  • Control variables: keep all non-tested variables constant.

Mass Transport and Circulation

Many animals have a heart and circulation because mass transport is necessary to overcome the limitations of diffusion in meeting the metabolic requirements of large, multicellular organisms with small surface area to volume ratios. Blood vessels have specific adaptations: arteries have thick walls with elastic tissue and smooth muscle to withstand high pressure from the heart; veins have thinner walls, wider lumens, and valves to prevent backflow of blood under low pressure; capillaries have walls that are one cell thick to provide a short diffusion distance for exchanging substances with tissues.

  • Diffusion limits: inadequate for deep body tissues in large organisms.
  • Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls to withstand high pulse pressure.
  • Veins: thin walls, large lumen, valves to prevent backflow.
  • Capillaries: single endothelial cell layer for rapid exchange.

The Mammalian Heart and Cardiac Cycle

The mammalian heart pumps blood through a double circulatory system. The cardiac cycle consists of three stages: atrial systole, where the atria contract and push blood into the ventricles through open atrioventricular valves; ventricular systole, where the ventricles contract, increasing pressure and closing atrioventricular valves while forcing semilunar valves open to push blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery; and cardiac diastole, where all chambers relax, and blood passively fills the atria and ventricles. Major blood vessels include the vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein, and aorta. Dissection of a mammalian heart allows the identification of atria, ventricles, valves, and thick-walled muscular left ventricles compared to thin-walled right ventricles.

  • Atrial systole: atria contract, ventricles relax, atrioventricular valves open.
  • Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, atrioventricular valves close, semilunar valves open.
  • Cardiac diastole: heart chambers relax, blood flows into atria and ventricles.

Gas Exchange and Fick's Law

Gas exchange surfaces have a large surface area to volume ratio, a short diffusion distance due to being thin, and a steep concentration gradient maintained by ventilation and blood flow. The rate of diffusion depends on these properties and is calculated using Fick's Law of Diffusion: Rate is proportional to (surface area × concentration difference) ÷ thickness of membrane. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange through millions of alveoli providing a massive surface area, capillary walls that are one cell thick, and a constant supply of blood to maintain the concentration gradient.

  • Fick's Law: Rate proportional to Area × Concentration Difference ÷ Thickness.
  • Alveoli adaptations: thin squamous epithelium, extensive capillary network, moist lining.

Haemoglobin and Oxygen Transport

Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four polypeptide chains, each containing a haem group with an iron ion. It transports oxygen by forming oxyhaemoglobin. The oxygen dissociation curve shows the relationship between percentage saturation of haemoglobin and partial pressure of oxygen. The sigmoidal curve occurs because the binding of the first oxygen molecule alters the protein's tertiary structure, making it easier for subsequent oxygen molecules to bind (positive cooperativity). The Bohr effect describes how an increase in carbon dioxide partial pressure decreases haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the right and unloading more oxygen in respiring tissues. Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, shifting its dissociation curve to the left, allowing it to extract oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta.

  • Haemoglobin structure: 4 polypeptide subunits, each with an iron-containing haem group.
  • Oxygen dissociation curve: sigmoidal shape due to cooperative binding.
  • Bohr effect: high carbon dioxide concentration shifts curve right, increasing oxygen unloading.
  • Fetal haemoglobin: higher oxygen affinity, curve shifts left compared to adult.

Cardiovascular Disease (CVD) and Risk Factors

Cardiovascular disease often begins with endothelial dysfunction, where damage to the arterial lining leads to an inflammatory response. White blood cells accumulate, absorbing cholesterol to form fatty streaks, which develop into atheromas or plaques. Plaque formation narrows arteries and raises blood pressure. The blood clotting process is triggered when damage exposes tissue factor; thromboplastin is released, catalysing the conversion of prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin. Thrombin then catalyses the soluble protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin fibres, which mesh with platelets to form a blood clot, potentially blocking coronary arteries and causing myocardial infarction.

  • Atherosclerosis sequence: endothelial damage, inflammatory response, plaque/atheroma formation, raised blood pressure.
  • Blood clotting cascade: thromboplastin released, prothrombin converted to thrombin, fibrinogen converted to fibrin.
  • Risk factors: genetics, high-fat/salt diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking, physical inactivity.

Health Studies and Risk Evaluation

Epidemiological data on illness and mortality rates help determine health risks. It is vital to distinguish between correlation and causation and to recognise conflicting evidence. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider sample selection, sample size, and whether the data collected is both valid and reliable. People's perception of risks often differs from actual risks due to underestimating or overestimating lifestyle factors. Body mass index (BMI) is calculated as mass (kg) divided by height squared (m squared), and waist-to-hip ratio are obesity indicators used alongside diet, exercise, and smoking cessation to reduce coronary heart disease risk.

  • BMI formula: mass (kg) ÷ height squared (m squared).
  • Correlation vs causation: correlation does not prove one variable causes another.
  • Study design evaluation: check for representative sample size, control of variables, validity, and reliability.

Treatments for Cardiovascular Disease (CVD)

Treatments for cardiovascular disease carry both benefits and risks. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure but can cause dizziness and fatigue. Statins lower blood cholesterol by inhibiting liver enzymes but may cause muscle pain and liver damage. Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors reduce blood clotting but increase the risk of uncontrolled bleeding from injuries.

  • Antihypertensives: reduce blood pressure; risk of dizziness and nausea.
  • Statins: lower blood cholesterol; risk of muscle damage and liver inflammation.
  • Anticoagulants and platelet inhibitors: reduce clotting risk; risk of haemorrhage.

Worked Examples

Calculating BMI: A person has a mass of 70 kg and a height of 1.75 m.

  • Square the height: 1.75 × 1.75 = 3.0625.
  • Divide mass by squared height: 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.86.
  • State the unit: 22.86 kg per m squared.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing condensation and hydrolysis: condensation joins molecules and releases water; hydrolysis splits molecules using water.
  • Stating correlation is proof of causation: correlation only shows a relationship, not a causal mechanism.
  • Forgetting the units in Fick's Law or BMI calculations: always include correct units in answers.
  • Confusing adult and fetal haemoglobin curves: fetal curve is to the left of the adult curve, indicating higher oxygen affinity at lower partial pressures.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how the structure of an artery is related to its function. Answer: Arteries have thick walls containing collagen for strength, elastic tissue to stretch and recoil under high pressure, and smooth muscle to constrict and dilate the lumen.
  2. Explain why high levels of LDL cholesterol increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Answer: LDLs transport cholesterol to tissues where they can deposit it in artery walls, leading to atheroma formation, narrowing of arteries, and increased blood pressure.
  3. Explain the significance of the Bohr effect in actively respiring tissues. Answer: Respiring tissues produce high levels of carbon dioxide, which lowers pH, causing haemoglobin to release more oxygen more readily.
  4. Explain how glycogen's structure relates to its function as an energy storage molecule in animals. Answer: Glycogen is branched, allowing rapid hydrolysis to release glucose monomers, and is insoluble so it does not affect water potential.
  5. State the role of thromboplastin in blood clotting. Answer: Thromboplastin is released from damaged tissue and catalyses the conversion of prothrombin into thrombin.

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper practice questions. Revise enzymes, gas exchange, and transport mechanisms next.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

HTML, CSS and the client-server model

HTML defines the structure and content of a web page using tags, such as headings and paragraphs. CSS controls how that content looks, including colour, layout and font size. Keeping structure and style separate means one stylesheet can change the appearance of many pages.

In the client-server model, a client such as a browser sends a request, and a server returns the requested resources. When a web page is requested, the browser uses the domain name to look up the server's IP address through the Domain Name System (DNS), then sends the request over HTTP or HTTPS.

Exam tip: describe a web request as a sequence: DNS lookup, request, server response, rendering in the browser.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Check yourself Trace a queue after enqueue(A), enqueue(B), dequeue(). title: Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment
content:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI14, Topic 5. Energy enters most ecosystems as light, is fixed by photosynthesis and then passes along food chains. Nutrients cycle, and human activity can disrupt those cycles.

  • Photosynthesis and limiting factors
  • Energy transfer through trophic levels
  • Nutrient cycles
  • Human impact

Key areas to revise

  • Photosynthesis overall reaction (5.1): light energy splits water strong bonds, hydrogen combines with carbon dioxide to form glucose, releasing oxygen.
  • Photophosphorylation of ADP (5.2): requires energy; ATP hydrolysis provides immediate biological energy.
  • Light-dependent reactions (5.3): light excites chlorophyll electrons, generating ATP, reducing NADP via cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and producing oxygen through water photolysis.
  • Light-independent reactions (5.4): carbon dioxide reduction via Calvin cycle using GP, GALP, RuBP, and RUBISCO; products form simple sugars used in respiration and biological molecules (polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids).
  • Chloroplast structure (5.5): thylakoids, grana, stroma, and membranes related to photosynthetic roles.
  • Spectra and chromatography (5.6, 5.7): absorption spectrum, action spectrum, pigment separation, and Rf value identification.
  • Core Practical 10 (5.8): investigating light intensity, wavelength, temperature, and carbon dioxide availability on aquatic plant photosynthesis rates.
  • Primary productivity (5.9): GPP, NPP, and plant respiration relationship where NPP = GPP − R.
  • Trophic transfer (5.10): calculating biomass and energy transfer efficiency between trophic levels as (energy transferred ÷ energy intake) × 100%.
  • Ecological terms (5.11): population, community, habitat, and ecosystem definitions.
  • Abiotic and biotic factors (5.12): controlling numbers and distribution of organisms.
  • Niche concept (5.13): accounts for organism distribution and abundance.
  • Core Practical 11 (5.14): quadrats, transects, distribution, abundance, and abiotic factor measurement.
  • Succession (5.15): stages from colonisation to climax community.
  • Climate change evidence (5.16): carbon dioxide levels, temperature records, pollen in peat bogs, dendrochronology, correlations, and causal relationships.
  • Anthropogenic causes (5.17): greenhouse gases and greenhouse effect.
  • Carbon cycle application (5.18): methods to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide.
  • Extrapolation and models (5.19): predictions, climate models, and limitations.
  • Climate change effects (5.20): changing rainfall patterns, seasonal cycles, distribution, development, and lifecycles.
  • Enzyme activity and temperature (5.21): Q10 calculation and metabolic impact.
  • Core Practical 12 (5.22): temperature effects on organism development (seedling growth, brine shrimp hatch rates) with ethical considerations.
  • Evolution (5.23): gene mutation and natural selection changing allele frequencies.
  • Speciation (5.24): isolation reducing gene flow leading to allopatric or sympatric speciation.
  • Scientific conclusions (5.25): evaluating controversial issues like climate change actions based on sources.
  • Conservation (5.26): reforestation, sustainable resources, and biofuels managing human needs and conservation conflicts.

Worked example

Calculate the net primary productivity if gross primary productivity is 14000 kJ m⁻² year⁻² and plant respiration is 5500 kJ m⁻² year⁻². Using NPP = GPP − R, NPP = 14000 − 5500 = 8500 kJ m⁻² year⁻².

Key points to remember

Examiners frequently note that students confuse GPP and NPP; always subtract plant respiration (R) from gross primary productivity to find net primary productivity. When calculating ecological efficiencies, ensure units match across trophic levels and multiply by 100 to yield a percentage. Remember that allopatric speciation requires geographical isolation, whereas sympatric speciation occurs within the same habitat via behavioural, temporal, or anatomical isolation. When discussing climate change evidence, distinguish between correlation and causal relationships explicitly in your exam answers.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

The Principle of Superposition

When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Coherence and Path Difference

Two sources are coherent if they share frequency and constant phase difference. Maxima occur where path difference = nλ; minima where it = (n + ½)λ.

Double-Slit (Young)

Fringe spacing x = λD/a (D = slit–screen distance, a = slit separation).

Example: λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m, a = 0.5 mm: x = 2.4 mm.

Red light gives wider fringes than blue; smaller slit separation also widens fringes.

Diffraction Grating

d sin θ = nθth order maximum. More slits → sharper, brighter maxima. The number of visible orders is the largest n with sin θ ≤ 1.

Example: 600 lines/mm → d = 1.67 μm; for 500 nm light, n_max = 3.

Stationary Waves

Two identical waves travelling opposite directions (e.g. wave + reflection) create nodes (no movement) and antinodes (max movement), spaced λ/2 apart. Strings and closed pipes resonate at f₁ = v/2L (fundamental) and harmonics.

Exam tips: always compute d from 'lines per mm' first; state 'path difference = nλ' explicitly in explain-the-fringe questions.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

title: Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Study Notes
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI12, Topic 4. Plant tissues are arranged to transport water, move sugars and carry out photosynthesis. Biodiversity measures and conservation methods show how ecosystems are monitored and protected.

Plant tissues

  • Xylem vessels are dead, hollow cells with lignified walls. They carry water and mineral ions up the plant.
  • Phloem sieve tube elements have sieve plates and few organelles. They carry sucrose and amino acids in both directions.
  • Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf. Sclerenchyma gives support through thick lignified walls.

Stomata and transpiration

  • Stomata open when guard cells become turgid by taking in water. They close when the guard cells become flaccid.
  • Transpiration is faster in high temperatures, dry air and wind, because these increase the water potential gradient out of the leaf.
  • Xerophytes reduce water loss with a thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata and hairs.

Measuring biodiversity

  • Species richness is the number of different species in a habitat.
  • Simpson's index of diversity is D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², where n is the number of individuals of each species and N is the total. For two species with 10 individuals each, D = 1 − (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.50.

Sampling

  • Quadrats estimate the abundance of sessile or slow-moving organisms, often as percentage cover.
  • Transects show how species change along an environmental gradient.
  • Mark-release-recapture estimates the population of a mobile animal with the Lincoln index: N = (n₁ × n₂) ÷ m₂. Here n₁ is the number marked in the first sample, n₂ the number caught in the second, and m₂ the number of marked animals in the second sample.

Conservation

  • In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, for example in national parks and reserves.
  • Ex situ conservation keeps species outside their habitat, for example in seed banks and zoos.
  • The IUCN Red List classifies species by their conservation status.

Exam tip: when you are asked to explain a transpiration result, relate it to water potential and the diffusion gradient out of the stomata.

title: Ethics and AI — Study Notes
content:
`# Ethics and AI

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

Ownership, licensing and AI bias

Copyright gives the creator legal protection over how their software and other original work is copied, distributed and changed. Copying software without permission is a breach of copyright and can be illegal. Open source software is released under licences that allow others to use, study and modify it, often on the condition that changes are shared in the same way.

An AI system learns from its training data. If that data over-represents some groups or reflects past prejudice, the system's outputs can be biased, and it may treat people unfairly without anyone intending it. Developers can reduce this by checking the training data and testing the system on a wide range of cases.

Exam tip: link each ethical point to a consequence for a real user, such as a person losing a job or a loan being refused unfairly.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴. Add the indices in the numerator to get 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴, then subtract the indices to get 2⁴ = 16. Check by a second method: 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256, and 256 ÷ 16 = 16. Both routes agree.

Fractional and negative powers

A negative index means a reciprocal: 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25. A fractional index with denominator n means an nth root: 16^(1/2) = 4, and 27^(2/3) = (27^(1/3))² = 3² = 9. Taking the root first and then raising the result to the power keeps the arithmetic small.

  • Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1, so 7⁰ = 1.
  • Do not multiply the base by the index: (2³)² = 2⁶, not 2⁵ and not 6.
  • Standard form for a number between 0 and 1 uses a negative index: 0.00047 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. TLS uses asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key at the start of a session.

A digital certificate binds a public key to an organisation. A trusted certificate authority signs it so that a browser can check the site's identity.

Exam tip: explain the hybrid approach: asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the bulk data.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

The number sets

Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on; integers add zero and negatives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, 1 and themselves.

Prime factors and HCF/LCM

Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree. The highest common factor uses the common primes at their lowest powers; the lowest common multiple uses every prime at its highest power. Venn diagrams sort numbers by properties such as even, square or prime.

Square roots and cube roots

The square root of a number is positive or negative: √16 = 4 but x² = 16 gives x = ±4. Check whether a root is exact or needs a calculator, and give a non-exact answer to the accuracy asked.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

Equivalent fractions and simplifying

Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number. Simplify by dividing both by their highest common factor. Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Find the lowest common denominator, rewrite each fraction over it, then add or subtract the numerators only. Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

Percentages

To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply by the decimal equivalent: 15% of 240 is 0.15 × 240 = 36. Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. Repeated percentage change multiplies by one plus the multiplier each time, so 5% increase twice is × 1.05 × 1.05.

title: Exam technique: Robotics & AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3, the examiner needs to see explanations, descriptions and justifications. For example, to answer a question on automated systems, a student must explain how sensors, processors and actuators work together, and describe how this relates to real-world applications. For AI characteristics, a student must justify how a particular characteristic, such as learning or problem-solving, is used in a given scenario.
### Traps
A common mistake is to confuse supervised and unsupervised machine learning. Correction: supervised learning uses labelled data, while unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data. Another mistake is to overlook the importance of ethics in AI development. Correction: students must consider the potential biases and consequences of AI systems. A third mistake is to fail to provide concrete examples when describing AI applications. Correction: students must tie each AI characteristic to a specific step in the scenario.
### Memory hooks
To remember the components of a robotic system, use the mnemonic SPAP: Sensors, Processors, Actuators and Power. To recall the types of machine learning, use the phrase SUR: Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement. When evaluating the benefits and concerns of robotics, consider the acronym PJD: Precision, Job displacement and Danger.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer the relevant questions. Students should allocate their time based on the mark allocation for each question, and make sure to leave time for review and revision.

title: Exam technique: Angles and Polygons
content:
### What earns the marks
For angle-chasing, justify earns marks for each reason stated alongside the value: angles on a straight line, vertically opposite, alternate, corresponding, and the circle theorems by name. For cyclic quadrilaterals, quote earns the theorem (opposite angles sum to 180) before the equation. For polygons, the formula (n - 2) x 180 stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: using adjacent instead of opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral. Correction: mark the diagram first. Error: answering each interior angle when the sum is asked. Correction: only divide at the very end. Error: treating any triangle in a circle as right-angled. Correction: the right angle needs the diameter as hypotenuse.
### Worked example
The sum of the interior angles of an n-sided polygon is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon (n = 8), each interior angle is 6 × 180 ÷ 8 = 135°, so each exterior angle is 45°. The exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°, which gives a quick check: 8 × 45 = 360.
### Check yourself
Find the interior angle of a regular hexagon. Use (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°. Explain why the exterior angle is 60° and why this matches 360 ÷ 6.

### Worked example

title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, cyber security threats and protection, malware, online safety, digital currency, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Cyber security

Cyber security protects data, systems and users from attack. A vulnerability is a weakness an attack can use; a threat is what exploits it.

  • Vulnerabilities: default or weak passwords, unpatched software, misconfigured access rights, unsecured or public Wi-Fi, removable media (memory sticks), insider threat, unencrypted data in transit.
  • Malware: virus (needs a host file and replicates when that file runs), worm (self-spreads across a network), trojan (disguised as useful software), spyware (records activity), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), adware.
  • Social engineering: phishing (fake email or site asks for details), pharming (malicious redirect via DNS or the hosts file), blagging (invented story), shoulder surfing, brute-force and dictionary attacks.
  • Technical attacks: interception / packet sniffing on an unsecured network, SQL injection (malicious input typed into a query field), denial of service and DDoS (flooding a service so it cannot respond), session hijacking.

Protection: strong unique passwords plus 2FA; biometric authentication (fingerprint, face); encryption so intercepted data is unreadable (plaintext is turned into ciphertext with a key — HTTPS/TLS does this on websites); firewalls filtering traffic by IP address and port; anti-malware that scans, blocks and quarantines; patching and updates; user access levels so staff reach only what they need; regular backups; user training; penetration testing to find holes first.

Answer shape: name the threat precisely (pharming is not phishing), then give the matched defence — pharming → keep DNS servers and hosts files secure and check HTTPS certificates.

4. Digital currency

A digital currency exists only in electronic form. A cryptocurrency (for example Bitcoin) is a decentralised digital currency secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain.

  • Blockchain: a distributed ledger — every node holds a copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an old record breaks the chain and is rejected by the network.
  • Keys and wallets: the owner holds a public key (the address others pay to) and a private key (proves ownership and signs a payment). A wallet stores these keys — lose the private key and the money is gone.
  • Transactions: broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and added to a block; the verifier (miner) is rewarded. No bank or central authority is involved.

Advantages: quick international transfers, low transaction fees, no central authority to fail or censor, a transparent ledger, and coins cannot be counterfeited. Disadvantages: the value is very volatile, payments are irreversible, mining uses large amounts of energy, it appeals to criminals and ransomware demands, it needs internet access and technical care, and there is little consumer protection if a wallet is lost or stolen.

5. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

6. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

7. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
