  • Fields from Currents
  • Electromagnetic Induction

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

title: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology
content:
Quick revision: Coordination, Response and Gene Technology

Biology — A2. Edexcel IAL Biology WBI15, Topic 8. Nervous and hormonal systems coordinate the body, and plants respond to light and gravity using hormones. Gene technology uses enzymes to cut, join and copy DNA for medicine, research and agriculture.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS, relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS, and motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors, all featuring Schwann cells wrapping around axons to form a myelin sheath that insulates the axon.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors such as muscles or glands to respond to a stimulus by generating action potentials that travel to neuromuscular junctions or gland endings.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc consists of a receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone in the grey matter of the spinal cord, motor neurone, and effector, with white matter containing myelinated axons ascending and descending to the brain.
  • 8.4 Action potentials are conducted along an axon via depolarisation caused by voltage-gated sodium ion channels opening and sodium ions rushing in, followed by repolarisation caused by voltage-gated potassium ion channels opening and potassium ions rushing out.
  • 8.5 Myelination allows saltatory conduction where the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, drastically increasing the speed of nerve impulse transmission.
  • 8.6 Synapses transmit impulses between neurones using neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine diffusing across the synaptic cleft, and the pupil dilates via radial muscles in dim light and contracts via circular muscles in bright light.
  • 8.7 Drugs affect nerve transmission such as nicotine mimicking acetylcholine, lidocaine blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, cobra venom blocking acetylcholine receptors, L-DOPA acting as a dopamine precursor to treat Parkinson's disease, and MDMA increasing neurotransmitter release.
  • 8.8 Rods in the retina detect light when photon absorption converts cis-retinal to trans-retinal, causing rhodopsin to break down into opsin and retinal, closing sodium cation channels, stopping sodium influx, and hyperpolarising the rod cell to initiate action potentials in optic neurones.
  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is harmless, preventing unnecessary energy expenditure.
  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (cranial and spinal nerves).
  • 8.11 Plant responses are controlled by phytochrome which changes form in red and far-red light affecting transcription, auxin (IAA) which causes cell elongation and affects transcription, and gibberellins which stimulate seed germination by promoting amylase transcription.
  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains by measuring starch breakdown under varying conditions.
  • 8.13 Coordination in animals is brought about through rapid, targeted nervous control and slower, chemical hormonal control travelling in the blood.
  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres control conscious thought and sensory processing, the hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, the pituitary gland secretes hormones, the cerebellum coordinates balance and voluntary movement, and the medulla oblongata controls involuntary functions like heart rate and breathing.
  • 8.15 Medical imaging techniques include MRI and CT for structural detail, fMRI for localized brain activity during tasks, and PET for metabolic activity using radioactive tracers.
  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals cause ill health, such as a shortage of dopamine in Parkinson's disease and low serotonin levels in depression, informing the design of new drugs.
  • 8.17 Therapeutic drugs and proteins can be produced using genetically modified organisms including transgenic plants, animals, and microorganisms like bacteria and yeast.
  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is produced by using restriction endonucleases to cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sites to yield sticky or blunt ends, and DNA ligase to join the sugar-phosphate backbones of the DNA insert and vector.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into host cells using vectors such as plasmids, bacteriophages, or through methods like electroporation, microinjection, and liposomes.
  • 8.20 Microarrays use fluorescently labelled cDNA to hybridise with fixed single-stranded DNA probes, identifying which genes are actively being transcribed in a cell.
  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the collection, storage, and computational analysis of large biological datasets such as genomic sequences and amino acid databases using software tools.
  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms carry risks such as gene transfer to wild relatives and ethical concerns, alongside benefits like increased crop yields, disease resistance, and mass production of essential medical proteins.

Worked example

Explain how lidocaine affects the transmission of a nerve impulse. Step 1: Identify that lidocaine is a local anaesthetic drug. Step 2: Relate its mechanism of action to axonal membranes. Lidocaine binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels on the axon membrane. Step 3: State the consequence on the action potential. Sodium ions cannot enter the axon, preventing the membrane from depolarising, so the action potential cannot be generated or propagated along the neurone, blocking pain signals to the CNS.

Key points to remember

Students often confuse hyperpolarisation in rod cells with depolarisation in axons; remember that in the dark rod cells are depolarised and releasing neurotransmitter, but light hyperpolarises them and stops neurotransmitter release.

When describing recombinant DNA, always mention the specific roles of both restriction endonucleases for cutting DNA and DNA ligase for sealing phosphodiester bonds, as omitting either loses credit.

For plant growth factors, make sure to link auxin and gibberellin action directly to transcription and protein synthesis rather than just simple cell stretching.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

title: Differentiation II — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation II

Product and Quotient Rules

  • (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  • (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²

Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Standard Derivatives

  • sin x → cos x; cos x → −sin x; tan x → sec²x
  • e^x → e^x; ln x → 1/x

Chain Rule Everywhere

d/dx [ln(3x)] = 3/(3x) = 1/x; d/dx [e^(2x)] = 2e^(2x); d/dx [sin²x] = 2 sin x cos x.

Implicit Differentiation

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. x, treating y as a function of x (terms in y pick up dy/dx).

Example: x² + y² = 25 → 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 → dy/dx = −x/y.

Parametric Curves

For x = f(t), y = g(t): dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).

Example: x = t², y = t³ gives dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

Exam tips: quote the rule you use; for tangent/normal on parametric curves, find t at the point first, and simplify implicit answers using the original equation.

Exam method: exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric rules

The derivative of eˣ is eˣ, and the derivative of e^(kx) is k e^(kx). The derivative of ln x is 1/x, and for ln(f(x)) the chain rule gives f′(x)/f(x). The derivative of sin x is cos x and of cos x is −sin x; for a function of kx, multiply by k.

When a product contains an exponential or trigonometric function, use the product rule d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Factorising the result, such as eˣ(1 + x), makes it easier to evaluate at a point.

Quotients use d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Write tan x as sin x/cos x when the quotient rule is easier, and remember that d/dx(tan x) = sec² x.

Second derivatives follow by differentiating again. Use them to classify stationary points, or to check the concavity of a curve, when the question asks for it.

Exam cue: Show each rule as you apply it. Method marks are awarded for a correct product or chain step even if the final arithmetic is wrong.

title:
Appendix U — Extended worked long answer on the immune response for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the immune response is the kind of question where many candidates have all the pieces but lose marks by not putting them in time order or by not saying the distinctions clearly. The best practice for it is to write the answer from the durable ideas and the immune-process appendix, and to check that the answer has the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order, with the distinctions in the right places. A model answer starts with the first line: the pathogen has entered through the breach in the skin, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. The answer then moves to the specific response: the antigens on the pathogen are recognised, B cells produce antibodies specific to those antigens, T cells help and control and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells, and memory B and T cells are formed. The answer then explains why the timing matters: on first exposure the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, but on later exposure the secondary response is faster and stronger because the memory cells are already present. The answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first.

If you write that answer with those points in that order, you hit the marks the question is after. You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. You hit the timing distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster and stronger because of memory. You hit the vaccination link, because you have said that vaccination primes the same memory system without the disease. You hit the process rather than the label, because you have said the sequence in time order and given the reasons for the sequence. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the immune-response long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write a shorter answer that only says the body produces white blood cells and antibodies and remembers the pathogen, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The practice for the immune-response question is to write the answer from the durable ideas and then to check the distinctions one by one, because each distinction is a mark and each missing distinction is a lost mark. Check that the non-specific versus specific distinction is there. Check that the B versus T distinction is there. Check that the primary versus secondary timing distinction is there. Check that the memory cell role is there. Check that the vaccination link is there. If all five are there, the answer is ready. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore not just to write the answer once, but to write it, check the distinctions, and practise the missing distinction until it is in the answer under time pressure. Appendix U — Extended worked long answer on the immune response for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the immune response is the kind of question where many candidates have all the pieces but lose marks by not putting them in time order or by not saying the distinctions clearly. The best practice for it is to write the answer from the durable ideas and the immune-process appendix, and to check that the answer has the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order, with the distinctions in the right places. A model answer starts with the first line: the pathogen has entered through the breach in the skin, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. The answer then moves to the specific response: the antigens on the pathogen are recognised, B cells produce antibodies specific to those antigens, T cells help and control and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells, and memory B and T cells are formed. The answer then explains why the timing matters: on first exposure the primary response is slower because the specific lymphocytes have to be activated and expanded, but on later exposure the secondary response is faster and stronger because the memory cells are already present. The answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first.

If you write that answer with those points in that order, you hit the marks the question is after. You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. You hit the timing distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster and stronger because of memory. You hit the vaccination link, because you have said that vaccination primes the same memory system without the disease. You hit the process rather than the label, because you have said the sequence in time order and given the reasons for the sequence. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the immune-response long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. The mark scheme takes marks off the almost-correct answer for the missing step or distinction or specificity, and the note is written to show you what the missing thing is and how to put it in under time pressure. If you can use the note to find the missing thing in your practice answers and put it in, you are practising the thing the mark scheme rewards, which is the difference between the correct answer and the almost-correct one. That is the use of the note against the real mark scheme: to show you the difference the mark scheme cares about, and to give you the material to close the difference under time pressure.

The mark scheme also rewards the ability to answer the question that is actually there, and that is the reason the note has the practice answers shaped for the question shapes rather than for the note itself. The practice answers are shaped for the immune-response question, the gene technology question, the coordination question, the cross-strand question, the description question, the comparison question and the evaluation question, because those are the shapes the mark scheme is built around. If you can write the practice answer in the shape of the question, you are writing for the marks the mark scheme gives, because the mark scheme gives marks for the shape as well as for the content. If you write the answer in the wrong shape, you are writing for a different kind of mark scheme, and you will lose the marks that the real one gives for the shape. The note is written to help you write in the right shape, and that is the use of the practice answers: to model the shape the marks are in, so that you can write in that shape under time pressure on the day.

The final point about the mark scheme is that it is the mark scheme you have to satisfy, not the note, so the note is successful if it helps you write answers that satisfy the mark scheme, not if it is itself a complete summary of everything the specification ever says. The note is long because the mark scheme rewards reasoning, sequence, distinction and specificity, and because those take space to lay out, but the note is only a tool for helping you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and a tool is only good if it is used well. The use that makes it good is to practise the answers under time pressure, to check the distinctions and the sequence and the reasoning against the note, and to close the gaps before the exam. If you use the note that way, it helps you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the success the note is aiming for. If you use the note as a thing to read once and then forget, it will not help you write the answers the mark scheme rewards, and that is the use it fails at. The note is long so that you can use it as a practice source, and the practice source is the use that makes it successful, because the practice source is the thing that builds the answers the mark scheme rewards.

Appendix Y — The final end-of-topic checklist for the whole biology-A2 wave in one place

The end-of-topic checklist for the whole wave is the thing that tells you whether the wave is really done or only mostly done, and it is the thing to check after the note is written and before you move on from the wave. The first thing the checklist should confirm is that every specification point in the wave has a place in the note, because if a point has no place, the wave is not done, and the missing point is the thing to add before the wave is finished. For this biology-A2 wave, the checklist is the set of specification points the note is built from: the photosynthesis stages and the ATP story, the light-dependent and light-independent reactions and the chloroplast, the absorption and action spectra and the Rf value, the GPP and NPP and the transfer efficiency, the ecology vocabulary and the biotic and abiotic factors, the succession and the fieldwork methods, the climate evidence and the greenhouse mechanism and the mitigation, the climate models and the limits, the enzyme and temperature and Q10 and the development practical, the evolution and allele frequency and speciation, the receptor and synapse and muscle and homeostasis and the endocrine and plant and gene technology topics. If all of those have a place in the note, the wave is complete in coverage. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the gap that the exam can test without warning. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the coverage is the first thing the checklist should confirm.

The second thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is not just covering the coverage but also the precision, because coverage without precision is what loses marks on the day. For this wave, the precision is the sequence and the distinctions: the synaptic calcium step, the sliding-filament idea with ATP and calcium, the insulin-glucagon opposition with negative feedback, the restriction enzyme and PCR and electrophoresis principles, the primary-versus-secondary timing, the non-specific-versus-specific distinction, the B-versus-T distinction, the herd-immunity-as-coverage distinction, the DNA-profiling-as-interpretation distinction, and the cross-strand recognition idea. If all of those are in the note with enough detail to be used under time pressure, the wave is complete in precision. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to add, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to cover all of those, and the precision is the second thing the checklist should confirm.

The third thing the checklist should confirm is that the note is usable under time pressure, because coverage and precision are not enough if they cannot be used under time pressure. For this wave, the usability is the practice answers and the one-page summary: the immune-response long answer, the gene technology long answer, the coordination long answer, the cross-strand answer, the description and comparison answers, the evaluation answers, and the one-page summary of the wave. If all of those can be produced and then checked against the note under time pressure, the wave is complete in usability. If one cannot, the one that cannot is the thing to practise, because the one that cannot is the mark that will be lost on the day. The note is long enough to support all of those, and the usability is the third thing the checklist should confirm. If the wave is complete in coverage, precision and usability, the wave is done, and the note has done its job for the wave. If the wave is missing one of those, the missing one is the thing to finish before the wave is done, and the note is there to finish it.

Appendix Z — Closing the wave: what to do when the wave passes the checklist and what to do when it does not

When the wave passes the checklist, the thing to do is to consolidate and then move on, because the wave is done and the next wave is the thing that now matters. The consolidation is the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, because those are the things that make the wave reachable on the day and the things that make the wave usable for the exam. If the wave passes the checklist and you also have the one-page summary and the four-hour review structure, the wave is not just done in coverage and precision and usability; it is also done in the form that makes it usable on the day, and that is the form that matters. The move on is to the next wave, which is the thing that the project is actually about, and the wave is the unit of progress. If the wave is done, the next wave is the thing to start, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and the waves are the thing that build the topic one wave at a time. The thing to do when the wave passes is therefore to consolidate it into the reachable form and then start the next wave, because that is the progress the project is built on.

When the wave does not pass the checklist, the thing to do is to find the missing piece and finish it, because the wave is not done until the missing piece is done, and the missing piece is the gap that will lose marks if it is left open. For this biology-A2 wave, the missing piece is sometimes a coverage gap, sometimes a precision gap, and sometimes a usability gap, and the thing to do is to find which kind of gap it is and finish that kind of gap before moving on. If it is a coverage gap, the thing to do is to add the missing specification point to the note. If it is a precision gap, the thing to do is to add the missing sequence or distinction or reasoning to the note. If it is a usability gap, the thing to do is to add the missing practice answer or one-page-summary piece to the note. The thing to do when the wave does not pass is therefore to find the missing piece and finish the kind of gap it is, because the gap is the thing that stands between the wave and the done state, and the done state is the thing the project is aiming for. The note is there to finish the gap, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what finishes the gap when the wave is not yet done.

The final thing to do when the wave does not pass is to set a time limit for finishing the gap, because the project is a set of waves and the waves are the units, and a wave that does not finish its gap is a wave that holds up the next wave, and the next wave is the thing that matters to the project. If the gap can be finished in the time limit, finish it and then move on, because that is the progress the project is built on. If the gap cannot be finished in the time limit, the thing to do is to add the reachable part of the gap and leave the rest for the next session, because the reachable part is the part that matters most and the rest can wait, and the project is built on reachable progress more than on perfect progress. The note is long enough to hold both the reachable part and the rest, because the note is the tool for the wave, and the tool is what holds the wave together while the gap is being finished. The wave is therefore finished when the gap is finished or when the reachable part is done and the rest is scheduled, because either way the wave is no longer blocking the next wave, and the next wave is the thing the project is built on. The decision is the thing to make when the wave does not pass, and the note is the tool that makes the decision usable, because the note is the place where the wave lives and the wave is the thing that has to be passed before the next wave can be started.

title: Web Technologies — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

1. HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>Page</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Heading</h1>
  <p>Paragraph with <strong>bold</strong> text</p>
  <img src="pic.jpg" alt="description">
  <a href="https://example.com">Link</a>
  <table><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>
</body>
</html>

Head holds metadata/title; body holds visible content; hypertext links via <a href>.

2. CSS

p { color: red; font-size: 14px; }
.highlight { background-color: yellow; }
#header { text-align: center; }

Element, class (.) and id (#) selectors; inline vs external stylesheets; separation of content (HTML) from presentation (CSS).

3. JavaScript and the DOM

document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello";
document.getElementsByClassName("item")[0].style.color = "blue";

DOM = the browser's object model of the page; JS reads/changes it for interactivity (validation, sliders, dynamic text). Events (click, submit) trigger functions.

4. How pages load

URL → DNS lookup → server request → HTML parsed → assets fetched → DOM built → render. Layers: structure (HTML) → presentation (CSS) → behaviour (JS).

Exam tips: write tags with correct closing pairs; explain DOM operations as "find element by id … then change property"; separate structure/presentation/behaviour in answers.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Functions

Sequences as functions

A sequence can be defined by a term-to-term rule (each term from the previous one) or a position-to-term rule (un in terms of n). A linear sequence has un = a + (n − 1)d, and the domain of a sequence is the positive integers.

Function notation

A function f maps each element of its domain to exactly one output. Write f(x) for the output at x, and find values by substitution. The range is the set of outputs the function can produce.

Composite functions

gf(x) means apply f first, then g: gf(x) = g(f(x)). The order matters in general, so fg and gf are usually different.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x². Then gf(x) = (2x + 3)² = 4x² + 12x + 9, while fg(x) = 2x² + 3.

Inverse functions

An inverse exists only when the function is one-to-one. To find f⁻¹(x), write y = f(x), rearrange to make x the subject, then swap x and y. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 3 gives y = 2x + 3, so x = (y − 3)/2 and f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

Exam technique

  • Write the domain of an inverse function explicitly when the question asks for it.
  • Check a composite function by substituting a simple value such as x = 1.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. To order decimals, compare digits from left to right, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places. Rounding to a given number of decimal places or significant figures looks at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

Written methods

Long multiplication and division are set out in columns with place value kept aligned. Estimate first by rounding each number to one significant figure; the estimate shows whether the exact answer is reasonable. Check using the inverse operation.

Order of operations

Brackets, then indices, then division and multiplication from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 19. Use a calculator's brackets key to enter long expressions in one go.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Study Notes
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

title: Exam technique: Probability Distributions
content:
### What earns the marks
For distribution tables, probabilities summing to 1 checked earns the first mark. For expectation, each x times p(x) summed earns the method mark. For variance, E(X squared) computed separately then subtracted earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: sigma used as variance. Correction: sigma is sd; square it. Error: E(X squared) computed as E(X) squared. Correction: square the x values first. Error: function-of-X expectation via E(X) substituted. Correction: sum g(x)p(x) directly.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. ### Check yourself Find P(Z < −1.5) using symmetry. It equals 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668. Explain why the symmetry of the curve allows this without a separate table lookup.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Quadratic questions usually ask for one of three things: the shape of the curve, the number and position of its roots, or a range of values for a parameter. Identify which one you need before you start.

Completing the square and the turning point

Write ax² + bx + c as a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a). The turning point is at x = −b/2a, and the sign of a tells you whether it is a minimum (a > 0) or a maximum (a < 0). The same form gives the least or greatest value of the expression.

Example: 2x² − 12x + 7 = 2(x − 3)² − 11. The minimum is at (3, −11), so the least value of the expression is −11.

Solving: factorising, formula or sketch

Try factorising first. If it does not factorise neatly, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. A rough sketch shows how many roots to expect and whether the answer is a set of values or an interval.

Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 does not factorise neatly. Here b² − 4ac = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

The discriminant D = b² − 4ac decides how many real roots an equation has. D > 0 gives two distinct real roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives no real roots. The same test works for intersections: a line and a curve meet where their equations share a solution, so form one quadratic and read its discriminant.

Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² − 4(4)(9) = 0, so k² = 144 and k = ±12. Check: with k = 12 the equation becomes (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter in the discriminant

When the discriminant contains an unknown constant, write the condition as an equation or inequality and solve it. A quadratic inequality needs a sketch or a sign table to give the final range.

Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. Solving gives k − 1 ≤ −4 or k − 1 ≥ 4, so k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

A line meeting a curve, and tangency

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Two intersections need D > 0, a tangent needs D = 0, and no intersection needs D < 0.

Example: the line y = x + 3 and the curve y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28, so there are two intersection points. For the line y = 4x + c to touch y = x² + 2x + 1, the equation x² − 2x + (1 − c) = 0 needs D = 0, so c = 0. The point of contact is (1, 4).

Solving an inequality from a sketch

Find the roots, sketch the parabola and read off the region. When a is positive, the curve is below the axis between its roots and above it outside them.

Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0. The curve is below the axis between its roots, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0 is the same as 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, which factorises as (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0. The solution is −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1. Multiplying by −1 reverses the inequality, which is the step students most often miss.

Exam technique

  • Name the job first: shape, roots, or a condition on a parameter.
  • Write D = b² − 4ac with its numbers before deciding anything.
  • Give answers in the form the question asks for, such as exact surds or inequalities.
  • For a parameter range, test a value on each side of a boundary to confirm the direction of the inequality.

title:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology WBI15

This revision note belongs to Edexcel International A2 Level Biology WBI15 and covers the cultivation and measurement of microorganisms, the structure and replication of bacteria and viruses, the routes of pathogen entry and the body's non-specific and specific defences, the distinction between bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics, the principles of aseptic technique and the investigation of antibiotic action, the use of polymerase chain reaction and gel electrophoresis in DNA analysis, DNA profiling in identification and forensic work, and the forensic estimation of time of death in a mammal using multiple independent indicators. Each bullet names the specification point it satisfies so you can map your own revision against the syllabus rather than treating the notes as a general summary.

Culturing Microorganisms and Aseptic Technique

Microorganisms are grown in the laboratory either as individual colonies on solid media or as suspended cultures in liquid broth. The aim of every handling step is to keep the culture pure, the environment clean, and the operator safe, and the technique that achieves this is aseptic technique — a set of linked practices that prevents unwanted microorganisms from entering a culture and prevents the culture from escaping into the environment.

  • 6.1 Aseptic technique is the standard for culturing microorganisms. It includes working near a flame so that convection currents carry airborne microbes away from the open vessel, sterilising inoculating loops by heating them in a flame until they glow, allowing the loop to cool before touching the culture so that living organisms are not killed on contact, flaming the necks of bottles and Petri dish lids before opening them, and closing plates after inoculation using tape that holds the lid down without sealing it completely, so that anaerobic conditions do not develop and any overgrowth is still visible.
  • The growth medium itself must be sterile before inoculation. Plates are poured from sterilised molten agar that has been cooled to a temperature that will not kill the organisms to be cultured but is still liquid enough to pour. The nutrients in the medium should match the organism being cultured — carbohydrate, nitrogen source, minerals and suitable pH — and selective or differential media may be used when the goal is to isolate one species from a mixed sample.
  • Static cultures on agar produce colonies: each colony arises from a single viable cell or clump of cells deposited on the surface or within the agar, so a colony is a genetically uniform population derived from one progenitor. Pure cultures are obtained by repeatedly streaking a loop across an agar surface so that the inoculum is progressively diluted, with the final streaks producing isolated colonies that can be picked and restreaked.
  • Liquid cultures are used when the goal is to obtain large amounts of biomass or to follow growth over time. The culture vessel is kept closed, the medium is sterilised before use, and the flask is often shaken or stirred to keep oxygen evenly distributed, because most organisms used in school and college laboratories are aerobic or facultatively aerobic and will grow poorly in a stagnant medium.
  • Safety is part of the technique, not an add-on. Pathogenic species must never be cultured on open benches, the temperature and incubation time must be chosen so that organisms do not adapt to human body temperature unless that is the explicit purpose of the work, and cultures are destroyed by sterilisation before disposal. The specification expects you to understand why aseptic technique matters for both purity and safety, not merely to recall a checklist.

Measuring Microbial Growth and the Growth Curve

Growth in a microbial population is a change in the number of viable cells over time, not a change in the size of individual cells. Several methods exist, each with a different sensitivity, cost and interpretation, and the specification names four in particular: direct cell counts, dilution plating, mass and turbidity.

  • 6.2 (i) Direct cell counts count individuals in a known volume. A counting chamber such as a haemocytometer has a grid of known area and depth, so the volume above each grid square is known; counting the cells in several squares and scaling up gives the number per unit volume. This method is fast for dense cultures but counts both living and dead cells unless a viability stain is used, and it is tedious for dilute samples.
  • 6.2 (ii) Dilution plating estimates viable count by spreading a measured volume of a diluted culture onto agar and counting the colonies that grow. Because each colony arises from a viable unit, the count is expressed as colony-forming units per cubic centimetre (CFU cm−3). A series of dilutions is plated so that at least one plate yields a statistically usable number of colonies — typically between 30 and 300 — and the count is scaled back up by the dilution factor and the plated volume. This method counts only living organisms that can form colonies on the medium used, and it is therefore the standard for viable counts.
  • 6.2 (iii) Mass measurements estimate growth by drying a known volume of culture and weighing the residue, or by wet mass. The most common laboratory proxy is turbidity: a dense suspension of cells scatters more light than a dilute one, so absorbance (optical density) measured in a spectrophotometer at an appropriate wavelength rises with cell concentration. Turbidity is quick and repeatable and is suitable for following growth in the same culture over time, but it is a proxy, not a count — it must be calibrated against a viable count or a standard curve before it can be read as cells per unit volume.
  • 6.2 (iv) Each method has a use case. Dry mass is useful when cells clump or are small and numerous; turbidity is useful for continuous monitoring; viable counts are essential when you need to know how many living cells are present; and direct counts are useful for a rapid total cell estimate. The choice depends on what question is being answered, not on convenience alone.

The Bacterial Growth Curve and Exponential Calculation

When a small inoculum is added to a fresh liquid medium under constant conditions, the population follows a stereotypical sequence. The lag phase is a period of metabolic adjustment in which cells are not yet dividing at a constant rate; the exponential, or log, phase is the period of maximal, roughly constant division rate in which each cell generation adds a fixed number of cells; the stationary phase arrives when resources are exhausted or waste accumulates and the rate of cell division equals the rate of cell death; and the death phase follows when the death rate exceeds the division rate.

  • 6.3 (i) The phases are lag, exponential, stationary and death. In the exponential phase the population doubles in a constant time, the generation time, so the increase is exponential rather than linear.
  • 6.3 (ii) The exponential growth rate constant can be calculated from the change in number over time. The standard model is N = N0 e^(kt), where N is the number at time t, N0 is the starting number, k is the growth rate constant, and e is the base of natural logarithms. The generation time (doubling time) is the time for the population to double: using the exponential relationship, t_d = ln 2 / k. The specification expects you to handle the calculation, not merely to name the curve.
  • Worked example: a culture has 2.0 × 10^4 CFU cm−3 at the start of the exponential phase and 3.2 × 10^5 CFU cm−3 after 90 minutes in the same phase. Find the growth rate constant and the generation time.
  • Step 1: State the exponential formula N = N0 e^(kt).
  • Step 2: Rearrange to solve for k: k = (1/t) ln(N / N0).
  • Step 3: Substitute N = 3.2 × 10^5, N0 = 2.0 × 10^4, t = 90 min: N/N0 = 16, ln 16 = 2.773, so k = 2.773 / 90 = 0.0308 min−1.
  • Step 4: Calculate the generation time: t_d = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / 0.0308 = 22.5 min. So the population doubles roughly every 22.5 minutes under these conditions.
  • A common exam trap is to use the wrong time base or to confuse the growth rate constant with the generation time. The constant k has units of inverse time; the doubling time is a time. If the question gives counts at two times, always check whether both counts genuinely belong to the exponential phase — if one is still in the lag phase, the exponential formula will give a misleading answer because the assumption of constant doubling is false.

Core Practical 13: Following Microbial Growth

Core Practical 13 asks you to investigate the rate of growth of microorganisms in a liquid culture, taking into account the safe and ethical use of organisms. In practice this means setting up a liquid culture of a suitable, non-pathogenic species, incubating it under controlled conditions, and following growth by turbidity or by viable counting at intervals, then plotting the growth curve and identifying the phases.

  • 6.4 Safety and ethics require using a safe species, sealing plates appropriately, not leaving cultures open, sterilising before disposal, and working near a flame. Ethical use of organisms means avoiding unnecessary suffering — in microbiology this is mostly about using non-pathogenic species and handling them in a way that prevents contamination and exposure — and about not using more material than is needed to obtain the data.
  • The practical outcome is a growth curve with at least some indication of the lag, exponential and stationary phases. If you measure turbidity, be clear that you are tracking a proxy for cell number and, if possible, calibrate it with a viable count. If you plate dilutions, be clear that you are measuring viable count and that the plates must be counted before colonies overgrow and merge.
  • A good exam answer explains why the measurement method was chosen, whether it counts total or viable cells, and how the data were converted into a growth curve. It also notes limitations: turbidity cannot distinguish live from dead cells, plating underestimates cells that do not form colonies on the medium used, and sampling at too few time points can make the phases hard to locate.

Structure of Bacteria and Viruses and the Lytic and Latent Cycles

Bacteria are prokaryotic cells: they are small, lack a membrane-bound nucleus, and carry their genetic material as a single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm together with smaller extra-chromosomal rings called plasmids. Viruses are not cells: they are much smaller, are built around a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA, never both in one particle) surrounded by a protein capsid, and may or may not have a lipid envelope taken from the host cell membrane. The specification names four viruses as examples — tobacco mosaic virus, Ebola virus, HIV and lambda phage — and asks you to compare their structure and to understand the difference between the lytic cycle, in which a virus replicates and lyses the host cell, and latency, in which the viral genome persists in the host without producing new particles for a period.

  • 6.5 (i) Bacteria are prokaryotes with a cell wall (in most species containing peptidoglycan), a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a nucleoid region containing the circular chromosome, and often plasmids. They do not have mitochondria, chloroplasts, endoplasmic reticulum or a Golgi body. Viruses have a nucleic acid core (DNA or RNA), a capsid made of protein subunits, and in some cases an envelope; they have no metabolism of their own and can only reproduce inside a host cell.
  • The four named viruses illustrate different structures. Ebola virus is an enveloped RNA virus with a filamentous shape; the envelope helps it enter host cells by membrane fusion. Tobacco mosaic virus is a rod-shaped RNA virus that infects plants; its rigid protein coat reflects its function in protecting the RNA between host cells. HIV is a retrovirus — an enveloped RNA virus that reverse-transcribes its RNA into DNA inside the host and integrates that DNA into the host genome, which is central to its ability to cause persistent infection. Lambda phage is a bacterial virus (bacteriophage) with a head (DNA) and a tail that attaches to the bacterial surface and injects its DNA; it can pursue either a lytic or a lysogenic pathway.
  • 6.5 (ii) In the lytic cycle the virus attaches, injects or enters its nucleic acid, uses the host's machinery to replicate viral nucleic acid and make viral proteins, assembles new particles, and then lyses the host cell to release them. In latency (often called lysogeny in bacteriophages) the viral genome integrates into or persists alongside the host genome and does not immediately produce new particles; it can be replicated along with the host genome and activated later by a trigger such as stress or immune suppression. The distinction matters because latency makes some infections hard to clear and to diagnose: the virus is present but not producing the particles that would be detected by a standard titre.
  • A useful way to remember the difference is that lytic means the virus kills the host cell in the same round of infection, whereas latent means the viral genome can sit quietly inside the host and be carried forward, reactivating later. For HIV, latency is a major clinical challenge because the virus hides in long-lived cells and can rebound if treatment stops.

Tuberculosis and HIV: Infection, Symptoms and Outcomes

Two named pathogens illustrate very different ways in which microbes cause disease: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a slowly growing bacterium, and human immunodeficiency virus, a fast-replicating retrovirus. Both persist in the body and both cause damage partly by the way the host responds to them, not only by direct destruction.

  • 6.6 (i) Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an aerobic, slow-growing bacterium with a waxy, lipid-rich cell wall that resists staining and resists many chemical treatments; this wall is one reason it survives inside host cells and is hard to treat. It is transmitted in droplets from an infected person, and after inhalation it is taken up by macrophages. In many people the immune response walls off the bacteria in granulomas and the infection remains latent, but if the response is insufficient or the bacterium reactivates, tissue destruction occurs, particularly in the lungs, leading to the symptoms of tuberculosis.
  • Tuberculosis symptoms include a persistent cough, often with blood-tinged sputum, chest pain, fatigue, weight loss, fever and night sweats. The disease can spread to other organs. The slow growth of the bacterium and its intracellular location make treatment long and the use of multiple drugs necessary, because a single drug leaves room for resistant survivors.
  • 6.6 (ii) HIV infects human cells, especially helper T cells, by binding to surface receptors and fusing with the cell membrane. Once inside, the viral RNA is reverse-transcribed into DNA, integrated into the host genome, and used to produce new viral particles that bud from the cell. The loss of helper T cells undermines the coordination of the adaptive immune response, leaving the person vulnerable to opportunistic infections and certain cancers; the late stage of untreated infection is acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, AIDS.
  • The progression from HIV infection to AIDS takes years in an untreated person because the immune system partially controls the virus for a time, but the virus is never fully cleared. The outcome illustrates the principle that disease symptoms can arise from the host's immune response and from opportunistic infection as much as from the virus directly.

Routes of Entry and the Body's Barriers

Pathogens reach internal tissues through defined routes, and the body has a layered set of barriers that reduce the chance of entry and of establishment. Understanding the route of entry matters because it explains the clinical picture and the likely means of control.

  • 6.7 (i) Major routes of entry include the respiratory route (inhaled droplets or aerosols reaching the lungs), the digestive route (contaminated food or water reaching the gut), the skin route (through cuts, punctures, insect bites or other breaches of the skin), the sexual route, and the parenteral route (directly into the blood or tissues, as with contaminated needles). Each route exposes the pathogen to a different environment and a different set of defences.
  • 6.7 (ii) Barriers include physical, chemical and microbial factors. Skin is the main physical barrier; its outer layer is tough and relatively dry, and it is continuously shed, removing attached organisms. Mucous membranes line the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts; mucus traps particles and cilia move them out of the respiratory tract. Chemical defences include stomach acid, which kills many ingested microbes, and enzymes such as lysozyme in tears and secretions, which damage bacterial cell walls. The normal flora of the skin, gut and other surfaces competes with pathogens for space and nutrients and can inhibit their growth, so disruption of the normal flora — for example by broad-spectrum antibiotics — can allow opportunistic pathogens to establish.
  • A good answer links the barrier to the route: stomach acid is useful against ingested pathogens but not against inhaled ones; skin is a barrier until it is breached; and the normal flora is a competitive barrier whose disruption can itself cause disease. The specification expects you to understand that the body is defended at the point of entry, not only after the pathogen has reached the blood or tissues.

Non-Specific Defence: Inflammation, Lysozyme, Interferon and Phagocytosis

Once a pathogen breaches a barrier or damage occurs, the body mounts a non-specific response that acts within minutes to hours and does not require prior exposure to the pathogen. This is the innate response, and it includes inflammation, lysozyme action, interferon and phagocytosis.

  • 6.8 (i) Inflammation is a coordinated local response to damage and to the presence of pathogens and their products. Damaged cells and resident immune cells release chemical mediators such as histamine and cytokines; these cause vasodilation, so more blood flows to the area (redness and heat), and increased vascular permeability, so plasma and cells leave the vessels (swelling and pain). The increased blood flow and permeability bring phagocytes, antibodies and complement proteins to the site, and the clotting response can wall off the area. Inflammation helps contain the infection and brings defences to the site, but it also produces the symptoms of inflammation.
  • 6.8 (ii) Lysozyme is an enzyme found in tears, saliva, nasal secretions and other body fluids; it breaks bonds in the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls, weakening or killing susceptible bacteria. It is one of the chemical barriers at body surfaces and in secretions, and it acts best against Gram-positive bacteria whose cell walls are more exposed, though it can affect Gram-negative species too.
  • 6.8 (iii) Interferons are proteins released by virus-infected cells that signal neighbouring cells to increase their defences; they do not kill the virus directly but make the local environment less favourable for viral replication, partly by activating genes that inhibit viral nucleic acid synthesis and partly by enhancing the activity of immune cells. Interferon is part of the early antiviral response and helps limit the spread of virus before the specific response is underway.
