  • Using a single indicator to estimate time of death as if it were precise: the estimate comes from combining several indicators, each affected by conditions, so the result is a range with uncertainty, not a fixed number.
  • Describing antibiotic action without distinguishing bacteriostatic from bactericidal: know that static stops growth and cidal kills, and that the choice can depend on the host''s ability to clear the infection.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how you would measure the growth of a liquid bacterial culture using turbidity, and state one limitation of this method. Answer: Measure the absorbance of the culture at a suitable wavelength at intervals using a spectrophotometer; as the culture grows, the suspension becomes more turbid and the absorbance increases; plot absorbance against time to follow growth. Limitation: turbidity measures a proxy for cell number and counts both living and dead cells, so it must be calibrated against a viable count and does not distinguish live from dead cells. (5 marks)
  2. Calculate the growth rate constant and doubling time for a culture that increases from 5.0 × 10^3 CFU cm−3 to 4.0 × 10^4 CFU cm−3 in 60 minutes during the exponential phase. Answer: Use N = N0 e^(kt); k = (1/t) ln(N/N0) = (1/60) ln(8) = 2.079/60 = 0.0347 min−1; doubling time t_d = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / 0.0347 = 20.0 min. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the structure of HIV and explain how it differs from the structure of a bacterium. Answer: HIV is a virus with a nucleic acid core (RNA), a protein capsid, and an envelope derived from the host membrane; it has no cell structure, no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no metabolism of its own. A bacterium is a prokaryotic cell with a cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a circular chromosome; it can metabolise and reproduce independently in suitable conditions. (5 marks)
  4. Explain the difference between natural active immunity and artificial passive immunity, giving an example of each. Answer: Natural active immunity is gained when the body produces its own response and memory after infection, e.g. recovering from a disease; artificial passive immunity is gained by injecting antibodies made elsewhere, e.g. antivenom, giving immediate but temporary protection with no memory. (4 marks)
  5. Describe how PCR is used to amplify a specific region of DNA and explain why a thermostable polymerase is needed. Answer: PCR uses repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers, and extension by DNA polymerase to double the target region each cycle; a thermostable polymerase such as Taq is needed because it must withstand the high temperature of the denaturation step without being destroyed, so the same enzyme can be used through many cycles. (5 marks)
  6. A forensic scientist is estimating the time of death of a mammal. Describe two indicators that could be used and explain why more than one is needed. Answer: Body temperature can be used soon after death because the body cools after death; rigor mortis can be used because muscles stiffen as ATP is depleted; extent of decomposition or insect succession can be used later. More than one indicator is needed because each changes at a rate that depends on conditions such as temperature, and no single indicator is precise enough on its own, so combining them gives a better estimate with a smaller range of uncertainty. (6 marks)
  7. Explain the difference between a bacteriostatic and a bactericidal antibiotic, and state why the distinction matters clinically. Answer: A bacteriostatic antibiotic stops bacteria from growing but does not necessarily kill them, relying on the host''s immune system to clear the infection; a bactericidal antibiotic kills bacteria. The distinction matters because a bacteriostatic drug may not be suitable when the host''s immune system is weak, whereas a bactericidal drug can be used to kill the pathogen directly. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one concrete example and one method, and by practising the calculations for exponential growth, respiratory quotient, and the antibody and PCR steps until you can write them from memory. Next, use this note alongside Core Practical 13, 14 and 15, and move on to Topic 7: Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment.

Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, logic expressions, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Integration — Study Notes
content:
Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

Rules and exam method

For xⁿ with n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Integrate term by term. The special case is ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. An indefinite integral needs + c; a definite integral does not.

For a definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Write the limits as [F(x)] between a and b, and substitute carefully: a negative limit raised to a power needs brackets.

The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ y dx when y ≥ 0 over the interval. If the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative, so take the modulus. If the curve crosses the axis, find the root and integrate each part separately, adding the moduli of the parts.

The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower) between their intersection points, found by solving the equations simultaneously.

Exam cue: Show the expanded antiderivative before substituting limits; method marks are given for a correct integration even when the arithmetic later slips.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Check yourself
Explain why the line of best fit should pass through (x̄, ȳ). Check that 2 × 5 + 2 = 12, so the line does pass through the mean point. State whether a prediction at x = 20 would be interpolation or extrapolation, and say why it is less reliable.

title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.
### Check yourself
A teacher samples 50 students from the first 50 names on the register. Name the sampling method and the main source of bias. This is a convenience sample, and the bias comes from the register order, which may not represent the whole school.

### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

Worked example: a full stationary-point analysis

Let y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5. Then dy/dx = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1). Stationary points occur when dy/dx = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1. The second derivative is d²y/dx² = 6x − 6. At x = −1 it is −12, which is negative, so there is a maximum; at x = 3 it is +12, so there is a minimum. Substitute back into the original equation for the y-coordinates: (−1, 10) is a maximum and (3, −22) is a minimum. Always state both coordinates.

Tangent and normal at a point

At x = 2, y = 8 − 12 − 18 + 5 = −17 and dy/dx = 12 − 12 − 9 = −9. The tangent has gradient −9 through (2, −17), so y + 17 = −9(x − 2). The normal is perpendicular, with gradient 1/9, so y + 17 = (1/9)(x − 2). Keep the equations in the form the question asks for, and do not mix the gradient of the normal with the tangent.

Rates of change: a chain rule example

The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³. If the radius increases at 0.5 cm/s, find the rate of change of volume when r = 3. dV/dr = 4πr², so dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt = 4π(9)(0.5) = 18π cm³/s ≈ 56.5 cm³/s. Linking the rates through the chain rule is the method being tested, so write the link explicitly.

Increasing and decreasing

The sign of dy/dx tells you whether the function is increasing (dy/dx > 0) or decreasing (dy/dx < 0). For y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5, the curve increases for x < −1, decreases between −1 and 3, and increases again for x > 3. State these intervals with the correct inequalities; an answer that says "x > −1" for the decreasing part loses the mark.

Common errors

  • Concluding a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone without a sign test or second derivative.
  • Substituting the x-value into dy/dx to give the y-coordinate of the stationary point.
  • Using the gradient of the tangent in the normal equation, instead of its negative reciprocal.
  • Forgetting the chain-rule factor when the rate of change question involves two variables.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Computer Science — A2. A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Key areas to revise

  • Simulation and Modelling
  • Sensors and Signals
  • Monitoring vs Control
  • Real-Time Considerations

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A simulation of traffic flow lets a designer test a new junction without building it. The model rests on assumptions, such as cars arriving at a fixed average rate, so its results are only as good as those assumptions and the real data used to set them. ### Check yourself Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a simulation rather than a real trial. An advantage is that it is safe and cheap to test extreme cases. A disadvantage is that it simplifies reality, so an unexpected real-world factor may be missing from the model.

title: Exam technique: Quadratics
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, the factorised form shown earns the first mark and each root earns credit after. For discriminants, the substitution with signs tracked earns the method mark and the root-count conclusion earns the second. For completing the square, the subtracted square earns the method mark and the turning point stated as a pair earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: negated root pairs from sign slips. Correction: expand-check each bracket. Error: one-sided k ranges. Correction: negative branch included. Error: negative length roots kept. Correction: reject with a reason stated.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

Reading a scatter diagram

Each point plots one pair of values. Positive correlation means y tends to rise as x rises; negative correlation means it falls. The strength of correlation depends on how closely the points cluster around a line. Correlation does not prove causation.

Lines of best fit

Draw a straight line through the middle of the points, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side, and use it to estimate values. Interpolation (inside the data range) is generally reliable; extrapolation (beyond the data) is less so and should be stated as an estimate.

Outliers

A point far from the general pattern is an outlier. Mention it in your answer and state whether it affects the conclusion, rather than ignoring it silently.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.
### Check yourself
Find the surface area of a cylinder with radius 2 cm and height 5 cm, leaving π in the answer. The curved surface is 2πrh = 20π and the two circles are 2πr² = 8π, giving 28π cm². Show each part before adding them.

title: Waves — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Waves

Physics — AS. A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • The Wave Equation
  • Intensity
  • Doppler Effect
  • EM Spectrum
  • Polarization

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A wave on a rope has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = fλ, or leaving wavelength in centimetres while using metres per second.
  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

### What earns the marks

title: Exam technique: Algebra Graphs
content:
### What earns the marks
For gradient and equation questions, calculate earns marks for a correct (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) computation with substitution shown, then the rearrangement to y = mx + c. For perpendicular lines, state earns the negative-reciprocal gradient explicitly before substituting. For curve questions, describe earns marks for roots, intercept and turning point each stated, and the axis of symmetry as an equation (x = 2, not just 2).
### Traps
Error: answering the midpoint when length is asked. Correction: re-read the final demand before computing. Error: giving the minimum value instead of its x-coordinate. Correction: label every coordinate pair fully. Error: keeping gradient 2 for a perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Correction: flip and negate first, then substitute.
### Worked example
Find the equation of the line through (0, 2) and (4, 10). The gradient is m = (10 − 2)/(4 − 0) = 2. Because the line crosses the y-axis at 2, the equation is y = 2x + 2. Check by substituting x = 4 to get 10, which is correct.
### Check yourself
Two lines are y = 3x − 1 and y = (−1/3)x + 5. Are they parallel, perpendicular, or neither? Their gradients multiply to 3 × (−1/3) = −1, so the lines are perpendicular. Parallel lines would have equal gradients, and the test is always the gradient.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

title: Exam technique: System Software and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS roles, each role tied to the scenario earns a mark: paging for oversized workloads, scheduling for shared CPUs. For malware, the propagation method contrasted (self-spreading worms vs host-bound viruses) earns both marks. For hashing, one-way verification plus salt against rainbow tables earns the pair.
### Traps
Error: single-driver answers for whole-OS management. Correction: name memory, processor, devices, security. Error: worms and viruses reversed. Correction: worms roam alone; viruses ride hosts. Error: encryption claimed where hashing belongs. Correction: password checks verify hashes, never decrypt.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.
### Check yourself
A nucleus with A = 64 has radius r = 1.2 x 64^(1/3) = 4.8 fm. State why doubling A does not double the radius. The radius grows with the cube root of A, so doubling A multiplies r by 2^(1/3), about 1.26.

### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Equations

Linear equations

Expand any brackets, collect the terms in x on one side and the constants on the other, then divide by the coefficient of x. When fractions appear, multiply every term by the lowest common denominator first.

Simultaneous linear equations

Use elimination (make the coefficient of one variable equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or substitution (rearrange one equation and put it into the other). Check the solution by substituting into the equation you did not use.

Example: 3x + 2y = 12 and x − y = 1. From the second equation x = y + 1. Substituting gives 3y + 3 + 2y = 12, so y = 9/5 and x = 14/5. Check: 3(14/5) + 2(9/5) = 12.

Quadratic equations

Factorise where possible, complete the square, or use the formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. The discriminant b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: two if positive, one if zero, none if negative.

Equations with algebraic fractions

Multiply through by the product of the denominators, excluding any values that make a denominator zero. The result is often a quadratic.

Example: 2/(x − 1) + 3/(x + 1) = 2. Multiplying by (x − 1)(x + 1) gives 5x − 1 = 2x² − 2, so 2x² − 5x − 1 = 0 and x = (5 ± √33)/4. Neither root equals ±1, so both are valid.

Exam technique

  • Keep answers exact (fractions and surds) unless the question asks for decimals.
  • Substitute each root back into the original equation when fractions are involved.

title: Ethics and AI — Study Notes
content:
`# Ethics and AI

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Check yourself
Evaluate the definite integral of 2x + 1 from 1 to 3. The antiderivative is x² + x, giving (9 + 3) − (1 + 1) = 10. Write both the antiderivative and the subtraction on the paper, because the method mark depends on them.

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

title: Exam technique: Operating Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
To earn full marks on this topic, students need to demonstrate their understanding of the operating system's roles and functions, as stated in 4.1. For example, when asked to explain how an OS manages memory, students should describe the process of paging and segmentation, and explain how virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full. The command words that appear in questions are explain, describe, and state. Explain earns the most marks, as it requires students to provide a detailed description of a concept, such as interrupts and buffers.
### Traps
One common mistake is to confuse the terms paging and segmentation. Paging refers to the process of dividing memory into fixed-size blocks, while segmentation refers to the process of dividing memory into variable-size blocks. Another mistake is to think that multitasking is the same as multithreading. Multitasking refers to the ability of an OS to run multiple processes simultaneously, while multithreading refers to the ability of a process to run multiple threads simultaneously.
### Memory hooks
A useful mnemonic to remember the functions of an OS is MANPS: Memory management, Application management, Network management, Process management, and Security. Another memory hook is to think of the OS as a manager that allocates resources, such as memory and I/O devices, to applications. A shortcut to understanding virtual memory is to think of it as a way to extend RAM to disk when RAM is full.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 10-15% of the total marks on the paper. Students should budget around 10-15 minutes to answer questions on this topic, depending on the length and complexity of the questions.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Check yourself
State which structure a printer queue uses and why, in one sentence that names the order of service. A print queue serves the first job submitted first, so it is first in, first out.

### Worked example

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.
### Check yourself
A point at (6; 8) has magnitude sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10. Explain why the magnitude is never the sum 6 + 8 = 14. The magnitude uses the root of the sum of squares, so the components do not add directly.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

Definitions

  • Displacement s: distance in a given direction (vector)
  • Velocity v: rate of change of displacement, v = ds/dt
  • Acceleration a: rate of change of velocity, a = dv/dt

Graphs

  • Gradient of a displacement–time graph = velocity
  • Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration
  • Area under a velocity–time graph = displacement
  • Area under an acceleration–time graph = change in velocity

SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)

EquationMissing
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Projectiles

Resolve into independent components: horizontal at constant velocity (s = ut), vertical under gravity (SUVAT).

Example: a ball fired at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30°: uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹, u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. Time of flight = 2u_y/g ≈ 2.04 s; range = uₓ × t ≈ 35 m.

Exam tips: state which direction is positive; projectile questions are two separate 1-D problems joined by time.

title: Organic Synthesis — Study Notes
content:
Organic Synthesis

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20. Organic synthesis plans a route from a starting material to a target molecule. You need to choose reagents and conditions, track functional groups and calculate the overall yield.

Planning a route

  • Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target: identify the functional group, then find a precursor that converts into it in one step.
  • Each step should be a known functional group interconversion with suitable reagents and conditions.
  • Carbon chain length can be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Key interconversions

  • Primary alcohol to aldehyde: distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further.
  • Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid: reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI).
  • Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol: NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄ for carboxylic acids and nitriles).
  • Alkene to haloalkane: addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol: steam with an acid catalyst.
  • Nitrobenzene to phenylamine: reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.

Yield calculations

  • Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ theoretical mass × 100.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product ÷ sum of molar masses of all products) × 100.

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Coordinate questions are multi-part: one part gives two points, the next gives a line, and the last asks for a proof or an area. Read the final part first, then pick the tools it needs.

Start from a question

The points A(−1, 4), B(5, 2) and C(3, −4) are given.

  1. Show that angle ABC is 90°.
  2. Find the area of triangle ABC.
  3. Find the equation of the line through A parallel to BC.

Part 1. The gradient of AB is (2 − 4)/(5 + 1) = −1/3. The gradient of BC is (−4 − 2)/(3 − 5) = 3. The product is −1, so AB is perpendicular to BC and the angle at B is 90°.

Part 2. AB² = 6² + 2² = 40 and BC² = 2² + 6² = 40, so AB = BC = √40. The right angle is at B, so the area is ½ × AB × BC = ½ × 40 = 20.

Part 3. Parallel lines share a gradient, so the line has gradient 3. Then y − 4 = 3(x + 1), which gives 3x − y + 7 = 0.

The tools

  • Distance: √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). When only a squared length is needed, leave out the root.
  • Midpoint: ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
  • Gradient: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1.
  • Equation of a line: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), using a known point and the gradient m. Rearrange into the form the question asks for.

Two lines: meeting, parallel or perpendicular

A meeting point satisfies both equations, so solve them together. Example: 2x − y = 1 and x + y = 5. Adding gives 3x = 6, so x = 2 and y = 3. Check: 4 − 3 = 1 and 2 + 3 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 3).

Perpendicular example: the line through (1, −3) perpendicular to 4x + y = 2. The given gradient is −4, so the required gradient is ¼. Then y + 3 = ¼(x − 1), which gives x − 4y − 13 = 0. Check at (1, −3): 1 + 12 − 13 = 0.

A circle and a line

Rewrite the circle x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 in centre–radius form by completing the square: (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 16. The centre is (3, −2) and the radius is 4.

Substitute the line y = x + 1 into the circle: x² + (x + 1)² − 6x + 4(x + 1) − 3 = 0 simplifies to 2x² + 2 = 0. Its discriminant is 0² − 4(2)(2) = −16 < 0, so there are no intersections and the line misses the circle.

Tangents and points against a circle

A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The point (3, 2) lies on the circle, since 9 + 4 − 18 + 8 − 3 = 0. The radius from (3, −2) to (3, 2) is vertical, so the tangent is horizontal: y = 2.

To test a point (x, y), substitute into (x − a)² + (y − b)² and compare with r². A smaller value means inside the circle, equal means on it, and larger means outside. For (1, 2): (1 − 3)² + (2 + 2)² = 20 > 16, so the point lies outside.

Traps that cost marks

  • Using the given gradient for a perpendicular line instead of its negative reciprocal.
  • Squaring the points instead of the coordinate differences when finding a length.
  • Rounding √40 early. Keep it as 2√10 when the question asks for an exact value.
  • Leaving a line in gradient form when the question asks for the ax + by + c = 0 form.

title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Check yourself
State the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer, and say which bit sets the sign. The range is -128 to +127, and the leftmost bit is the sign bit with weight -128.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

Worked example: building a binary search tree

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1 and 6 in that order. The first value, 8, becomes the root. Since 3 is less than 8, it goes to the left; 10 goes to the right. The value 1 is less than 8 and less than 3, so it sits to the left of 3. The value 6 is less than 8 and greater than 3, so it sits to the right of 3. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) then lists the values in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10.

Complexity of the main operations

  • Search, insert and delete in a balanced tree take O(log n) time, because each comparison discards about half the remaining nodes.
  • If the values are inserted in sorted order, the tree becomes a chain and the same operations degrade to O(n).
  • Hash table lookup takes O(1) on average but gives no ordering, so a hash table cannot list the data in sorted order.

Choosing between the structures

A stack, a queue and a linked list each store a collection, but they differ in how items are added and removed. A stack is last in, first out. A queue is first in, first out. A linked list allows insertion and deletion at a known position without shifting other items. The exam question usually asks you to justify the choice, so state the access pattern the data needs.

Appendix R — Extended worked long answer on the immune response for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the immune response is the kind of question where many candidates have all the pieces but lose marks by not putting them in time order or by not saying the distinctions clearly. The best practice for it is to write the answer from the durable ideas and the immune-process appendix, and to check that the answer has the non-specific first line, the specific response, the timing, the memory and the vaccination link in the right order, with the distinctions in the right places. A model answer starts with the first line: the pathogen has entered through the breach in the skin, the immediate non-specific responses include the local inflammation and the arrival of phagocytes, and phagocytosis is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens. The answer then relates it to vaccination: vaccination exposes the immune system to the antigen without the disease, so the memory is formed without the person having to suffer the infection first.

You hit the non-specific versus specific distinction, because you have said that the first line is non-specific and the specific response is specific. You hit the cell distinction, because you have said that B cells make antibodies and T cells help and control and deal with infected cells. You hit the timing distinction, because you have said that the primary response is slower and the secondary is faster and stronger because of memory. Check that the memory cell role is there. Check that the vaccination link is there. If all five are there, the answer is ready. Appendix S — Extended worked long answer on the gene technology techniques for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the gene technology techniques is the kind of question where candidates most often lose marks by knowing the name of each technique but not the principle and the purpose. The best practice for it is to write the answer technique by technique, with the principle and the purpose for each, and then to add the application and the limit if the question asks for it. A model answer starts with restriction enzymes: restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, and some cuts leave sticky ends, which are short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with another piece of DNA cut with the same enzyme, so that the two pieces can be joined by DNA ligase. The answer then says why that matters: the specificity of the cut and the matching of the sticky ends are what make cloning possible, because they let a wanted piece of DNA be inserted into a vector at a predictable place. The next technique is PCR: PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, and the cycles are denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by a heat-stable polymerase, so that the target sequence doubles each cycle. The answer then says why that matters: PCR lets a small sample of a specific sequence be amplified enough to study or use, and it is used in diagnostics and forensics, but the result is a specific target, not a random copy of the whole genome.

The next technique is gel electrophoresis: gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field, and DNA moves toward the positive electrode with smaller fragments moving faster, so the result is a banding pattern by size. The answer then says why that matters: the separation by size is what lets the fragments be resolved and compared, and a gene probe can then be used to detect a specific fragment by hybridisation, with the probe being a labelled complementary sequence. The next technique is the vector and transformation: a vector such as a plasmid carries foreign DNA into a host cell, and transformation is the uptake of the DNA, and a selectable marker lets you identify the transformed cells, with insertional inactivation used when the wanted DNA is inserted into a marker gene so that recombinant cells can be distinguished from non-recombinant ones. The answer then says why that matters: the vector and transformation are what put the DNA into the host, and the marker is what lets you find the cells that took it up, because not all cells do.

You hit the principle for restriction enzymes, which is cutting at specific sequences and using sticky ends and ligation to join. You hit the purpose for PCR, which is amplifying a specific sequence in vitro by repeated cycles with a heat-stable polymerase. You hit the principle for electrophoresis, which is separation by size in an electric field, with DNA moving to the positive electrode and smaller fragments moving faster. You hit the purpose for the probe, which is detecting a specific fragment by hybridisation with a labelled complementary sequence. You hit the principle and purpose for the vector and transformation and the marker, which is carrying DNA into a host and selecting the cells that took it up, with insertional inactivation as one way to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the gene technology long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write a shorter answer that only names the techniques, you have the labels but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The practice for the gene technology question is to write the answer technique by technique and then to check that each technique has both the principle and the purpose, because the mark is usually in the principle and the purpose together, not in the name alone. Check that restriction enzymes have the specific cut and the sticky end and the ligation. Check that PCR has the specific amplification and the cycles and the heat-stable polymerase. Check that electrophoresis has the size separation and the movement to the positive electrode and the smaller-faster idea. Check that the probe has the complementary labelled sequence and the hybridisation. Check that the vector and transformation have the carrying of DNA and the selection of transformed cells and the optional insertional inactivation. If all of those are there, the answer is ready. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore to write the answer, check the techniques one by one, and practise the missing technique until its principle and purpose are in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the gene technology question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support.

Appendix T — The final consolidation pass before the exam: how to tie the topic together one more time

The final consolidation pass before the exam is the pass where you tie the topic together one more time, because by then you should know enough of the detail to need the tying rather than the learning. The tying is the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions, all in one place in your head, so that when a question appears you can reach for the right idea, the right example and the right distinction without having to reconstruct the whole topic from scratch. The way to do the tying is to say the four durable ideas one more time, each with one anchor and one distinction, and to check that you can say them under time pressure. Say the control idea with the reflex arc or the insulin-glucagon system as the anchor and the nervous-versus-hormonal distinction. Say the layered defence idea with the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one side and the antibody and memory cell response on the other, and the non-specific-versus-specific distinction. Say the timing idea with the primary and secondary response and vaccination as the anchor and the memory-cell distinction. Say the matching idea with restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis as the anchors and the principle-versus-label distinction. If you can say those four durable ideas with their anchors and their distinctions under time pressure, you have the tying, and the tying is what lets you answer the topic on the day without panic.

The second part of the consolidation pass is to say the edge cases one more time, because the edge cases are the ones that separate a good answer from a very good one, and they are the ones that are easiest to blur when writing fast. Say the neuromuscular junction versus the synapse, with the sequence the same and the postsynaptic cell and outcome different. Say the rod versus the cone, with both photoreceptors but different sensitivity, colour and light level. Say the restriction enzyme versus the probe, with cutting and joining versus detecting. Say the somatic versus the germ-line therapy, with individual versus heritable. Say the herd immunity versus the individual immunity, with coverage and transmission versus the individual. Say the primary versus the secondary response, with slower versus faster and stronger because of memory. If you can say those edge cases one more time, you are ready for the questions that test them, and those are the questions that often decide the top marks. The consolidation pass is therefore not about learning new detail, but about making sure the distinctions you already know are still there and are still precise enough to be said under time pressure.

The third part of the consolidation pass is to do one last timed practice of each of the three kinds of question the topic sets: one description, one comparison and one evaluation. Pick one description question from the immune response, the gene technology techniques or the coordination receptors, and write the answer under time pressure. Pick one comparison question from nervous versus hormonal, primary versus secondary, or specific versus non-specific, and write the answer under time pressure. Pick one evaluation question from vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy or GM organisms, and write the answer under time pressure. Check each answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. The consolidation pass is then the last chance to close the gaps before the exam, and the last chance to make sure the answer you write under time pressure is the answer that earns the marks, not just the answer you can write with unlimited time. If the three timed answers are good, the exam is ready. If they are not, the gaps are the thing to close before the exam, and the note is there to close them.

The final part of the consolidation pass is to trust the durable ideas and the tying, and not to try to cram every detail at the last minute, because the last minute is too late for detail and too early for panic, and the right use of it is to reinforce the tying. If you have the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions, you can answer most of the topic, because those are the framework that the detail fits into. If you try to cram the detail at the last minute, you are likely to blur the distinctions you already have, and the distinctions are the marks. The consolidation pass is therefore about reinforcing the tying, not about adding more detail, and the note is there to reinforce the tying by giving you the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions in one place to reach for on the day. If you can reach for them under time pressure, the note has done its job, and the topic is ready for the exam in the form the exam is actually in.
