The practice is therefore not just to write the answer once, but to write it, check the distinctions, and practise the missing distinction until it is in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the immune-response question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support.

Appendix S — Extended worked long answer on the gene technology techniques for practice under time pressure

A long answer on the gene technology techniques is the kind of question where candidates most often lose marks by knowing the name of each technique but not the principle and the purpose. The best practice for it is to write the answer technique by technique, with the principle and the purpose for each, and then to add the application and the limit if the question asks for it. A model answer starts with restriction enzymes: restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, and some cuts leave sticky ends, which are short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with another piece of DNA cut with the same enzyme, so that the two pieces can be joined by DNA ligase. The answer then says why that matters: the specificity of the cut and the matching of the sticky ends are what make cloning possible, because they let a wanted piece of DNA be inserted into a vector at a predictable place. The next technique is PCR: PCR amplifies a specific DNA sequence in vitro through repeated cycles, and the cycles are denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by a heat-stable polymerase, so that the target sequence doubles each cycle. The answer then says why that matters: PCR lets a small sample of a specific sequence be amplified enough to study or use, and it is used in diagnostics and forensics, but the result is a specific target, not a random copy of the whole genome.

The next technique is gel electrophoresis: gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size in an electric field, and DNA moves toward the positive electrode with smaller fragments moving faster, so the result is a banding pattern by size. The answer then says why that matters: the separation by size is what lets the fragments be resolved and compared, and a gene probe can then be used to detect a specific fragment by hybridisation, with the probe being a labelled complementary sequence. The next technique is the vector and transformation: a vector such as a plasmid carries foreign DNA into a host cell, and transformation is the uptake of the DNA, and a selectable marker lets you identify the transformed cells, with insertional inactivation used when the wanted DNA is inserted into a marker gene so that recombinant cells can be distinguished from non-recombinant ones. The answer then says why that matters: the vector and transformation are what put the DNA into the host, and the marker is what lets you find the cells that took it up, because not all cells do.

If you write that answer with the principle and the purpose for each technique, you hit the marks the question is after. You hit the principle for restriction enzymes, which is cutting at specific sequences and using sticky ends and ligation to join. You hit the purpose for PCR, which is amplifying a specific sequence in vitro by repeated cycles with a heat-stable polymerase. You hit the principle for electrophoresis, which is separation by size in an electric field, with DNA moving to the positive electrode and smaller fragments moving faster. You hit the purpose for the probe, which is detecting a specific fragment by hybridisation with a labelled complementary sequence. You hit the principle and purpose for the vector and transformation and the marker, which is carrying DNA into a host and selecting the cells that took it up, with insertional inactivation as one way to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant. If you can write that answer under time pressure, you are ready for the gene technology long question, because you have the kind of answer that question is built from. If you write a shorter answer that only names the techniques, you have the labels but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The practice for the gene technology question is to write the answer technique by technique and then to check that each technique has both the principle and the purpose, because the mark is usually in the principle and the purpose together, not in the name alone. Check that restriction enzymes have the specific cut and the sticky end and the ligation. Check that PCR has the specific amplification and the cycles and the heat-stable polymerase. Check that electrophoresis has the size separation and the movement to the positive electrode and the smaller-faster idea. Check that the probe has the complementary labelled sequence and the hybridisation. Check that the vector and transformation have the carrying of DNA and the selection of transformed cells and the optional insertional inactivation. If all of those are there, the answer is ready. If one is missing, the missing one is the thing to practise before the next session, because the missing one is the mark that will be lost on the day. The practice is therefore to write the answer, check the techniques one by one, and practise the missing technique until its principle and purpose are in the answer under time pressure. That is the practice that makes the gene technology question answerable, and it is the practice the note is designed to support.

Appendix T — The final consolidation pass before the exam: how to tie the topic together one more time

The final consolidation pass before the exam is the pass where you tie the topic together one more time, because by then you should know enough of the detail to need the tying rather than the learning. The tying is the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions, all in one place in your head, so that when a question appears you can reach for the right idea, the right example and the right distinction without having to reconstruct the whole topic from scratch. The way to do the tying is to say the four durable ideas one more time, each with one anchor and one distinction, and to check that you can say them under time pressure. Say the control idea with the reflex arc or the insulin-glucagon system as the anchor and the nervous-versus-hormonal distinction. Say the layered defence idea with the skin barrier and phagocytosis on one side and the antibody and memory cell response on the other, and the non-specific-versus-specific distinction. Say the timing idea with the primary and secondary response and vaccination as the anchor and the memory-cell distinction. Say the matching idea with restriction enzymes, PCR and electrophoresis as the anchors and the principle-versus-label distinction. If you can say those four durable ideas with their anchors and their distinctions under time pressure, you have the tying, and the tying is what lets you answer the topic on the day without panic.

The second part of the consolidation pass is to say the edge cases one more time, because the edge cases are the ones that separate a good answer from a very good one, and they are the ones that are easiest to blur when writing fast. Say the neuromuscular junction versus the synapse, with the sequence the same and the postsynaptic cell and outcome different. Say the rod versus the cone, with both photoreceptors but different sensitivity, colour and light level. Say the restriction enzyme versus the probe, with cutting and joining versus detecting. Say the somatic versus the germ-line therapy, with individual versus heritable. Say the herd immunity versus the individual immunity, with coverage and transmission versus the individual. Say the primary versus the secondary response, with slower versus faster and stronger because of memory. If you can say those edge cases one more time, you are ready for the questions that test them, and those are the questions that often decide the top marks. The consolidation pass is therefore not about learning new detail, but about making sure the distinctions you already know are still there and are still precise enough to be said under time pressure.

The third part of the consolidation pass is to do one last timed practice of each of the three kinds of question the topic sets: one description, one comparison and one evaluation. Pick one description question from the immune response, the gene technology techniques or the coordination receptors, and write the answer under time pressure. Pick one comparison question from nervous versus hormonal, primary versus secondary, or specific versus non-specific, and write the answer under time pressure. Pick one evaluation question from vaccination, monoclonal antibodies, DNA profiling, gene therapy or GM organisms, and write the answer under time pressure. Check each answer against the model and the appendix that covers the same ground, and note the gaps. The consolidation pass is then the last chance to close the gaps before the exam, and the last chance to make sure the answer you write under time pressure is the answer that earns the marks, not just the answer you can write with unlimited time. If the three timed answers are good, the exam is ready. If they are not, the gaps are the thing to close before the exam, and the note is there to close them.

The final part of the consolidation pass is to trust the durable ideas and the tying, and not to try to cram every detail at the last minute, because the last minute is too late for detail and too early for panic, and the right use of it is to reinforce the tying. If you have the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions, you can answer most of the topic, because those are the framework that the detail fits into. If you try to cram the detail at the last minute, you are likely to blur the distinctions you already have, and the distinctions are the marks. The consolidation pass is therefore about reinforcing the tying, not about adding more detail, and the note is there to reinforce the tying by giving you the durable ideas, the anchors and the distinctions in one place to reach for on the day. If you can reach for them under time pressure, the note has done its job, and the topic is ready for the exam in the form the exam is actually in.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).
### Check yourself
Describe the enlargement that maps a triangle with vertices (1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 3) onto one with vertices (2, 2), (4, 2), (2, 6). The scale factor is 2, and the centre must be stated: it is found by joining corresponding points, and the centre is the origin.

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Study Notes
content:
Forces and equilibrium

Moment of a force

  • The moment of a force about a point is the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force: moment = F × d⊥. Unit: N m.
  • Only the perpendicular component of the force produces a turning effect. A force that passes through the pivot has zero moment.

Principle of moments

For a body in equilibrium the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

Couples

A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action do not coincide. It produces a turning effect without a resultant force. The moment of a couple is F × d, where d is the perpendicular separation, and it is the same about every point.

Conditions for equilibrium

  • The resultant force in every direction is zero.
  • The resultant moment about any point is zero.

For three coplanar, non-parallel forces in equilibrium, the lines of action must meet at a single point.

Centre of gravity

The centre of gravity is the point through which the weight of a body appears to act. For a uniform symmetrical body it lies at the geometric centre.

Worked example: a uniform beam of weight 100 N rests horizontally on two supports at its ends. Each support carries half the weight, 50 N, because the beam is symmetrical and in equilibrium.

Exam tips: state the pivot you take moments about. Draw the perpendicular distance, not the slant distance. Show that the resultant force is zero in each direction before you use the principle of moments.

Conditions for equilibrium

A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force on it is zero and the resultant moment about any point is zero. For a body in equilibrium under three coplanar forces, the lines of action meet at a single point. The moment of a force about a pivot is Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action. Taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown reaction force, which makes this a useful method in exam questions.

Exam tip: show the resolution of forces into horizontal and vertical components before you apply the equilibrium equations.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes

Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.
### Check yourself
Trace a binary search for 9 in the sorted list 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Record the middle index at each step and state the number of comparisons. It finds 9 at the middle on the first comparison.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.

title: Chemical Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13. In a closed system a reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and reverse rates are equal. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

The equilibrium constant Kc

  • For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). Only species in solution or gas phase appear in the expression.
  • Kc is constant for a given temperature. Changing concentration or pressure shifts the position but not the value of Kc.
  • The units of Kc depend on the stoichiometry. For N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc has units of mol⁻² dm⁶.

Worked example

  • For H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI, at equilibrium [HI] = 1.60, [H2] = 0.20 and [I2] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³. Kc = 1.60² / (0.20 × 0.20) = 64.

Partial pressure and Kp

  • In gas equilibria, the partial pressure of a gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
  • Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations. For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2, Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).

Effect of changes

  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction. For an exothermic forward reaction, Kc decreases as temperature rises.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached but not the position or Kc.

Exam tip: a change in temperature is the only change that alters Kc. Concentration, pressure and catalyst changes alter the position or rate, but not the constant.

ABANDORNANDNORXOR

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

Selection and iteration in practice

Selection uses IF and CASE structures to choose between paths, and a branch runs only when its condition is true. Iteration repeats a block of code. A count-controlled loop, such as FOR, runs a known number of times. A condition-controlled loop, such as WHILE or REPEAT, runs until a condition changes. A WHILE loop may run zero times, but a REPEAT loop always runs at least once.

A well-written program uses meaningful identifiers, indents its code to show structure, and includes comments that explain why a piece of code exists. Subroutines split a large problem into smaller tasks that can be tested separately.

Exam tip: choose the loop type from whether the number of repetitions is known in advance.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Inequalities

Linear inequalities

Solve in the same way as an equation, with one rule: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.

Example: 3(2x − 1) ≥ x + 4 gives 6x − 3 ≥ x + 4, so 5x ≥ 7 and x ≥ 7/5.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve the related quadratic equation first, then sketch the parabola to see where it lies above or below the axis. Do not divide by an expression in x unless its sign is known.

Example: x² − 2x − 8 < 0 factorises to (x − 4)(x + 2) < 0. The parabola is below the x-axis between its roots, so −2 < x < 4.

Example: x² > 9 has roots ±3, and the parabola is above the axis outside them, so x < −3 or x > 3.

Regions on a graph

A strict inequality such as y > 2x + 1 is drawn with a dashed boundary line, and a non-strict one with a solid line. Test a point not on the line to decide which side to shade.

Exam technique

  • Write the answer as an inequality or as an interval, as the question requires.
  • Test one value inside the solution set to confirm the answer.

title: Alkenes — Study Notes
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 5. Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond, which makes them far more reactive than alkanes. Their addition reactions are a central part of organic synthesis.

Structure and bonding

  • A C=C double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The pi bond is an electron cloud above and below the plane of the atoms, and it is the reactive part.
  • The carbons of a C=C bond are planar, with bond angles of about 120°.

Addition reactions

  • Hydrogen adds across the double bond in the presence of a nickel catalyst to form an alkane.
  • Halogens (for example bromine water) add across the double bond: a colour change from orange to colourless is the test for an alkene.
  • Steam adds across the double bond in the presence of phosphoric acid to form an alcohol.
  • Hydrogen halides add to give halogenoalkanes; with unsymmetrical alkenes the Markovnikov rule predicts the major product.

Polymerisation

  • Addition polymers form when many alkene monomers join together. Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are examples.
  • The repeat unit is drawn with the double bond opened and the bonds extended through brackets.

Isomerism

  • Restricted rotation about the C=C bond allows E/Z isomers when each carbon carries two different groups.

Exam tip: when drawing a polymer, show the repeat unit with the bonds extending outwards, and do not leave a dangling double bond.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

Algorithm design in practice

A good algorithm is correct, efficient and easy to follow. Designers begin by breaking the problem into smaller parts, a method called decomposition. Each part is then written as a step, and the steps are tested with sample data, including data at the limits of the input range.

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm in plain structured English before it is coded in a specific language. It makes the logic clear, so it can be checked and changed without worrying about syntax. Flowcharts show the same logic with symbols for input, process, decision and output.

Exam tip: trace the algorithm step by step with a table of values to show that it produces the expected output.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Distance and midpoint

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): length AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

Gradients

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where x₂ ≠ x₁. A horizontal line has m = 0; a vertical line has no gradient.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines (neither vertical nor horizontal) satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1.

Equations of a straight line

  • Gradient–intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept.
  • Point–gradient form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
  • General form: ax + by + c = 0, with gradient −a/b.

Example: Find the line through P(2, −1) perpendicular to y = 3x − 4. The perpendicular gradient is −1/3, so y + 1 = −1/3 (x − 2). Multiply by 3: 3y + 3 = −x + 2, giving x + 3y + 1 = 0.

Intersection of two lines

Solve the two equations simultaneously, by substitution or elimination. Lines with equal gradients and no common point are parallel.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 7. Substituting gives x + 2x + 1 = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2 and y = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r².

The expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). Complete the square in x and y to convert between the forms.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 has g = −3, f = 2, c = −3. Centre (3, −2), radius √(9 + 4 + 3) = 4.

Tangents

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Find the radius gradient from the centre to the point, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Exam technique

  • Sketch the figure first, and check whether the question asks about a line, a circle or both.
  • Keep exact values (fractions and surds) until the final step unless decimals are requested.
  • Check that a line passes through a given point by substituting its coordinates.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13. ### Check yourself Find (1 + 2i)(3 − i). The answer is 5 + 5i. Check by expanding: 3 − i + 6i − 2i² = 3 + 5i + 2 = 5 + 5i.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Check yourself
A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm and a perpendicular height of 4 cm. Find its area. Use ½(a + b)h = ½ × (5 + 9) × 4 = 28 cm². State the units and show the substitution before the final value.

### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.
### Check yourself
State the nth term of a sequence from its sum. Find Sₙ, then subtract Sₙ₋₁. Do not differentiate Sₙ, because the sum is a discrete function.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.
### Check yourself
A box plot has its median closer to the lower quartile than to the upper quartile. Which way is the data skewed, and what words should the answer use? The data is positively skewed, because the longer right-hand part of the box shows the upper values are more spread out.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Coulomb's Law

F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Uniform Fields

Between parallel plates: E = V/d, constant.

Example: 2 kV across 5 mm: E = 400 kV m⁻¹. An electron feels F = eE ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N toward the positive plate.

Potential

V = W/q, scalar; E = −dV/dr. Potential energy of q at V is qV.

Capacitance

C = Q/V (farads). Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV².

Combinations: parallel adds (C = C₁ + C₂); series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite to resistors).

Example: 10 μF and 20 μF in series: 1/C = 1/10 + 1/20 → C ≈ 6.7 μF.

Charging and Discharging

Exponential: V = V₀ e^(−t/RC). Time constant RC: after one RC, V falls to 37%. Half-life t½ = 0.69 RC.

Exam tips: field points from high to low potential; in discharge problems identify which quantity (V, Q or I) decays — all share the same exponential factor.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1. Nearly every question here is the same three-step job: translate the geometry into equations, solve them, then read the answer back against the diagram.

Core results

  • Distance between (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²).
  • The midpoint is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular lines satisfy m₁m₂ = −1.

Finding the equation of a line

With a point and a gradient, use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). With two points, find the gradient first. Give the answer in the form the question requests: y = mx + c, or ax + by + c = 0 with integer coefficients when it asks for that form.

Example: find the line through (−2, 5) perpendicular to 3x − 4y = 1. The given line has gradient 3/4, so the required gradient is −4/3. Then y − 5 = −4/3(x + 2), which rearranges to 4x + 3y − 7 = 0.

Intersections of a line and a curve

Points of intersection satisfy both equations at once, so substitute one into the other. The resulting quadratic has two roots, one repeated root, or no real roots, and the discriminant tells you which. Parallel lines give no intersection, and a repeated root means the line touches the curve.

Example: y = 2x − 1 and x² + y² = 10. Substituting gives 5x² − 4x − 9 = 0, so (5x − 9)(x + 1) = 0. The points are (9/5, 13/5) and (−1, −3).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r². Expanding gives the general form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, where the centre is (−g, −f) and the radius is √(g² + f² − c). To test a point, substitute its coordinates: a value below r² means inside, equal means on the circle, above means outside.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 has centre (3, −2) and radius √(9 + 4 + 12) = 5.

Tangents and normals

A tangent touches the circle at one point and is perpendicular to the radius through that point. Find the gradient of the radius from the centre, take the negative reciprocal for the tangent, then use the point–gradient form. The normal is the radius itself, so it passes through the centre.

Example: the tangent to (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25 at (7, 1). The radius has gradient 3/4, so the tangent has gradient −4/3, and its equation is 4x + 3y − 31 = 0.

Exam technique

  • Draw a rough diagram first; it shows whether a point should be inside or outside a circle before any algebra is done.
  • With a "show that" instruction, finish with the exact expression that was asked for.
  • To check a tangent, confirm that the distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours

  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

4. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

title: Acid-base Equilibria — Study Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 14. Acids and bases are defined by proton transfer. The strength of an acid is given by its dissociation constant, and pH calculations, buffers and titrations all follow from it.

Strong and weak acids

  • A strong acid dissociates completely in water, so [H⁺] equals the acid concentration. For 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl, [H⁺] = 0.010 and pH = 2.00.
  • A weak acid dissociates only partly. For HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] / [HA].
  • pKa = −log10 Ka. A smaller pKa means a stronger acid.

pH calculations

  • pH = −log10[H⁺]. For a base, find pOH = −log10[OH⁻] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K.
  • Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶ at 298 K.
  • For a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ NaOH solution, [OH⁻] = 0.050, pOH = 1.30 and pH = 12.70.

Buffers

  • A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (for example ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate). It resists large pH changes.
  • The pH of a buffer is given by pH = pKa + log([A⁻] / [HA]). When [A⁻] = [HA], pH = pKa.
  • Adding a small amount of strong acid is absorbed by the conjugate base, so the pH changes only slightly.

Titrations and indicators

  • Strong acid with strong base: the equivalence point is pH 7.
  • Weak acid with strong base: the equivalence point is above pH 7, so phenolphthalein (pH 8.3 to 10) is suitable.
  • Strong acid with weak base: the equivalence point is below pH 7, so methyl orange (pH 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable.
  • Choose an indicator whose colour change lies within the steep vertical section of the titration curve.

Exam tip: when pH is asked for a weak acid, calculate [H⁺] from Ka and the concentration before taking the logarithm.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Check yourself
Two events are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.2. Are they independent? No. P(A and B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) = 0.06, so the events are dependent. Mutually exclusive events are always dependent when both have non-zero probability.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Basics

A wave transfers energy without net transfer of matter.

  • Transverse: oscillation ⊥ propagation (EM waves, water surface)
  • Longitudinal: oscillation ∥ propagation (sound)

The Wave Equation

v = fλ. Frequency f is set by the source; speed v by the medium.

Example: sound at 340 m s⁻¹, f = 512 Hz: λ = 340/512 ≈ 0.66 m.

Intensity

I = P/A. Intensity ∝ amplitude² — doubling the amplitude quadruples the intensity.

Doppler Effect

Observed frequency changes with relative motion: f′ = f(v ± v_o)/(v ∓ v_s). Approaching sources sound higher.

Example: an ambulance passing you: high pitch approaching, low pitch receding.

EM Spectrum

Radio → micro → IR → visible (400–700 nm) → UV → X-ray → gamma. All travel at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in vacuum.

Polarization

Only transverse waves can be polarised — proof that light is transverse. Malus' law: I = I₀ cos²θ between polariser axes.

Exam tips: distinguish wave speed (set by medium) from frequency (set by source); in Doppler problems, signs depend on approach or recession.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Check yourself
A price falls from £80 to £68. Find the percentage decrease. The decrease is £12, so the percentage is 12/80 × 100 = 15%. Show the divisor is the original price and not the new one.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For full marks on Database Systems questions, the examiner needs to see explanations of relational concepts, correct SQL syntax, and descriptions of DBMS features. The command words calculate, show that, explain, describe, justify, and state are used. For example, to justify why a relational database is used, cite reduced redundancy and flexible queries, relating to statement 9. Working and reasons must be shown for explain and justify questions.
### Traps
Common mistakes include not aliasing joined tables, incorrect use of SQL keywords, and not considering data integrity. Corrections include using aliases like s, l, f, writing SQL keywords in uppercase, and considering validation rules and access rights.
### Memory hooks
To remember the benefits of a relational database, use the mnemonic REDUCE: Reduced redundancy, Easy queries, Data integrity, Unique identifiers, Concurrent access, and Efficient storage. Another hook is to always write SQL keywords in uppercase and alias joined tables. A sanity check for SQL queries is to ensure the correct use of SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and JOIN.
### Timing
Database Systems questions typically account for 9 marks and should be budgeted around 15-20 minutes. This allows time to read the question, plan the answer, and write a clear and concise response.

### Traps

### Worked example
Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2023–2025): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

For example, a question may ask students to explain the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT loop, or to describe how to declare and use a 2D array. Working and reasons must be shown to support answers.
### Traps
Common mistakes include using the wrong loop type, such as using a WHILE loop when a REPEAT loop is needed, or vice versa. Another error is failing to declare variables before use, or using the wrong data type. Additionally, students may forget to close files after use, or use the wrong file mode.
### Memory hooks
To remember the different data types, students can use the mnemonic INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE. To recall the difference between a procedure and a function, students can think of a procedure as a recipe that performs a task, while a function is a recipe that returns a value. When working with 2D arrays, students can use the pattern of looping over rows first, then columns.
### Timing
This topic typically accounts for 20-30% of the paper, and students should budget around 30-40 minutes to answer questions on programming concepts. Students should aim to spend around 10-15 minutes on each question, depending on the mark value and complexity.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check yourself
Explain why the rate must be scaled before you use the formula. The rate is given per minute, but the interval is 2 minutes, so λ must be the rate multiplied by the interval, giving 6 and not 3.

### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table

Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).
