title: Algebra — Inequalities — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins — Study Notes
content:
Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 19. Amines, amides, amino acids and proteins contain nitrogen. The lone pair on nitrogen controls basicity, and the amide and peptide links join molecules into polymers.

Amines

  • Primary amines have one alkyl group on the nitrogen, for example ethylamine.
  • Alkyl groups push electron density onto nitrogen, so ethylamine is a stronger base than ammonia.
  • In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so it is a weaker base than ammonia.
  • Amines form salts with acids: CH₃NH₂ + HCl gives CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻.
  • Preparation: a haloalkane heated with excess ethanolic ammonia gives a primary amine. The excess ammonia limits further substitution. A nitrile reduced by LiAlH₄ gives a primary amine.

Amides

  • An acyl chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine to form an amide. Ethanoyl chloride with ammonia gives ethanamide.
  • Hydrolysis of an amide with hot dilute acid gives a carboxylic acid and an ammonium salt.

Amino acids and zwitterions

  • Amino acids contain –NH₂ and –COOH. In the solid and near neutral pH they exist as zwitterions, ⁺H₃NCH(R)COO⁻, with no net charge.
  • At the isoelectric point the zwitterion has no net charge. In strong acid it is a cation; in alkali it is an anion.
  • Amino acids can be separated by electrophoresis because their charge depends on pH.

Peptides and proteins

  • A peptide link forms when the –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of another, releasing water.
  • Proteins have primary (sequence), secondary (alpha helices and beta sheets, held by hydrogen bonds) and tertiary structures. Complete hydrolysis with hot acid gives amino acids.

Exam tip: when comparing base strength, explain the availability of the nitrogen lone pair, not just the names of the groups.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

A function maps each input in the domain to exactly one output in the range.

Composite Functions

fg(x) means f(g(x)) — apply g first, then f. Order matters.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x². Then fg(x) = 2x² + 1 but gf(x) = (2x + 1)².

Inverse Functions

f⁻¹ reverses f: f⁻¹f(x) = x. To find it, swap x and y in y = f(x) and rearrange.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2 gives f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3.

An inverse exists only if f is one-one. If not, restrict the domain (e.g. f(x) = x² for x ≥ 0 has f⁻¹(x) = √x). Graphically, y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, and the range of f becomes the domain of f⁻¹.

Transformations

NotationEffect on y = f(x)
f(x) + atranslation up by a
f(x + a)translation left by a
a f(x)vertical stretch, factor a
f(ax)horizontal stretch, factor 1/a
−f(x)reflection in the x-axis
f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

Exam tips: state the domain of any inverse; when combining transformations, translations inside the bracket act in the opposite direction to the sign.

Composite and inverse functions: exam method

fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f, so read the composite from the right. Check that the output of g lies in the domain of f before you combine them; restricted domains are a common examiner target.

To find f⁻¹(x), write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject. The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one on the domain given; restrict the domain (for example x ≥ 0 for a quadratic) when the question asks for it.

The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x, so the point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer.

Exam cue: State the domain and range of an inverse when asked, and write fg and gf separately when order matters.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For trust, the CA signature chain described earns both marks: CA binds key to identity, browsers check against roots. For bulk data, symmetric speed plus asymmetric key exchange earns the hybrid pair. For verification, re-hash and compare stated earns the integrity mark with mismatch meaning change.
### Traps
Error: encryption claimed to stop phishing. Correction: valid TLS carries fake sites too; check identity. Error: hashes claimed to prove authorship. Correction: hashes prove integrity, signatures prove authorship. Error: self-claims accepted as trust. Correction: only CA signatures establish it.

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Newton's Laws

  • A body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force.
  • F = ma — the resultant force equals mass × acceleration.
  • Forces occur in pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, on different bodies.

Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant accelerates at 5 m s⁻².

Weight and Mass

Weight W = mg — a force in newtons; mass in kg is invariant. A 70 kg person weighs about 687 N.

Momentum

p = mv (vector, kg m s⁻¹). Resultant force = rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.

Conservation: in a collision with no external forces, total momentum is unchanged.

  • Elastic: kinetic energy also conserved
  • Inelastic: some KE becomes heat/sound

Example: a 3 kg trolley at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1 kg trolley and they couple: 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m s⁻¹.

Friction and Connected Bodies

Draw free-body diagrams, then apply F = ma along each axis. For a towed car and trailer, the tow-bar tension appears as an internal pair (equal and opposite).

Exam tips: 'constant velocity' means zero resultant force, not zero friction; impulse questions want FΔt = Δp.

title: Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Key areas to revise

  • Exact Values
  • Key Identities
  • Solving Equations
  • Graphs and Transformations
  • Using Identities

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2 sin x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Rearrange to sin x = −1/2. The reference angle is 30°, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° − 30° = 330°. Both answers go in the final line, because a question that asks for "all solutions in the interval" loses marks when one is missing.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at the calculator value and missing the second solution in the interval.
  • Giving answers in degrees when the question asks for radians, or the reverse. Check the units against the question before writing the final answer.
  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a trig expression that could be zero, which loses solutions. Factorise and set each factor to zero instead.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

Exam method: Poisson probabilities

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, … The mean and the variance are both equal to λ, so the parameter is found directly from either quantity given in the question.

Use the calculator's Poisson function or the formula with the exact value of e^(−λ). When a question asks for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r), add the separate probabilities, or subtract the complement from 1.

The rate must match the interval. If events occur at 4 per hour and the question asks about a 30-minute period, the new mean is 2. Always rescale λ to the period in the question.

A Poisson model is appropriate for counts of events that occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.

Exam cue: Check the rescaling of λ first; it is the most common error in Poisson questions, and it costs the whole question.

title: Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — Study Notes
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression

Edexcel IAL Biology WBI11, Topic 2. DNA holds the code for proteins. Gene expression copies that code into mRNA and then builds the protein. Cell membranes control what enters and leaves the cell.

Cell membranes

  • The fluid mosaic model describes a phospholipid bilayer with proteins that move within it.
  • Cholesterol stabilises the membrane and reduces its fluidity at high temperature. Glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface act as cell recognition sites.
  • Channel and carrier proteins control facilitated diffusion and active transport.

DNA structure and replication

  • DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each nucleotide has a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and one base: adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine.
  • Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and cytosine pairs with guanine (three hydrogen bonds).
  • Replication is semi-conservative: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds the helix, and DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the new strand.

Protein synthesis

  • Transcription takes place in the nucleus. RNA polymerase makes a complementary mRNA copy of one gene. RNA contains uracil instead of thymine.
  • Translation takes place on ribosomes. A codon is three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid. tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon that matches the codon.
  • The genetic code is degenerate: several codons can code for the same amino acid. It is also universal and non-overlapping.

Mutations

  • A substitution changes one base. It may be silent, or it may change one amino acid.
  • A deletion or insertion of one or two bases causes a frameshift that alters every codon after the mutation.

Exam tip: when you explain a mutation, say what happens to the codon, then to the amino acid, then to the protein's shape and function.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Internal Energy

Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Specific Heat and Latent Heat

  • Heating: Q = mcΔθ (c = specific heat capacity)
  • Phase change: Q = mL (L = specific latent heat)

Example: melting 0.2 kg ice: Q = 0.2 × 334,000 ≈ 67 kJ — no temperature change during the change.

Mixtures: heat lost = heat gained.

Gas Laws

  • Boyle: pV = constant (T fixed)
  • Charles: V/T = constant (p fixed)
  • Pressure law: p/T = constant (V fixed)
  • Combined/ideal: pV = nRT, R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹

Example: 2 mol at 300 K in 0.05 m³: p = nRT/V = 2 × 8.31 × 300/0.05 ≈ 100 kPa.

Kinetic Theory

½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT — temperature measures mean translational KE. Also pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩.

Exam tips: use kelvin in every gas equation; in mixture problems, work per substance with a common final temperature.

title: Algebra — Graphs — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

title:
Appendix A — Practical microbiology and the reasoning behind aseptic technique

The microbiology part of this topic is the part where the practical details matter as well as the theory, because the practicals are where the ideas become observable and where the candidate has to think about safety, purity and interpretation. Aseptic technique is the first practical idea to be precise about, because it is the one that is worth marks both as a safety measure and as a purity measure, and because candidates often say it is “just about being clean” rather than about controlling the movement of microbes. The precise idea is that aseptic technique is the set of practices that reduce the chance of unwanted microbes contaminating the culture and reduce the chance of the cultured microbes escaping to contaminate the workspace, the room or the people. If you say only that it is about being clean, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning, because the question is usually about why the technique is needed, not just what it is called.

The practicals on culturing also matter because they are the place where the candidate has to think about what a pure culture is and why it matters. A pure culture is one where only one species or strain is present, so that the observations and results can be attributed to that organism rather than to a mixture. If you cannot say why a pure culture matters, you cannot say why aseptic technique matters, because aseptic technique is the way you aim to keep the culture pure and keep it contained at the same time. The two ideas are connected, and the question usually expects you to see that connection rather than to treat purity and safety as unrelated. If you can say that a pure culture is needed so the results can be attributed to one organism, and that containment is needed so the organism does not escape, you have the practical microbiology idea in a form that scores marks.

The disposal and sterilisation ideas are also important, because they are the end point of the practical reasoning. Equipment that has touched the culture has to be sterilised before reuse or disposal, so that the cultured microbes are destroyed and the risk of spread is reduced. Waste that has touched the culture has to be disposed of safely, so that it does not become a source of contamination or infection. A good answer says that sterilisation and safe disposal are part of the practical, and that they matter because the culture is a living population that can multiply and spread if it is not controlled. If you can say that, you have the disposal idea in a form that scores marks. If you just say “the equipment is cleaned,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is about.

Appendix B — Microbial growth, the phases and the reasons for the shape of a growth curve

The growth curve is the idea in this topic where a candidate can get the shape right but still lose marks by not saying why the shape exists. The shape exists because microbial growth depends on the environment, and the environment changes as the culture grows: resources are used up, waste builds up, space and conditions change, and those changes affect the rate of growth and eventually the rate of death. A good answer says that a culture goes through lag, exponential, stationary and decline phases, and that the phases reflect the changing conditions in the culture rather than being an arbitrary pattern. If you can say that, you have the growth-curve idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say the phases are lag, log, stationary and death without saying why, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The exponential phase is the phase where the population is increasing as fast as the conditions allow, and it is the phase that matters most for questions about growth rate, because that is where the rate is highest and where the idea of exponential increase is easiest to state. The lag phase is where the organisms are adapting to the new conditions, so the rate is low at first. The stationary phase is where growth is balanced by death, so the population is roughly stable. The decline phase is where death exceeds growth, so the population falls. A good answer can describe those without exact timings, because the point is the pattern and the reason for it. If you can describe the pattern and say why it occurs, you have the answer the examiners are after. If you only memorise the names of the phases without the reason, you are vulnerable on the “explain” questions, which are where the marks often sit.

The factors that affect growth are the other part of the growth topic, and they are the part where candidates most often forget that the organism matters. A thermophile and a mesophile have different temperature ranges; an aerobe and an anaerobe have different oxygen requirements; and different organisms have different pH and water-activity and nutrient requirements. A good answer says that growth depends on factors such as temperature, pH, water availability, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitors, and that the optimum and range depend on the organism. It does not say that all microbes have the same requirements, because they do not, and it does not say that only one factor matters at a time, because in practice several factors interact. If you can say that, you have the growth-factor idea in a form that scores marks. If you only list the factors without saying that the organism determines the range, you have the label but not the reasoning, and that is where the mark is lost.

Appendix C — Pathogens, infection and disease, and the difference between the two ideas

The difference between infection and disease is one of the ideas in this topic where a vague answer can lose marks even when it sounds reasonable. Infection means the microorganism is present and multiplying in or on the body; disease means the harm that results. A person can be infected without obvious disease, and a person can be diseased from a cause that is not an infection in the narrow sense. If you can say that, you have the distinction. If you use the two words as if they mean the same thing, you lose the precision that the mark is after. The distinction matters because it is the basis for saying that a pathogen is a microorganism that can cause disease, not that every microorganism always does, and not that infection always causes the same amount of harm in every case.

The ways a bacterium can cause disease are also worth being precise about, because a candidate who says “bacteria cause disease” without saying how is usually leaving marks on the table. Pathogenic bacteria can damage tissues directly, they can produce toxins, and they can trigger host responses that themselves cause harm. A good answer says that the damage can come from the bacterium itself, from a toxin it makes, or from the response to it, and that the same organism may do more than one of those. If you can say that, you have the pathogenesis idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “bacteria make you ill,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

Viruses are different in a way that candidates often miss when they are writing too fast. A virus is not a cell, and it cannot reproduce on its own; it has to get inside a host cell and use the host’s machinery. That is the central idea, and it is the idea that explains why the virus is not treated as a living cell in the normal sense and why the antiviral logic is different from the antibacterial logic in some cases. A good answer says that a virus has genetic material inside a protein coat, that some have an envelope, that viruses lack the machinery to reproduce independently, and that they must use a host cell. If you can say that, you have the virus idea in a form that scores marks. If you say that a virus is a very small bacterium, you have lost the distinction that the mark is after. If you say that a virus can reproduce outside a host, you have lost the central idea entirely, and that is one of the mistakes the examiners expect to see from a weak answer.

Appendix D — The first line of defence, and why non-specific matters

The first line of defence is the part where candidates often lose marks by treating non-specific defence as if it were the same kind of thing as specific immunity. It is not. The first line is the barriers and the non-specific responses: skin, mucous membranes, tears, saliva, stomach acid, inflammation and phagocytosis. These act against a broad range of pathogens rather than one particular type, which is what makes them non-specific. A good answer says that the first line includes physical and chemical barriers and non-specific responses such as inflammation and phagocytosis, and that these are non-specific because they act broadly rather than against one particular antigen. It does not say that the first line is the same as specific immunity, because it is not, and it does not say that non-specific defences are always enough, because they are not. If you can say that, you have the first-line idea in a form that scores marks.

Phagocytosis is the process in the first line that is usually worth a little structure, because that is where the mark often lives. A phagocyte engulfs the pathogen into a phagosome, the phagosome fuses with a lysosome, and the enzymes and other contents of the lysosome destroy the pathogen. A good answer says that, and also says that phagocytosis is non-specific, so it is not aimed at one particular antigen in the way the antibody response is. If you can say that, you have the phagocytosis idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “phagocytes eat pathogens,” you have the label but not the mechanism, and the mark is in the mechanism, because that is what the exam is testing when it asks about phagocytosis specifically.

Inflammation is the other non-specific response that is worth a little structure, because it is the one where candidates most often confuse the response with the infection. Inflammation is the local response to injury or infection, bringing more blood flow and more phagocytes and other defences to the area, and producing the classic signs such as redness, heat and swelling. A good answer says that inflammation is a non-specific response that helps contain and clear the problem, and that it can happen after injury as well as after infection, so it is not the same thing as the infection itself. If you can say that, you have the inflammation idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “inflammation means you are infected,” you have lost the distinction, because inflammation is the response, not the infection, and the mark is in seeing that distinction.

Appendix E — Antigens and antibodies and the structure behind the specificity

The specificity of the immune response is the idea that makes the specific defences different from the non-specific ones, and it is the idea that the antigen-antibody question is usually really about. An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or other molecule on the surface of a pathogen or on another cell, that the immune system recognises and responds to. An antibody is a protein produced in response to a specific antigen, and it binds to that antigen and helps neutralise, mark or remove the pathogen. The important point is that the response is specific, because each antibody has a binding site that fits one antigen. A good answer says that, and also says that antigens are not only on pathogens, because that is a common overstatement that loses precision. If you can say that, you have the antigen-antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The structure of the antibody is the detail that explains why the specificity exists, and that is the detail worth knowing if the question asks about it. An antibody has a constant region and variable regions that form the antigen-binding site, and the shape of the binding site is what makes it specific to one antigen. A good answer says that the constant region is the same across the antibody class and the variable regions make the binding site, and that the shape of the binding site is what gives the specificity. It does not say that the antibody is a generic killer regardless of shape, because the shape is the point. If you can describe the constant and variable regions and say why the binding site matters for specificity, you have the antibody-structure idea in a form that scores marks.

The ways antibodies help are also worth being precise about, because a candidate who says “antibodies kill pathogens” is usually leaving marks on the table. Antibodies can neutralise pathogens or toxins, they can mark them for destruction, and they can help other defences deal with them. A good answer says that antibodies help by neutralising, marking or aiding removal, rather than acting as a single universal killer. If you can say that, you have the antibody-function idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “antibodies destroy pathogens,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is about when the question asks how antibodies work.

Appendix F — B cells, T cells and the reasoning behind the two arms of the specific response

The distinction between B cells and T cells is one of the standard marks on this topic, and it is the distinction that candidates lose most often when they blur both into “immune cells.” B cells are associated with the humoral response and with antibody production; T cells are associated with the cell-mediated response and with helping and controlling the immune response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. Both are lymphocytes, but they have different roles. A good answer says that, and also says that the response is integrated, so it is not as if the two arms are unrelated. If you can say that, you have the B-cell and T-cell idea in a form that scores marks. If you blur them into one vague category, you lose the distinction that the mark is after.

Memory cells are the detail that makes the immune response more than a one-time event, and that is the detail worth knowing if the question asks about memory or about vaccination. After an immune response, memory B and T cells persist, and they allow a faster and stronger response on later exposure to the same antigen. A good answer says that memory cells are responsible for the secondary response and for the basis of vaccination, and that the secondary response is faster and stronger than the primary response. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point. If you can say that, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks.

The vaccination link is the one that often brings the memory idea and the specific response idea together, and that is the link worth making explicit. Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body is primed for real exposure. A good answer says that vaccination works by priming the immune system with the antigen without disease, producing memory cells, so the secondary response is ready if the real pathogen is met. It does not treat vaccination as a separate magic trick from the immune response, because it is part of the same system. If you can say that, you have the vaccination idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “vaccines stop you getting ill,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

Appendix G — Herd immunity, epidemiology and the population side of the topic

Herd immunity is the idea in this topic where the population view is most important, because the question is usually about the group, not just about the individual. Herd immunity happens when enough people are immune that the pathogen has difficulty spreading through the population, so that even people who are not immune are less likely to be exposed. A good answer says that herd immunity depends on coverage, not on every individual being immune, and that it reduces transmission through the population. It does not say that herd immunity makes every individual immune, because it does not, and it does not say that it works without coverage, because coverage is the point. If you can say that, you have the herd immunity idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “vaccination protects everyone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning about coverage and transmission.

Epidemiology is the other population idea in the topic, and it is the one where candidates most often lose marks by saying it is only about counting cases. Epidemiology is the study of the patterns, causes and control of disease in populations. It looks at who is affected, where, when and at what rate, and it is used to identify risk factors and causes and to inform control measures. A good answer says that, and also says that epidemiology points to associations that then need explanation, so it is not a guarantee of causation on its own. If you can say that, you have the epidemiology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “epidemiology is the study of diseases in populations” without saying what that study involves, you have the label but not the reasoning. The reasoning is what the mark is after, because the question is usually about what epidemiology does, not just what it is called.

The population side of the topic is the side where the practical and the public-health ideas meet, and that is the side worth keeping in view. The same ideas that matter in a small practical culture, purity, safety, growth and interpretation, also matter in a population, where the questions are about spread, risk and control. If you can say that the topic has both a small-scale and a large-scale side, and that the large-scale side depends on the same kinds of reasoning, you have the topic as a connected whole rather than as three unrelated lists. That is the view that the higher marks are after, because the higher marks are about the connections, not just the parts.

Appendix H — Forensic biology and the reasoning behind the evidence, not just the evidence types

Forensic biology is the part of the topic where candidates most often lose marks by listing evidence types without saying why they matter or what their limits are. The precise idea is that forensic biology uses biological evidence, especially DNA, to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people, objects or scenes, and that the evidence is interpreted rather than taken as a simple yes-no answer on its own. A good answer says that, and also says that the value of the evidence depends on how it was collected, whether it was contaminated, and whether the interpretation matches the question. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA can identify people,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning about interpretation and limits.

DNA profiling is the technique in this topic where the reasoning about the method matters as much as the result. DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples, and a match can identify a person or link a sample to a scene, while a mismatch can exclude a person. The result depends on the quality of the sample and the comparison, and on the context, so it is not a simple absolute proof in every sense without context. A good answer says that DNA profiling compares the patterns of variation in DNA, that the differences between individuals are what make it possible, and that the result is interpreted in context. It does not say that DNA profiling is proof in a magic sense, because the context and the sample quality matter. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “DNA fingerprinting identifies someone,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning about the pattern and the interpretation.

The care with biological evidence is the other idea in this topic that is worth saying explicitly, because it is the idea that connects forensics to the same reasoning as microbiology culturing. Contamination, chain of custody and context are all things that affect whether the evidence is meaningful, and a candidate who cannot say that is usually left with only the label of “biological evidence” and no reasoning about what makes it reliable or not. A good answer says that biological evidence has to be collected and preserved properly, that contamination must be avoided, that the chain of custody matters, and that the interpretation depends on the context. If you can say that, you have the forensic care idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “blood is evidence,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after when the question asks about handling or interpretation.

Appendix I — Typical mistakes, revisited with the reasoning behind them

The mistakes in this topic are worth revisiting with the reasoning behind them, because that is the way to stop making them under time pressure. The reason candidates say all bacteria are pathogens is that they are thinking of disease, not of the whole group. The fix is to remember that bacteria include harmless and useful ones as well. The reason candidates say viruses are cells is that they are thinking of “small living thing” rather than of the cell structure. The fix is to remember that viruses are particles with genetic material and a coat and no independent metabolism. The reason candidates say aseptic technique is just about tidiness is that they are thinking of neatness rather than of controlling the movement of microbes. The fix is to remember that aseptic technique is about purity and containment at the same time. The reason candidates say microbial growth is a steady increase is that they are thinking of “more and more” rather of the limits that end exponential growth. The fix is to remember the phases and the reasons for the shape.

The reason candidates say the first line of defence is always enough is that they are thinking of “the body has defences” rather of the fact that pathogens can still get through. The fix is to remember that the first line is non-specific and often insufficient, which is why the specific response exists. The reason candidates say antibodies kill pathogens in one uniform way is that they are thinking of “antibodies are the good guys” rather of the different roles antibodies play. The fix is to remember neutralisation, marking and aiding removal as different roles. The reason candidates blur B cells and T cells is that they are thinking of “lymphocytes” as one thing rather than of the different roles the two kinds play. The fix is to remember antibody production for B cells and cell-mediated roles for T cells, with memory as the shared outcome. The reason candidates say herd immunity means every individual is immune is that they are thinking of “everyone is protected” rather of the transmission logic. The fix is to remember coverage and reduced spread.

The reason candidates say DNA profiling is absolute proof without context is that they are thinking of “DNA is unique” rather of the interpretation of the sample. The fix is to remember sample quality, contamination, chain of custody and the context of the comparison. The reason candidates say the mere presence of blood is proof of guilt or innocence is that they are thinking of “blood is incriminating” rather of the meaning of the evidence. The fix is to remember that presence is not the same as a meaningful match, and that the evidence has to be interpreted. If you can remember the reasoning behind each mistake, you are less likely to make it when you are writing fast, because the reasoning gives you something to reach for instead of the vague wrong idea. That is the use of revisiting the mistakes with the reasoning behind them, and it is the use that matters on the day.

Appendix J — How the three strands of the topic connect when the question crosses them

The three strands of the topic, microbes, immunity and forensics, are connected in a way that the cross-strand questions test, and the connection is the reasoning you have to be able to move between. Microbiology gives you the pathogens and the way they grow and spread, and the practical care that matters with living cultures. Immunity gives you the defence system that fights them, from barriers and phagocytosis through antibodies and memory cells. Forensics gives you the use of biological evidence, especially DNA, to identify and link, with the care and interpretation that make the evidence meaningful. If you can move between these strands, you can answer the cross-strand questions, which are often the ones where the marks are concentrated because they test understanding rather than labels.

The cleanest cross-strand connection is the reasoning about contamination, because it appears in microbiology culturing and in forensic evidence for different but related reasons. In microbiology, contamination ruins the purity of the culture and can introduce the wrong organism. In forensics, contamination can make the evidence unreliable or misleading. In both cases, the reasoning is that the result is only as good as the way it was obtained and handled, and that the meaning depends on the context. If you can say that, you can answer the cross-strand question that asks you to compare or relate the care needed in the two cases, because you have the reasoning rather than a separate label for each.

Another cross-strand connection is the reasoning about recognition, because the same idea of recognition appears in antigens and antibodies and in DNA profiling, though in different forms. In immunity, the body recognises antigens and produces specific antibodies. In DNA profiling, the method compares patterns of variation in DNA that distinguish individuals. In both cases, the idea is that the system can tell one thing from another by recognising specific features, and that the result is meaningful only if the recognition is reliable and the comparison is relevant. If you can say that, you can answer the cross-strand question that asks you to relate the two kinds of recognition, because you have the reasoning rather than a set of unrelated labels.

The final cross-strand connection is the reasoning about memory and specificity in immunity and the reasoning about identification and variation in forensics. Both strands are about telling things apart and responding to them in a way that is specific and useful: the immune system tells one antigen from another and remembers it; the forensic method tells one individual’s DNA pattern from another’s and uses that to identify or exclude. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand view that makes the topic a connected whole, and that is the view that the higher-mark questions are after. If you only see the three strands as separate, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that span them. The note is long enough to cover the strands separately and together, and that is the use of the length: to make the connections visible as well as the parts.

Appendix A — Practical microbiology and the reasoning behind aseptic technique

The microbiology part of this topic is the part where the practical details matter as well as the theory, because the practicals are where the ideas become observable and where the candidate has to think about safety, purity and interpretation. Aseptic technique is the first practical idea to be precise about, because it is the one that is worth marks both as a safety measure and as a purity measure, and because candidates often say it is “just about being clean” rather than about controlling the movement of microbes. The precise idea is that aseptic technique is the set of practices that reduce the chance of unwanted microbes contaminating the culture and reduce the chance of the cultured microbes escaping to contaminate the workspace, the room or the people. If you say only that it is about being clean, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning, because the question is usually about why the technique is needed, not just what it is called.

The practicals on culturing also matter because they are the place where the candidate has to think about what a pure culture is and why it matters. A pure culture is one where only one species or strain is present, so that the observations and results can be attributed to that organism rather than to a mixture. If you cannot say why a pure culture matters, you cannot say why aseptic technique matters, because aseptic technique is the way you aim to keep the culture pure and keep it contained at the same time. The two ideas are connected, and the question usually expects you to see that connection rather than to treat purity and safety as unrelated. If you can say that a pure culture is needed so the results can be attributed to one organism, and that containment is needed so the organism does not escape, you have the practical microbiology idea in a form that scores marks.

The disposal and sterilisation ideas are also important, because they are the end point of the practical reasoning. Equipment that has touched the culture has to be sterilised before reuse or disposal, so that the cultured microbes are destroyed and the risk of spread is reduced. Waste that has touched the culture has to be disposed of safely, so that it does not become a source of contamination or infection. A good answer says that sterilisation and safe disposal are part of the practical, and that they matter because the culture is a living population that can multiply and spread if it is not controlled. If you can say that, you have the disposal idea in a form that scores marks. If you just say “the equipment is cleaned,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is about.

Appendix B — Microbial growth, the phases and the reasons for the shape of a growth curve

The growth curve is the idea in this topic where a candidate can get the shape right but still lose marks by not saying why the shape exists. The shape exists because microbial growth depends on the environment, and the environment changes as the culture grows: resources are used up, waste builds up, space and conditions change, and those changes affect the rate of growth and eventually the rate of death. A good answer says that a culture goes through lag, exponential, stationary and decline phases, and that the phases reflect the changing conditions in the culture rather than being an arbitrary pattern. If you can say that, you have the growth-curve idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say the phases are lag, log, stationary and death without saying why, you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

The exponential phase is the phase where the population is increasing as fast as the conditions allow, and it is the phase that matters most for questions about growth rate, because that is where the rate is highest and where the idea of exponential increase is easiest to state. The lag phase is where the organisms are adapting to the new conditions, so the rate is low at first. The stationary phase is where growth is balanced by death, so the population is roughly stable. The decline phase is where death exceeds growth, so the population falls. A good answer can describe those without exact timings, because the point is the pattern and the reason for it. If you can describe the pattern and say why it occurs, you have the answer the examiners are after. If you only memorise the names of the phases without the reason, you are vulnerable on the “explain” questions, which are where the marks often sit.

The factors that affect growth are the other part of the growth topic, and they are the part where candidates most often forget that the organism matters. A thermophile and a mesophile have different temperature ranges; an aerobe and an anaerobe have different oxygen requirements; and different organisms have different pH and water-activity and nutrient requirements. A good answer says that growth depends on factors such as temperature, pH, water availability, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitors, and that the optimum and range depend on the organism. It does not say that all microbes have the same requirements, because they do not, and it does not say that only one factor matters at a time, because in practice several factors interact. If you can say that, you have the growth-factor idea in a form that scores marks. If you only list the factors without saying that the organism determines the range, you have the label but not the reasoning, and that is where the mark is lost.

Appendix C — Pathogens, infection and disease, and the difference between the two ideas

The difference between infection and disease is one of the ideas in this topic where a vague answer can lose marks even when it sounds reasonable. Infection means the microorganism is present and multiplying in or on the body; disease means the harm that results. A person can be infected without obvious disease, and a person can be diseased from a cause that is not an infection in the narrow sense. If you can say that, you have the distinction. If you use the two words as if they mean the same thing, you lose the precision that the mark is after. The distinction matters because it is the basis for saying that a pathogen is a microorganism that can cause disease, not that every microorganism always does, and not that infection always causes the same amount of harm in every case.

The ways a bacterium can cause disease are also worth being precise about, because a candidate who says “bacteria cause disease” without saying how is usually leaving marks on the table. Pathogenic bacteria can damage tissues directly, they can produce toxins, and they can trigger host responses that themselves cause harm. A good answer says that the damage can come from the bacterium itself, from a toxin it makes, or from the response to it, and that the same organism may do more than one of those. If you can say that, you have the pathogenesis idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “bacteria make you ill,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is after.

Viruses are different in a way that candidates often miss when they are writing too fast. A virus is not a cell, and it cannot reproduce on its own; it has to get inside a host cell and use the host’s machinery. That is the central idea, and it is the idea that explains why the virus is not treated as a living cell in the normal sense and why the antiviral logic is different from the antibacterial logic in some cases. A good answer says that a virus has genetic material inside a protein coat, that some have an envelope, that viruses lack the machinery to reproduce independently, and that they must use a host cell. If you can say that, you have the virus idea in a form that scores marks. If you say that a virus is a very small bacterium, you have lost the distinction that the mark is after. If you say that a virus can reproduce outside a host, you have lost the central idea entirely, and that is one of the mistakes the examiners expect to see from a weak answer.

Appendix D — The first line of defence, and why non-specific matters

The first line of defence is the part where candidates often lose marks by treating non-specific defence as if it were the same kind of thing as specific immunity. It is not. The first line is the barriers and the non-specific responses: skin, mucous membranes, tears, saliva, stomach acid, inflammation and phagocytosis. These act against a broad range of pathogens rather than one particular type, which is what makes them non-specific. A good answer says that the first line includes physical and chemical barriers and non-specific responses such as inflammation and phagocytosis, and that these are non-specific because they act broadly rather than against one particular antigen. It does not say that the first line is the same as specific immunity, because it is not, and it does not say that non-specific defences are always enough, because they are not. If you can say that, you have the first-line idea in a form that scores marks.

Phagocytosis is the process in the first line that is usually worth a little structure, because that is where the mark often lives. A phagocyte engulfs the pathogen into a phagosome, the phagosome fuses with a lysosome, and the enzymes and other contents of the lysosome destroy the pathogen. A good answer says that, and also says that phagocytosis is non-specific, so it is not aimed at one particular antigen in the way the antibody response is. If you can say that, you have the phagocytosis idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “phagocytes eat pathogens,” you have the label but not the mechanism, and the mark is in the mechanism, because that is what the exam is testing when it asks about phagocytosis specifically.

Inflammation is the other non-specific response that is worth a little structure, because it is the one where candidates most often confuse the response with the infection. Inflammation is the local response to injury or infection, bringing more blood flow and more phagocytes and other defences to the area, and producing the classic signs such as redness, heat and swelling. A good answer says that inflammation is a non-specific response that helps contain and clear the problem, and that it can happen after injury as well as after infection, so it is not the same thing as the infection itself. If you can say that, you have the inflammation idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “inflammation means you are infected,” you have lost the distinction, because inflammation is the response, not the infection, and the mark is in seeing that distinction.

Appendix E — Antigens and antibodies and the structure behind the specificity

The specificity of the immune response is the idea that makes the specific defences different from the non-specific ones, and it is the idea that the antigen-antibody question is usually really about. An antigen is a molecule, usually a protein or other molecule on the surface of a pathogen or on another cell, that the immune system recognises and responds to. An antibody is a protein produced in response to a specific antigen, and it binds to that antigen and helps neutralise, mark or remove the pathogen. The important point is that the response is specific, because each antibody has a binding site that fits one antigen. A good answer says that, and also says that antigens are not only on pathogens, because that is a common overstatement that loses precision. If you can say that, you have the antigen-antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The structure of the antibody is the detail that explains why the specificity exists, and that is the detail worth knowing if the question asks about it. An antibody has a constant region and variable regions that form the antigen-binding site, and the shape of the binding site is what makes it specific to one antigen. A good answer says that the constant region is the same across the antibody class and the variable regions make the binding site, and that the shape of the binding site is what gives the specificity. It does not say that the antibody is a generic killer regardless of shape, because the shape is the point. If you can describe the constant and variable regions and say why the binding site matters for specificity, you have the antibody-structure idea in a form that scores marks.

The ways antibodies help are also worth being precise about, because a candidate who says “antibodies kill pathogens” is usually leaving marks on the table. Antibodies can neutralise pathogens or toxins, they can mark them for destruction, and they can help other defences deal with them. A good answer says that antibodies help by neutralising, marking or aiding removal, rather than acting as a single universal killer. If you can say that, you have the antibody-function idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “antibodies destroy pathogens,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the reasoning is what the mark is about when the question asks how antibodies work.

Appendix F — B cells, T cells and the reasoning behind the two arms of the specific response

The distinction between B cells and T cells is one of the standard marks on this topic, and it is the distinction that candidates lose most often when they blur both into “immune cells.” B cells are associated with the humoral response and with antibody production; T cells are associated with the cell-mediated response and with helping and controlling the immune response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. Both are lymphocytes, but they have different roles. A good answer says that, and also says that the response is integrated, so it is not as if the two arms are unrelated. If you can say that, you have the B-cell and T-cell idea in a form that scores marks. If you blur them into one vague category, you lose the distinction that the mark is after.

Memory cells are the detail that makes the immune response more than a one-time event, and that is the detail worth knowing if the question asks about memory or about vaccination. After an immune response, memory B and T cells persist, and they allow a faster and stronger response on later exposure to the same antigen. A good answer says that memory cells are responsible for the secondary response and for the basis of vaccination, and that the secondary response is faster and stronger than the primary response. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point. If you can say that, you have the memory idea in a form that scores marks.

The vaccination link is the one that often brings the memory idea and the specific response idea together, and that is the link worth making explicit. Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body is primed for real exposure. A good answer says that vaccination works by priming the immune system with the antigen without disease, producing memory cells, so the secondary response is ready if the real pathogen is met. It does not treat vaccination as a separate magic trick from the immune response, because it is part of the same system. If you can say that, you have the vaccination idea in a form that scores marks. If you only say “vaccines stop you getting ill,” you have the label but not the reasoning, and the mark is in the reasoning.

Both strands are about telling things apart and responding to them in a way that is specific and useful: the immune system tells one antigen from another and remembers it; the forensic method tells one individual’s DNA pattern from another’s and uses that to identify or exclude. If you can say that, you have the cross-strand view that makes the topic a connected whole, and that is the view that the higher-mark questions are after. If you only see the three strands as separate, you are likely to lose the marks on the questions that span them. The note is long enough to cover the strands separately and together, and that is the use of the length: to make the connections visible as well as the parts.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

title: Data Representation — Study Notes
content:
Data Representation

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): binary/hex, two's complement, BCD, text/image/sound encoding, file sizes, compression.

1. Number systems

  • Binary place values 128…1; hex digits 0–9, A–F; one hex digit = one nibble (4 bits).
  • Conversions: binary ↔ decimal ↔ hex. 0101 1010 → 5A; FF = 255.
  • BCD: 4 bits per decimal digit — 0029 → 0000 0000 0010 1001. Used in clocks/calculators; easier digit conversions, more bits than pure binary.

2. Two's complement (signed)

MSB is negative: −128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. −5 = 1111 1011. Range 8-bit: −128…+127.

Negating: invert bits, add 1. Subtraction: add the negated number — 7 − 5 = 7 + (−5) = 0000 0111 + 1111 1011 = 0000 0010.

3. Text

ASCII 7-bit (128 chars) → extended sets; Unicode for all scripts (UTF-8 variable width). Character sets map codes to glyphs; uppercase/lowercase codes differ by one bit.

4. Images and sound

  • Bitmap: pixels; colour depth = bits per pixel. File size (bits) = W × H × depth. Metadata (width, height, depth) stores dimensions.
  • Sound: sample rate (Hz), resolution (bits per sample), track duration × channels. Higher rate/depth = better fidelity, larger files.

5. Compression

  • Lossless (RLE, ZIP): exact restore — text/code must use it. RLE example: AAABBBCC → 3A3B2C; effective with runs.
  • Lossy (JPEG, MP3): discards perceptually minor data — photos/music OK, text never.

Exam tips: show full working in conversions; for size questions write the formula first with units; state the reason a compression type suits the file.

Binary addition and overflow

Binary addition follows the same carry rule as denary, except that 1 + 1 = 10 (0 carry 1). For example, 0110 + 0111 = 1101. A register or storage location has a fixed number of bits, so a result that needs more bits than are available overflows and gives a wrong answer. Programmers and examiners look for an overflow error when the carry out of the leftmost bit is set.

Exam tip: state the number of bits used. Overflow depends on that width, not on the value of the numbers alone.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:

title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

Discriminant and inequalities: exam method

For ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b² − 4ac. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Use this without solving the equation when the question asks about the nature of the roots.

To find the values of k for which a quadratic has no real roots, require b² − 4ac < 0 and solve the resulting inequality in k.

To solve a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the U-shaped (a > 0) or inverted-U (a < 0) curve, and read off the region above or below the axis. For x² − 5x + 6 < 0 the roots are 2 and 3, and the solution is 2 < x < 3.

Exam cue: Completing the square gives the turning point (p, q) and shows the minimum or maximum value directly.

title: Entropy and Energetics — Study Notes
content:
Entropy and Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12. Enthalpy alone does not decide whether a reaction happens. Entropy measures how energy and matter are spread out, and the Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict feasibility.

Entropy

  • Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be dispersed. Its standard unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  • Entropy increases when a solid melts or dissolves, when a liquid evaporates, and when the number of gas molecules increases.
  • Entropy decreases when gas molecules condense or when a crystal forms from solution.
  • Standard entropy values are given in data books. The entropy change for a reaction is ΔS = Σ S(products) − Σ S(reactants).

Gibbs free energy

  • The Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is in kelvin. ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ and ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating.
  • A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative. When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

Total entropy change

  • The total entropy change is ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings. For the surroundings, ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

Temperature and feasibility

  • For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG becomes negative above the temperature T = ΔH / ΔS. High temperature therefore makes the reaction feasible.
  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

Worked example

  • For CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K, so the decomposition becomes feasible above about 1100 K.

Exam tip: always convert kJ to J before subtracting TΔS, and state the temperature in kelvin.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

Congruent triangles

Two triangles are congruent when they match on one of four conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA or AAS (two angles and a side), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and a side) for right-angled triangles. SSA is not a condition. Name the congruence test in every proof.

Similar shapes and scale factors

Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. The linear scale factor k multiplies lengths, k² multiplies areas and k³ multiplies volumes. To find a missing side, set up the ratio of corresponding sides and cross-multiply.

Transformations in geometry questions

A translation is described by a column vector, a rotation by its centre, angle and direction, a reflection by its mirror line and an enlargement by its centre and scale factor. Image points are checked by measuring the same distance from the centre or the mirror line.

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.
### Check yourself
For the same pdf, state why P(X = 1) is zero before you calculate anything. A single point has zero width, so its area is zero.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2023–2025): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.
